articles.title: Diplomatic visits attempt to hold off all-out US-Iran war
articles.body:
Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi emphasised that Iran and Russia have the "closest strategic relationship in history" following talks with his Russian counterpart Sergey Lavrov in Tehran. Meanwhile, US President Donald Trump said the United States continues to hit Iran hard "economically and militarily" and praised Russian President Vladimir Putin for "laying off Iran"
The war in Yemen intensifies, as the Houthis stuck government forces in a training camp, killing over 50 and wounding more than 200
Israeli attacks continue on Gaza, occupied West Bank, south Lebanon and southern Syria
And so we continue our live coverage of the day...
Iran says Iraq will expel exiled Kurdish opposition members
Iran's ambassador to Iraq said on Tuesday that Baghdad had agreed to "expel" or hand over members of Iranian Kurdish opposition groups who have taken refuge on the Iraqi side of the border.
The announcement came after senior Iraqi security officials repeatedly told AFP that Baghdad was refusing to do so, fearing for the lives of the Kurdish exiles.
Iraq's autonomous Kurdistan region, an oil-rich area in the north of the country, has long hosted camps and bases for Iranian Kurdish rebel groups, which Tehran labels terrorists who serve US or Israeli interests.
"During a meeting of the joint security commission—attended by the Iranian delegation and the Iraqi National Security Adviser—the two parties agreed to expel the members of the Iranian separatist terrorist groups from the Iraqi Kurdistan region or hand them over to Iran," ambassador Mohammad Kazem Al-Sadegh wrote on X.
The hijab row, Israel, and cracks in Azerbaijan-Turkey ties
"The European Parliament consists of these Islamophobes, and this must always remain in focus," Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev said on 15 September, accusing the West of waging an "undeclared war" against Islam.
Yet just days later, the Azerbaijani government stepped up its enforcement of restrictions on Islamic headscarves in schools, triggering social media campaigns and protests both inside the country and abroad.
This is not the first time Azerbaijan has attempted to ban the hijab in schools. WikiLeaks cables revealed that, as early as 2007, Ramiz Mehdiyev, then head of the Presidential Administration, had expressed concern over the growing number of women wearing headscarves.
The United Nations insisted Tuesday that aid must immediately be allowed to enter Yemen's third-biggest city Taiz, besieged by pro-Iran Houthi fighters blocking all supplies.
"Humanitarian aid must be immediately allowed to enter the city and its passage must be facilitated," UN rights chief Volker Turk said in a statement, warning that civilians were being placed "at grave risk".
Turkey submits Mecca pact to parliament for ratification
Turkey has submitted a defence pact with Pakistan and Saudi Arabia to parliament for ratification, three parliamentary sources said on Tuesday, moving NATO's second-largest army closer to a formal mutual defence pledge with Riyadh as it faces Houthi attacks.
The three countries signed the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement in August, under which an armed attack on one member is considered an attack on all. A joint statement issued when they signed the deal did not specify what each country had committed to.
At an emergency meeting of the alliance in Riyadh earlier this month, they agreed to ensure the "rapid deployment" of military forces and capabilities in Saudi Arabia.
Turkey, which has a robust defence industry, has condemned Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, expressed willingness to help meet Riyadh's military technology needs and agreed to join a Saudi-led coalition to ensure navigational safety in the Red Sea.
Parliamentary ratification is required for Turkey to formally approve the agreement.
Macron gets 200,000 tonnes extra diesel per month from Gulf
French President Emmanuel Macron has secured the delivery of an additional 200,000 tonnes of diesel per month from the United Arab Emirates and Bahrain during a tour of the Gulf, the French presidency said Tuesday.
He obtained commitments for around 100,000 tonnes per month from the Emirates, while an additional 100,000 tonnes monthly will be secured during a stop in Bahrain later in the day, the Elysee Palace said.
With the addition of deliveries from Saudi Arabia, France has commitments for 295,000 tonnes per month, representing just over 10 percent of its consumption, the presidency added.
Macron is undertaking a tour of key energy suppliers in the Gulf in an effort to secure oil and diesel supplies and bring down prices in France, after a weekend of violent protests sparked by soaring living costs.
He is visiting the UAE, Bahrain and Qatar, all of which have been thrown into turmoil since February by the US-Iran war.
Israeli strikes and gunfire killed at least four Palestinians, including a married couple and a 17-year-old, in separate incidents in the Gaza Strip on Tuesday, health officials said.
Medics said an Israeli airstrike killed Akram Yassin and his wife Dina Abu Baker in an apartment in Gaza City.
The Israeli military said it struck a militant in the area, without giving further details.
In Khan Younis, in the south, medics said a 17-year-old boy was killed by Israeli gunfire near the Qizan Al-Najar neighbourhood, while another was killed by Israeli gunfire in the Zeitoun suburb east of Gaza City, taking Tuesday's death toll to at least four.
UK to fly RAF missions defending Saudi against Houthis
Britain will deploy Royal Air Force fighter jets on defensive missions to help protect Saudi Arabia from escalating Houthi attacks, Bloomberg reported on Tuesday, citing British officials familiar with the matter.
RAF Typhoon fighter jets will help defend Saudi cities and infrastructure against aerial attacks by the Iran-backed group, while Britain will also provide an Atlas A400M transport aircraft and military advisers, the report said.
Britain's Ministry of Defence did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Iran prolongs talks in stalemate to influence US midterms
Iran has deliberately prolonged talks with the US to try to weaken Donald Trump politically ahead of November's US midterm elections, senior officials say, while fears of renewed military action and deep distrust of Washington have reinforced Tehran's reluctance to strike a quick deal to end the war.
Three senior Iranian officials and an Iranian insider, speaking on condition of anonymity, said Tehran was convinced the US president was ready to resort to renewed attacks to try to break the stalemate in the eight-month-old war.
"Iran is preparing for renewed Israeli and US attacks, not for a deal with America to end the war," one of the officials said. "The clerical establishment is determined not to give Trump a political victory."
The United Nations reported on Tuesday that the estimated number of displaced people has become more than 250,000 inside Yemen since the resumption of hostilities.
Death toll rises to 60 in Houthi strike on Yemen army camp
The death toll from a Houthi missile strike on a government military camp in southern Yemen rose to 60 people, primarily new recruits, making it the deadliest strike since fighting in the country erupted three months ago, Yemeni officials said Tuesday.
At least a dozen people were still missing a day after the Iranian-backed rebels hit the al-Alam training camp in the southern province of Shabwa with ballistic missiles, three officials said.
Monday's strike was part of a recent surge of fighting in Yemen, which started when forces from the internationally-recognized government and Saudi-led coalition launched airstrikes on Houthi-held Sanaa International Airport in July, shattering a 2022 ceasefire deal that largely stopped fighting in the country's civil war.
IRGC says two tankers hit mines, set ablaze south of Hormuz
Two tankers were set ablaze and brought to a halt south of the Strait of Hormuz after hitting Iranian mines, the Revolutionary Guards' Navy said in a statement shared by state media on Tuesday, without saying when the tankers were hit.
The statement also said a US drone was downed by Iran on Monday night.
Strait of Hormuz. [Getty]
Saudi says intercepted Houthi missile targeting Riyadh
Saudi forces on Tuesday intercepted a ballistic missile aimed at the kingdom's capital, said a spokesman for the Riyadh-led coalition backing Yemen's government, after authorities issued a danger warning and AFP journalists reported hearing blasts.
The kingdom "intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched by the terrorist Houthi militia towards Riyadh", Turki Al-Malki said in a post on X.
The Saudi capital on Tuesday was shaken by two blasts, according to AFP journalists, after authorities issued an alert warning of potential danger.
"A warning has been issued by the National Early Warning Platform in Riyadh City to alert for a potential danger," the Saudi civil defence said in a statement on X.
Iran shot down an American drone over the Strait of Hormuz at dawn today, according to Tasnim.
A statement by Iran's Revolutionary Guard stated that the fifty-fourth US Army MQ9 drone was intercepted and destroyed in the airspace of the Strait of Hormuz, by modern advanced air defense system of the Revolutionary Guard’s air-space force, and under the guidance of the country’s integrated air defense network.
Palestinians in the war-torn coastal enclave who have lost family members and homes view Trump's endorsement as a clear sign that their suffering will continue without meaningful US pressure on Israel to change course.
Across the occupied West Bank, the olive harvest, one of Palestine’s most cherished cultural traditions, is underway.
But every year, Israeli settlers have a tradition of their own: attacking farmers and disrupting the harvest in whatever ways they can.
Olive farming supports the livelihoods of roughly 100,000 Palestinian families.
But the economic toll of Israeli settler attacks and military operations has been devastating, with tens of millions in damages caused to the industry last year.
And this year, settler attacks across the West Bank are occurring at the highest rate ever recorded by the UN.
Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis said on Monday they carried out several attacks against Saudi energy, airport and military targets, including an Aramco site in Yanbu, the Shaybah oilfield, King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh and Abha airport.
There was no immediate Saudi confirmation and Reuters could not immediately verify the claims.
Pakistan army chief Asim Munir to visit Tehran today
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Tuesday that Russia and Iran have "never" worked so closely, as Moscow seeks to play a mediating role in the Middle East war.
Araghchi hosted his Russian counterpart Sergey Lavrov in Iran on Monday, in his first visit since the outbreak of the conflict.
"We covered everything from Europe to West Asia, including Lebanon, Palestine, Ukraine and Yemen. Also focused on expansion of economic and nuclear cooperation," Araghchi wrote on X.
"Never in our history have Iran and Russia worked as closely as now."
Lavrov said ahead of the visit that Moscow's efforts "aimed at preventing the return of a large-scale war", with talks stalled between the United States and Iran.
His visit came after Russian President Vladimir Putin told his Iranian counterpart Masoud Pezeshkian this month that Moscow was prepared to contribute to mediation efforts.

articles.title: Social Democrat warns foreign labor risks creating master-servant society
articles.body:
Social Democratic finance spokesperson Kaare Dybvad Bek has warned that Denmark risks developing a society divided between those providing low-paid services and those becoming dependent on them.
“What do we become as human beings if we slowly let low-paid Africans and Asians do everything that is not immediately manageable?” Dybvad Bek said Monday during a budget debate in the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament.
He questioned whether Danes lose practical skills and the ability to learn when they rely on foreign workers, delivery services such as Wolt and artificial intelligence for routine tasks.
Dybvad Bek referred to German philosopher Georg Hegel’s theory that a master becomes increasingly helpless as a servant performs more of the work.
He said individual consumers were not responsible for the development.
“It is up to us politicians to stop the flow of underpaid labor that forms the basis for these services,” he said.
Dybvad Bek argued that goods and services should be priced at a level that allows workers to earn a living wage.
He also warned that Denmark could create new parallel societies if foreign workers remain socially separated from the people they serve.
The comments came as Dybvad Bek presented a government proposal requiring employers to finance Danish lessons for workers from countries outside the European Union before they arrive.
He said companies should help pay for the integration of workers from whom they profit.

Lego named Denmark’s most valuable brand at 114 billion DKK
Lego has Denmark’s most valuable brand, with an estimated value of 114 billion DKK, according to a report by British consultancy Brand Finance.
The Danish toy company’s brand value increased by 54 percent from the previous year, business newspaper Børsen reported.
Nordea placed second with a brand value of 46.2 billion DKK, while shipping company Maersk ranked third.
“Lego is an exceptional brand, regardless of how you measure it,” Brand Finance Chief Operating Officer Mike Rocha told Børsen.
Brand Finance calculates how much a company would hypothetically have to pay to license its brand if it did not own it.
The consultancy said Lego’s financial performance contributed to the increase in value.
Lego recorded revenue of 83.5 billion DKK in 2025, an increase of 12 percent from the previous year and the highest annual total in the company’s history.
Growth accelerated during the first half of 2026, when Lego’s revenue rose by 21 percent compared with the same period in 2025.
Lego declined to comment to Børsen on the Brand Finance report.
MobilePay launches digital proof of age for use in Danish stores
MobilePay’s nearly 4.8 million Danish users will be able to document their age through the payment app when shopping in physical stores.
The feature will appear under the app’s “Wallet” menu in an update being gradually released from Tuesday, Vipps MobilePay said.
Users can add a passport-style photograph to the digital proof, which displays only their name, photo and age category.
Vipps MobilePay product manager Dennis Kvade said the need to confirm age and identity was increasing both online and in physical stores.
“It is not particularly practical to bring your passport on a night out,” he said, adding that existing age checks can also be vulnerable to fraud.
Supermarket chain Rema 1000 will accept MobilePay’s proof of age. Its employees will receive information about the feature.
However, the MobilePay document is not an official identification card and cannot replace a passport, health insurance card or driving licence.
It is intended for situations in stores and nightlife venues where young people must show they are old enough to purchase restricted products such as alcohol.
Individual businesses can decide whether to accept it, meaning users cannot assume it will be recognized everywhere.
Denmark’s Agency for Digital Government launched AltID earlier in 2026 as the country’s first official digital proof of age and identification app for both online and in-person use.
Pensioners occupy Aarhus rehabilitation center to protest closure
Between 10 and 12 pensioners occupied Rehabiliteringshøjskolen in Risskov on Tuesday and locked staff outside to protest its planned closure.
The demonstration began after the Aarhus City Council decided to close the residential rehabilitation center at the end of 2026, TV2 Østjylland reported.
“The folk high school cannot raise the dead, but it can keep them alive,” read one sign displayed in a window.
The center provides residential stays lasting two to five weeks, during which people receive support and guidance from a healthcare team.
Protester Torben Blom said the program had been crucial after both his legs were amputated.
“It has meant that I have become a human being again,” he said.
The center opened in 2018 but will close because Denmark’s healthcare reform requires Aarhus Municipality to transfer certain responsibilities and buildings to the regional authority.
Health and Care Alderman Metin Lindved Aydin of the Social Liberal Party said the municipality could not afford to build a similar facility during the next four years.
He said the reform required the municipality to save 185 million DKK.
Aydin said other rehabilitation services would remain available but acknowledged that they would differ from the existing program.
He described the occupation as a new form of senior activism and called it “refreshing” and “brave,” while saying he could not encourage illegal occupations.
Aydin said he would not call the police.
Danish home sales fall 12 percent as higher rates slow market
Denmark’s housing market is showing signs of slowing after a strong start to 2026, according to transaction figures from property portal Boligsiden.
A total of 7,709 homes were sold in September, 12 percent fewer than in the same month last year.
Housing transactions during the first nine months of 2026 were three percent below the corresponding period in 2025.
Apartment sales have fallen most sharply. Eight percent fewer apartments have been sold nationwide this year, while Copenhagen has recorded a decline of 23 percent.
Brian Friis Helmer, personal finance economist at AL Sydbank, said rising mortgage rates could partly explain the slowdown.
Fixed-rate mortgages have recently fluctuated between four and five percent, compared with 3.5 percent at the beginning of the year.
Higher prices for gasoline, natural gas and electricity are also reducing the money households have available, he said.
However, strong employment and rising inflation-adjusted incomes continue to support the housing market.
Sales of houses and terraced homes are also below last year’s level. Holiday home sales, by contrast, have increased by 4.5 percent.
Boligsiden communications director Birgit Daetz said the increase indicates that many households remain financially secure because holiday homes are traditionally purchased during periods of economic strength.
Rising property values and the possibility of rental income may also make such purchases more affordable, she said.
Copenhagen mayor disputes Frederiksen’s claims about meat in nursing homes
Copenhagen Lord Mayor Sisse Marie Welling of the Socialist People’s Party has accused Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen of presenting an inaccurate picture of food policies in the city’s nursing homes.
Frederiksen wrote on Instagram that a Copenhagen proposal could prevent nursing home residents from receiving the meat they want.
“It is a lack of respect for the elderly person’s right to make decisions for themselves,” Frederiksen wrote. “Those people in nursing homes who have toiled and slaved for our country must of course be allowed to eat meat.”
Welling rejected the claim.
“The elderly must naturally have the food they know and like. For many of them, that involves meat,” she wrote.
Welling said individual nursing homes can decide how to plan menus and how much meat to serve. She said residents’ nutritional needs should take priority over climate concerns.
The dispute follows debate over Copenhagen’s food and meal strategy, which aims to make municipal meals more sustainable and reduce purchases of beef.
A consultancy analysis reported that some nursing homes had rejected residents’ birthday requests for beef because of carbon reduction targets.
The study surveyed 200 nursing home residents and 607 people receiving meals at home.
Between 58 and 60 percent were satisfied with the food, while 8 to 13 percent reported little or no satisfaction.
Several nursing home residents criticized meat quality and said beef rarely appeared on menus. The analysis also found that residents wanted greater influence over their meals.
More than half of surveyed Danish teachers feel stressed every week
More than half of teachers in a new union survey said they experience stress daily or weekly, with most attributing it to their working conditions.
The survey by Danmarks Lærerforening, the Danish Union of Teachers, included responses from 1,901 public school teachers and kindergarten class leaders.
Sixteen percent said they felt stressed at work every day, while 36 percent experienced stress weekly and 23 percent monthly.
Nine in 10 of those experiencing stress said workplace conditions were responsible.
“We are facing a working environment problem in the public schools, while at the same time many teachers choose to leave,” union chair Gordon Ørskov Madsen said.
More than one in three respondents said they had taken sick leave from teaching because of stress.
Teachers identified classroom disruption, insufficient preparation time, heavy workloads and difficulty obtaining help for pupils with special needs as major pressures.
Some also reported that parents expected them to resolve conflicts between pupils that occurred outside school.
Nana Vaaben, an associate professor at University College Copenhagen, said teachers can experience moral stress when they know pupils need help but lack the authority to provide it.
Respondents identified fewer teaching hours, more preparation time and better support for pupils with special needs as the measures most likely to reduce stress.
The union plans to raise those proposals in upcoming negotiations with the government and other labor market parties.
Denmark and Vietnam to establish strategic partnership
Denmark and Vietnam will establish a strategic partnership during Vietnamese President Tô Lâm’s state visit to Denmark this week.
Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen of the Social Democrats and Lâm are expected to formally enter into the agreement Tuesday, the Prime Minister’s Office said.
The partnership will build on a 2023 agreement covering areas including climate policy, green growth and the transition to cleaner energy.
The Prime Minister’s Office did not provide further details about the new agreement.
“I am pleased that we, here on the 55th anniversary of Denmark’s diplomatic relations with Vietnam, are now further strengthening Danish-Vietnamese cooperation,” Frederiksen said.
“In an unpredictable world, we need strong partnerships. Both for Denmark and for the EU,” she added.
The agreement is being announced during a state visit by Lâm and his spouse, Ngô Phương Ly.
Independent authority to investigate police strikes against photographers
The Independent Police Complaints Authority will investigate reports that police officers struck two press photographers with batons during demonstrations in Copenhagen on Saturday.
The photographers worked for Danish newspapers Politiken and Ekstra Bladet and were involved in separate incidents during demonstrations for and against remigration.
Copenhagen Police referred the cases to the independent authority, known as DUP, following criticism from both newspapers.
“The Copenhagen Police in no way wish to place obstacles in the way of the press carrying out their work,” police said.
Politiken reported that its photographer was struck several times, had his camera smashed and received treatment at an emergency room.
Ekstra Bladet’s photographer said he was struck on the arm with a baton despite carrying cameras and visible press credentials.
Politiken editor-in-chief Christian Jensen described the incident as a serious attack on press freedom.
“The police make the press their adversary by preventing us from doing our job, which is also about witnessing the police’s exercise of their power,” he wrote.
Ekstra Bladet editor-in-chief Knud Brix also called the reported incident “completely unacceptable.”
The Danish Union of Press Photographers and the Danish Union of Journalists have requested a meeting with the national police commissioner.
They want police leadership to explain how similar incidents will be prevented and how journalists will be protected while covering demonstrations.
Delayed UN climate reports could weaken action before COP33, Danish expert warns
Global climate efforts could face serious setbacks if the UN climate panel does not publish its next assessment reports before the COP33 summit in 2028, a Danish climate expert has warned.
“Without the reports, countries will stand on a basis that is less comprehensive. They will lack crucial knowledge,” said Adrian Lema, head of the National Centre for Climate Research at the Danish Meteorological Institute.
He said countries could spend time debating scientific facts instead of agreeing on action.
“The consequence may be that we set climate action back years, and that uncertainty is created about some of the progress we have achieved,” Lema said.
COP33 will include the next major review of countries’ progress under the 2015 Paris Agreement.
A weeklong meeting of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, known as the IPCC, ended Friday without agreement on a budget or timetable for the reports.
Lema attended as Denmark’s lead negotiator and wanted the reports published well before COP33.
Saudi Arabia, Russia, Iran, India and China argued that publication before the summit was unnecessary, he said.
IPCC decisions require consensus rather than majority votes.
Lema said an agreement remained possible but had become more difficult.
“If we can get enough countries to say it loud and clear, then the few who disagree will be under a different pressure,” he said.
Copenhagen begins separate collection of used diapers for recycling
The City of Copenhagen began installing separate waste bins for used diapers in residential courtyards and municipal day-care centers Monday.
Diapers previously had to be placed with residual waste and were incinerated. They will now be processed at Denmark’s first diaper treatment facility.
“There is a major climate benefit in recycling the diapers instead of incinerating them,” Climate, Environment and Technology Mayor Line Barfod of the Red-Green Alliance said.
The city estimates that between 85 and 94 percent of diaper waste, including liquids and feces, can be converted into new materials.
Cellulose and the contents of the diapers will become biofiber used to produce biogas, electricity and district heating.
Plastic components can be recycled into products such as car interiors. Superabsorbent polymers can become binding material for the construction industry.
Collection will expand to municipal nursing homes, senior housing and other city institutions in February 2027.
Residents of detached houses and members of allotment garden associations will also be able to join the program next year. The scheme is expected to be fully implemented in 2029.
The bins will accept diapers for children and adults, incontinence pads, paper-based cloths and wet wipes without plastic or bamboo. Menstrual hygiene products are excluded.
Diaper waste must be placed in an ordinary plastic trash bag sealed with a tight knot.
Study finds misogynistic TikTok content can appear within minutes
Young male TikTok users can encounter misogynistic content within minutes, even when they do not actively search for it, according to a Danish study.
Researchers from the Center for Digital Pedagogy and Analyse & Tal created eight fictional profiles representing men ages 16 to 19 interested in fitness, dating, investing and gaming.
After the profiles interacted with videos about those subjects, researchers allowed them to scroll automatically for one hour.
Content associated with the “manosphere” appeared after an average of three minutes. In one case, it appeared after 21 seconds.
The manosphere refers to online communities and content that degrade women or support restricting their rights and opportunities.
Researchers also examined one year of viewing data provided by 29 men ages 15 to 22. They identified an average of five to six manosphere videos in each participant’s weekly feed.
The researchers said this was a minimum estimate but emphasized that the 29 participants were not representative of all young men.
Employment and Equality Minister Ane Halsboe-Jørgensen of the Social Democrats called for stronger social media regulation and more discussion in schools and homes.
TikTok said it takes the findings seriously.
“We proactively remove 98.1 percent of the videos that violate our rules on hate and hateful behavior,” Nordic communications director Lukasz Lindell said.
TikTok said it was also working to diversify recommendations and interrupt repetitive content patterns.
Government wants employers to fund Danish lessons for foreign workers
The Danish government wants employers to pay for Danish lessons for workers from countries outside the European Union before they arrive in Denmark.
Social Democratic finance spokesperson Kaare Dybvad Bek announced the proposal Monday during the Folketing’s debate on the government’s 2027 budget bill.
“It provides a saving of 100 million DKK, but first and foremost it sends a clear signal that people who come to the country to work must speak Danish,” he said.
Dybvad Bek said the issue concerned Denmark’s understanding of itself as a society.
More foreign workers have entered the restaurant and service industries in recent years, particularly in Copenhagen. This has led to more customers being served in English rather than Danish, he said.
During the debate, Dybvad Bek also argued that Danes risk losing practical skills when they rely on food delivery services such as Wolt and artificial intelligence for manageable tasks.
He also referred to planned restrictions affecting what he called “underpaid African agricultural workers.”
Dybvad Bek further criticized Nepalese and Iranian nationals who, he said, use Denmark’s education system to enter the labor market while avoiding other requirements.
Regional trains suspended between Odense and Fredericia after cable damage
Regional train services between Odense and Fredericia have been suspended until at least 2 p.m. Monday because of a severed cable.
DSB, Denmark’s national rail operator, has ordered rail replacement buses and updated its journey planner.
InterCity and express trains continue to operate on the route, although passengers may experience longer travel times.
“In Odense and Fredericia, there are staff in orange vests who can assist with guidance,” DSB said.
Banedanmark, the state agency responsible for Denmark’s railway infrastructure, is working to repair the damaged cable.
Train services on the route were expected to return to full capacity Monday after several days of disruptions. The cable damage means that this is no longer possible.
Passengers have experienced longer journeys and fewer trains between the two cities since a fire damaged a relay hut near Aarup in western Funen on October 9.
The hut contained electronic equipment used by the railway’s signaling system. The fire caused signal failures between Middelfart and Odense, disrupting services on Funen and across Denmark.
Even after more trains return, services will continue at reduced speeds near Aarup Station, where trains will temporarily be unable to stop.
Sunny Monday to give way to rainy and windy week in Denmark
Denmark can expect sunshine Monday before rain and stronger winds arrive during the rest of the week.
“On Monday, we have a beautiful autumn day in store,” Danish Meteorological Institute meteorologist Marie Timm said. “There will be some high-altitude clouds in the sky, but otherwise it is a beautiful day where there will be sun for everyone.”
After overnight temperatures fell close to freezing in some areas, daytime temperatures will rise to between 9 and 13 degrees Celsius.
Winds will generally be light to moderate, although coastal areas could experience fresher conditions.
Tuesday will begin dry with some sunshine before clouds and rain move across Denmark from the southeast.
The islands will receive rain during the morning and early afternoon, while northern Jutland will be affected later.
Timm said the amount of rain and strength of the wind remained uncertain because forecasts continued to change.
Another weather front will bring rain from the west Wednesday, with only brief dry periods expected.
Widespread rain is also forecast Thursday, followed by stronger southerly winds and further rain Friday.
Daytime temperatures from Tuesday through Friday will range from 8 to 13 degrees, while nighttime temperatures will remain between 5 and 10 degrees.
Timm advised people to bring rainwear rather than umbrellas because of the expected wind.
One in three Danish teachers reports verbal abuse from pupils
One in three Danish public school teachers experienced rude or abusive language from pupils during the previous week, according to a new survey.
Four in 10 teachers said such incidents occurred daily or several times a week, education trade publication Folkeskolen reported.
The survey was completed by 1,901 teachers and kindergarten class leaders between August 26 and September 14, 2026.
Teachers reported comments including “You fucking bad teacher,” “You are a damn idiot” and “You don’t boss me around.”
Lars Peter Sønderbo Andersen, a senior researcher in occupational and environmental medicine at Regional Hospital Gødstrup, said the language damages teachers’ working environment and undermines their authority in classrooms.
He said the problem has worsened in recent years.
In a similar survey conducted almost 10 years ago, one in four teachers reported being called derogatory terms such as “bitch,” “idiot” or “whore” at least once a month.
Danmarks Lærerforening, the Danish Union of Teachers, described the new findings as concerning.
“Some of these statements are quite severe, and we can hear from the inquiries we receive that it affects the teachers when they are spoken to like that,” union representative Thomas Andreasen said.
He called for schools to establish clear, shared rules for acceptable language. He also said having more permanent teachers in classrooms could help.
Denmark contacts more than 25 countries seeking prison spaces
Denmark has contacted more than 25 European countries about potentially renting prison spaces as its correctional system faces record overcrowding.
“The Danish Prison and Probation Service is in a serious situation,” Justice Minister Nicolai Wammen of the Social Democrats said. “We must do everything we can to resolve the capacity challenges in Danish prisons.”
Denmark already has an agreement to rent 300 prison spaces in Kosovo for foreign nationals sentenced to deportation. However, delays mean the renovated prison is not expected to begin accepting inmates until late 2027 or early 2028.
The original plan expected inmates to begin serving sentences there in early 2023.
Wammen called the Kosovo agreement important but said additional measures were needed to relieve Denmark’s prisons.
The Justice Ministry declined to identify the countries it contacted or disclose the correspondence. It said publication could risk damaging Denmark’s foreign policy interests.
Estonia’s Justice Ministry confirmed that Denmark had not entered discussions with it. Estonia is concentrating on an existing agreement under which it began receiving inmates from Sweden in 2026.
At the end of September, Denmark had about 4,650 inmates but only 4,300 prison spaces, according to the Prison Officers’ Union.
The union calculated the average occupancy rate at 105.4 percent, the highest recorded level. It stood at 102.7 percent in 2025.
Denmark rejects Russian proposal for maritime and air security agreement
Russia has urged Denmark to enter into a security agreement intended to prevent incidents at sea and in the air, Danish broadcaster TV 2 reported.
The Russian Embassy in Denmark said Russia had previously made the same proposal.
“Today, one can only note that Russia’s initiative for de-escalation has not been met with understanding,” the embassy wrote.
The appeal follows a September incident in which the Russian frigate Soobrazitelny fired two flares toward a Danish military helicopter in international waters near Gedser.
According to the Danish Armed Forces, the flares were fired without warning while the Fennec helicopter was photographing the frigate during a routine mission.
Russia’s ambassador to Denmark, Vladimir Barbin, later accused the helicopter of acting “provocatively.”
The embassy said an agreement could provide a legal framework for preventing similar incidents.
Defence Minister Jeppe Bruus of the Social Democrats rejected the proposal.
“Russia’s aggressive behavior clearly and deliberately violates the international rules by which the country is already bound,” he said. “As long as that is the case, entering into more agreements that are not complied with does not solve the problem.”
The embassy said Russia had protested through diplomatic channels over similar incidents in 2025 and 2026.
Eight arrested during demonstration and counterprotests in Copenhagen
Eight people were arrested Saturday in connection with a demonstration organized by the movement Det Danske Folk in central Copenhagen.
Three arrests occurred before the demonstration began at 2 p.m. in Kongens Nytorv, Copenhagen Police Deputy Inspector Jakob Hansen said.
Two people were arrested after being “in disagreement about some things,” while another was arrested for refusing to provide their name to police.
Five more people were arrested around 5 p.m. as the demonstration ended at Højbro Plads.
“As the demonstration is dispersed, there are smaller groups that begin putting on masks and initiating confrontations with others,” Hansen said. “We have to prevent that, and that leads to a clash with the police.”
Officers drew their batons during the confrontation.
Police did not disclose why the five people were arrested or how many people were involved. It was also too early to specify possible charges against any of the eight people.
The demonstrators marched from Kongens Nytorv toward Christiansborg Palace Square. Counterprotesters gathered at several locations along the route.
Det Danske Folk promoted the demonstration with slogans supporting what it called “fair and realistic remigration” and opposing Islamization, Sharia law and social control.
The counterprotesters gathered under the slogan “No to remigration.”
Electricity’s share of Danish energy use rises to 23.4 percent
Electricity accounted for 23.4 percent of Denmark’s total energy consumption in 2025, an increase of 1.5 percentage points from the previous year.
Green Power Denmark, an industry organization representing the Danish energy sector, said the increase was driven mainly by electric vehicles and the district heating sector’s use of electric boilers and heat pumps.
The organization said growing electrification is gradually reducing Denmark’s reliance on oil and natural gas.
“We are freeing ourselves from what is happening in the Middle East and American politics,” Green Power Denmark chief executive Kristian Jensen said.
He said Danish energy prices remain affected by developments abroad because the country still relies on prices set by global markets.
Denmark’s electrification rate rose by only 3.8 percentage points in total from 2016 through 2024, making the 1.5-point increase in 2025 significant.
Green Power Denmark wants electricity to account for 60 percent of total energy consumption by 2035.
Jensen said achieving that target would require industrial companies to replace natural gas with electricity and heat pumps.
He pointed to iron foundries and food producers, including dairy group Arla, as examples of industries already using heat pumps.
Such changes could reduce companies’ carbon dioxide emissions and energy costs while improving their competitiveness, Jensen said.
Figures for Denmark’s electrification rate in 2026 are not yet available.
The 21-year-old singer has gone from posting piano videos on TikTok to becoming one of Denmark’s biggest pop stars. On Friday, she received the top prize at DR’s annual P3 Guld music awards.
Danish singer Annika has won P3 Prisen, the main award at one of Denmark’s most prominent annual music events, P3 Guld.
The 21-year-old received the award Friday evening at DR Koncerthuset in Copenhagen, a year after being nominated for the same prize but losing out to Danish band Aphaca.
P3 Guld is the annual music awards show organised by P3, the youth-oriented music and entertainment radio station run by Danish public broadcaster DR.
The event celebrates artists who have made a significant impact on Danish music over the past year, with P3 Prisen regarded as its main award.
Annika, whose full name is Annika Wedderkopp, was selected by a P3 jury ahead of fellow nominees Zar Paulo and producer Anton Westerlin, who is also her boyfriend.
“With an authentic foundation in her own life, Annika creates massive hits about breakups and infatuations, about doubt and a steely belief that everything will naturally work out,” the jury said.
From TikTok to the Danish charts
Annika’s rise has been rapid.
She began by posting videos of herself singing at the piano on TikTok before breaking through with “Knuser hjerter” in 2024.
She followed it with several successful releases, including “Så længe jeg er sexy”, and won P3 Talentet, the event’s talent award, that same year.
Last year, she released her debut album “AW”, which includes “Stolt”, a collaboration with Danish rapper Lamin. She also opened Roskilde Festival’s Orange Stage, the festival’s largest and most prestigious stage.
Previous recipients of P3 Prisen include some of Denmark’s best-known contemporary artists, including The Minds of 99, Tobias Rahim, Artigeardit, Lamin, Tina Dickow and Jada.
Other winners
Several other awards were presented at Friday’s ceremony.
Guldimund and Saveus won P3 Lytterhittet – the listeners’ choice award – for their song “Vil du noget?”.
Zar Paulo received P3 Live, an award recognising an artist who has distinguished themselves on Denmark’s live music scene. The award returned this year after previously being presented in 2001 and 2009.
Danish-Faroese artist Friða Saiya won P3’s Næste, a new award that has replaced P3 Talentet and highlights emerging artists.
Criticism over lack of women
This year’s P3 Guld also faced criticism before the ceremony over the gender balance among its performers.
Twelve men and two women were scheduled to perform during the evening.
Ditte Christiane Jensen, head of editorial at DR Ung, defended the lineup in a written response to Ritzau.
“Talent, creativity and artistic quality are not about gender,” she said.
“This year’s lineup was put together based on the artists and bands that have left a significant mark on the music year and in P3’s universe.”
Source: Ritzau
Trump: Greenland deal biggest real estate deal ever
The US president says he “got it for nothing” after signing a new defence agreement with Denmark and Greenland that expands the American military presence on the island.
US President Donald Trump has described a new defence and security agreement with Denmark and Greenland as potentially “the biggest real estate deal that has ever been made”.
Speaking at a Republican campaign rally in Dalton, Georgia, Trump portrayed the agreement as a major achievement for the United States.
“What do you think of the deal I made on Greenland? Got it for nothing,” Trump told supporters.
“It is probably the biggest real estate deal that has ever been made.”
Trump was campaigning ahead of the US midterm elections on November 3.
His comments come after months of tension over Greenland, an autonomous territory within the Kingdom of Denmark. Trump has repeatedly said that the United States wants control and ownership of Greenland, arguing that the island is crucial to American national security.
Two new US military bases
The United States, Denmark and Greenland signed a new security and defence agreement on Greenland at the end of September following lengthy negotiations.
The agreement was signed at the United Nations in New York shortly after Trump addressed the UN General Assembly.
It allows the United States to establish two additional military bases in Greenland.
The US currently operates Pituffik Space Base in northwestern Greenland, which plays an important role in missile warning, space surveillance and Arctic security.
The new agreement also opens the possibility of deploying parts of the planned US Golden Dome missile defence system in Greenland. The system is intended to protect the United States against threats including missiles and drones.
Despite Trump’s description of the agreement as a “real estate deal”, it does not transfer ownership of Greenland to the United States.
Trump’s comments came as Republicans campaign to retain control of Congress in the November midterm elections. Democrats are currently polling more strongly in the race for the House of Representatives, while control of the Senate remains more uncertain.
Republicans currently hold majorities in both chambers.
Source: Ritzau
Denmark’s shift from fossil fuels to electricity is accelerating
Electric cars, heat pumps and electric boilers are driving a sharp increase in the share of Denmark’s energy consumption covered by electricity.
Denmark is becoming increasingly electrified as electric cars, heat pumps and electric boilers replace fossil fuels.
Electricity accounted for 23.4 percent of Denmark’s total energy consumption in 2025, according to figures highlighted by industry organisation Green Power Denmark.
That was an increase of 1.5 percentage points in just one year.
The increase is significant. Between 2016 and 2024, the share of electricity in Denmark’s total energy consumption rose by only 3.8 percentage points.
The acceleration is being driven particularly by the growing number of electric cars and by district heating companies investing in electric boilers and heat pumps.
Kristian Jensen, CEO of Green Power Denmark, says the development will gradually make Denmark less dependent on imported oil and natural gas – and therefore less exposed to international energy prices and geopolitical developments.
“We are freeing ourselves from what is going on in the Middle East and American politics,” Jensen told Ritzau.
“When Danes experience that gasoline, diesel and electricity have become more expensive than they were a year ago, it is because we are still dependent on the price set in the rest of the world.”
Target: 60 percent by 2035
Green Power Denmark wants electricity to account for 60 percent of Denmark’s total energy consumption by 2035.
Reaching that level will require a much faster transition in Danish industry, according to Jensen.
He points to heat pumps as one of the technologies that can help companies replace natural gas with electricity. Iron foundries and food producers, including dairy group Arla, have already demonstrated that large heat pumps can be used in industrial production.
Jensen argues that other companies should follow their example.
“It will not only reduce the companies’ CO2 emissions, it will also reduce energy expenses and thereby improve their competitiveness,” he said.
Figures for Denmark’s electrification rate in 2026 are not yet available, but Green Power Denmark expects the shift towards electricity to continue.
Source: Ritzau
Denmark’s oldest-ever person was a member of the Danish Nazi party
Records show that 112-year-old Kirsten Schwalbe joined Denmark’s Nazi party during the German occupation. She says she did so at her husband’s request and did not sympathise with Nazism.
Kirsten Schwalbe, who this week became the longest-living Dane in recorded history, was a member of Denmark’s Nazi party during the German occupation.
The 112-year-old joined the National Socialist Workers’ Party of Denmark (DNSAP) in August 1941, according to Kristeligt Dagblad.
Her name appears in the Bovrup registry, a record of people who were members of DNSAP. Two historians have independently confirmed to the newspaper that the entry matches Schwalbe’s date of birth and address, although her surname is misspelled as “Schalbe”.
Schwalbe has confirmed that both she and her former husband were members of the party, but says she only joined because her husband urged her to do so.
She rejected the suggestion that she had sided with Nazi Germany.
“Not at all. I barely knew what it was, because I have never taken an interest in politics,” she told TV Midtvest when asked whether she had sympathised with the Nazis.
Schwalbe said she found it unfair that she should have to “pay for it” more than 70 years later, adding that “back then, wives didn’t look into such things”.
Membership does not show level of involvement
DNSAP was founded in 1930 and was strongly inspired by Adolf Hitler’s German Nazi Party, the NSDAP.
But Charlie Krautwald, a historian at the University of Copenhagen, cautioned against drawing conclusions about Schwalbe’s level of involvement from the registry alone.
The record shows that a person joined the party, he told Kristeligt Dagblad, but not why they joined, how long they remained a member or whether they paid membership fees.
A person could therefore appear in the registry without having been active in the party.
TV Midtvest has followed Schwalbe for several years and manages an Instagram account about her life. Two of the broadcaster’s employees have also recently published a book about her.
Her membership of DNSAP had not previously been mentioned. TV Midtvest editor-in-chief Marc Killigren Akselsen told Kristeligt Dagblad that the broadcaster had not known about it.
Schwalbe, who lives in Struer in western Jutland, became the longest-living Dane on record on Wednesday, when she reached the age of 112 years and 218 days.
Source: Ritzau
Nets error causes duplicate charges for customers in three Nordic countries
A technical error at payment provider Nets has caused some customers in Denmark, Sweden and Norway to be charged twice for the same purchase.
Nets said the incorrect transactions would be removed later Friday and the duplicate charges reversed.
The company provides payment systems across the Nordic region. In Denmark, it operates Dankort and processes payments made with Visa and Mastercard.
Nets discovered the error Thursday, according to company press director Peter Glüsing Pedersen.
“I don’t know how many it involves, but considering that we have around a handful of million transactions daily, it is a very small part of them,” he said. “We are talking about a couple of thousand in Denmark.”
Customers who notice a duplicate transaction can contact their bank, Pedersen said.
Work partially resumes at Fehmarn Belt site after cyberattack
Construction has partially resumed at the Fehmarn Belt tunnel site in Rødbyhavn after a cyberattack disrupted the main contractor’s IT systems.
The attack targeted systems belonging to Femern Link Contractors, known as FLC, during the night into Monday, state-owned infrastructure company Sund & Bælt said.
Several IT systems at the construction site remain affected, but work has resumed in some areas.
Earthworks are continuing without disruption, while some concrete work can also be carried out. Production of reinforcement steel has continued inside the site’s steel processing hall.
Sund & Bælt expects the main production facility in Rødbyhavn to resume operations soon but did not provide a specific timeframe.
The National Special Crime Unit, Denmark’s specialized police division for serious and complex crime, is investigating the cyberattack.
The Fehmarn Belt tunnel is under construction between Rødbyhavn in Denmark and Puttgarden in Germany. Once completed, it is expected to reduce travel time between the two countries to seven minutes by train and 10 minutes by car.
Lidl has Denmark’s cheapest basket of organic groceries, analysis finds
Lidl offers the lowest prices on a selected basket of organic groceries among seven Danish supermarket chains, according to an analysis by price-monitoring service Madprisluppen.
A basket containing 22 organic products cost 355.20 DKK at Lidl. The same basket cost 449.60 DKK at Meny, the most expensive chain in the comparison.
Madprisluppen said the Lidl basket was 26 percent cheaper than the one at Meny.
“We want to make it easier for Danes to make room for organics in everyday life, and here price plays an important role,” Lidl Denmark purchasing director Peer Sandtner said.
Rema 1000 was the second-cheapest supermarket, with its basket costing only 5 DKK more than Lidl’s.
SuperBrugsen was the second-most expensive, though its total was almost 35 DKK below Meny’s.
The analysis also included Netto, 365discount and Føtex. Prices were recorded from October 9 through October 12.
Products included milk, eggs, vegetables and dry goods. Meat was excluded because Madprisluppen found it difficult to identify comparable products across the chains.
The monitoring service also found that supermarkets carry fewer organic products than they did six years ago. Organic prices have increased, and such products appear in special offers less frequently than non-organic groceries.
Norway to lend 10-meter Viking boat to Danish museum for 10 years
A Norwegian Viking boat will be displayed at Moesgaard Museum near Aarhus under an unusual 10-year loan agreement.
The oak boat is almost 10 meters long and nearly two meters wide. It was among three smaller vessels discovered when archaeologists excavated Norway’s Gokstad ship in 1880.
The Gokstad ship is Norway’s largest preserved Viking ship.
“The boat is a very important cultural treasure from the Viking Age, and it is not an everyday occurrence that we grant permission for such a boat to be taken out of the country,” Kaare Stang of Riksantikvaren, Norway’s cultural heritage authority, said.
The three smaller boats had been chopped into pieces, possibly as part of a burial ritual, according to archaeologists.
The Museum of Cultural History in Norway owns the boat and applied for permission to lend it to Moesgaard Museum for a new exhibition.
Norwegian authorities normally approve loans for no more than three years. Moesgaard Museum must therefore submit a report on the boat’s condition every three years during the loan period.
Stang said Norwegian authorities trusted the Danish museum to protect the boat but emphasized that it must eventually return to Norway.
No arrival date has been announced.
Moesgaard Museum already displays a 6.5-meter Gokstad boat that was used to transport crews and exchange orders between warships.
Copenhagen establishes support groups for parents of children missing school
A new parents’ association has signed a four-year agreement with the City of Copenhagen to establish support groups for families whose children experience prolonged, involuntary school absence.
Such absence is often connected to poor well-being and is considered concerning when a pupil misses at least 20 percent of school for two consecutive quarters. That corresponds to about 10 days per quarter.
The first groups will be funded by Copenhagen and include eight to nine parents who meet approximately once a month, education news outlet Folkeskolen.dk reported.
A family therapist will lead the meetings, with a parent from Forældrekommissionen, or the Parents’ Commission, also participating.
Louise Gielov and Jens Langorn helped establish the association after their family appeared in the Danish public broadcaster DR documentary “Skolens tabte børn,” which showed daily life with children unable to attend school.
The couple received more than 1,000 messages from parents in similar situations after the documentary aired.
The association now has 2,545 members and aims to establish parent groups across Denmark. It also plans to use families’ experiences to promote earlier intervention and broader changes to prevent school absence.
The proportion of pupils with prolonged concerning absence increased from 2.4 percent in the 2019-2020 school year to 5.1 percent in 2024-2025.
The association has also secured 7 million DKK from foundations.
Dane becomes first European participant to receive combined flu and Covid vaccine
A 65-year-old Dane will become the first person in Europe to receive a new combined influenza and Covid-19 vaccine as part of a clinical trial Friday.
The trial will examine whether one injection can protect against both diseases as effectively as, or better than, the two separate vaccines currently used, Danish public broadcaster DR reported.
The first participant will receive the vaccine at Gentofte Hospital.
“We are investigating whether one shot with this new vaccine is just as effective or potentially better than the two shots given today at preventing hospitalizations with influenza and Covid-19,” said Tor Biering-Sørensen, a professor and senior physician at Herlev and Gentofte Hospital who is leading the trial.
About 165,000 Danes have agreed to participate. More than 300,000 people are expected to join over the next two years.
Half of the participants will receive one dose of the combined vaccine. The other half will receive separate influenza and Covid-19 vaccinations.
People age 65 and older in Denmark are automatically invited to receive free vaccinations against both diseases. The Danish Health Authority said about 1.3 million residents received invitations in September.
People with chronic illnesses or other conditions placing them at increased risk are also eligible for the free program.
The vaccines are intended to reduce the risk of severe illness and hospitalization during the winter respiratory infection season.
Frederiksen rejects calls for Zelenskyy to soften criticism of Trump
Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen of the Social Democrats says she has not heard any European leaders criticize Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy for his comments about US President Donald Trump.
Zelenskyy has said he feels “betrayed” by Trump, prompting reports that some European Union leaders believe he has damaged Ukraine’s relationship with the United States.
“There is no one who has said that. There is no one who has hinted at that. And if there were, I would disagree,” Frederiksen said Friday before an EU summit.
Three EU diplomats told the Financial Times on Thursday that European leaders planned to give Zelenskyy an “empathetic, but firm” message that he should reduce his public criticism of Trump.
Frederiksen rejected that approach.
“I could not dream of going in and placing restrictions on what a democratically elected European president must be allowed to say,” she said.
Frederiksen added that democratically elected leaders must be able to discuss their disagreements openly.
“One has to be able to defend oneself, and one has to be able to defend one’s country. I do not act as a judge over other people’s words,” she said.
Denmark faces rainy Friday before cooler and windier weekend
Denmark’s weekend will begin with mild and rainy weather before turning cooler and windier, with some periods of sunshine.
Friday will be cloudy, with rain spreading from Jutland toward Funen and Zealand, according to Danish Meteorological Institute meteorologist Sandra Nygaard. Bornholm is expected to remain dry.
Temperatures will range from 12 to 17 degrees Celsius, with the warmest conditions in southeastern Denmark.
Jutland could receive up to five millimeters of rain, while smaller amounts are expected farther east.
Clouds and light rain will move across eastern Denmark Friday evening and overnight into Saturday, while conditions will begin clearing from the west.
Temperatures could approach freezing during both weekend nights. However, the forecast does not currently indicate overnight frost. The coldest period is expected overnight into Sunday, when temperatures could fall to three degrees in northern Jutland.
Saturday may bring rain early, followed by mostly dry weather and possible sunshine. Stronger winds will make conditions feel colder than Friday.
Coastal areas can expect fresh to strong winds, while Bornholm could experience gale-force winds and strong gusts.
On Sunday, southwestern Denmark may receive clouds and rain. Most other areas can expect dry weather with some or considerable sunshine and temperatures of up to 12 degrees.
Archaeologists uncover more than 1,000 graves in Copenhagen park
Archaeologists have excavated more than 1,000 graves containing human remains beneath Hans Tavsens Park in Copenhagen’s Nørrebro district.
The park, located next to Assistens Cemetery, was previously used as a burial ground for Copenhagen’s poorest residents. Victims of the city’s 1853 cholera epidemic are among those buried there.
“We can use it to gain insight into the poor population from this period and Copenhagen’s history,” Museum of Copenhagen archaeologist Olivia Persson told Danish public broadcaster DR.
The excavation is taking place before Hans Tavsens Park and the neighboring Hans Tavsens Gade are redeveloped into a connected green space.
The project will also allow the park to collect water during cloudbursts, helping prevent flooding of nearby roads and basements as Denmark experiences wetter weather.
Construction began in autumn 2025 as part of the City of Copenhagen’s plan for managing extreme rainfall. The redevelopment is expected to be completed in spring 2028.
Most of the remains will be transferred to the University of Copenhagen’s Anthropological Laboratory for storage and examination. Some will undergo additional analysis, while the remainder will be reburied in the park.
Researchers will examine the health of selected individuals. They will also study how the graves were arranged to better understand religious and cultural attitudes toward death among Copenhagen’s poorer population at the time.
Greenland parliament backs temporary ban on deep-sea mining
Greenland’s parliament unanimously adopted a resolution Thursday directing the government to draft legislation temporarily banning deep-sea mining.
The proposed ban would remain in effect through December 31, 2029, with the possibility of two-year extensions.
Naalakkersuisut, Greenland’s government, supported the considerations behind the resolution. It said it would introduce a bill for the temporary ban during parliament’s spring 2027 session.
The ban must therefore pass as legislation before taking effect.
WWF Greenland, the local branch of the World Wide Fund for Nature, called the decision “an important step in the right direction,” according to AFP.
“With this decision, Greenland has the opportunity to send a strong signal that the protection of the ocean, nature and the Greenlanders’ livelihood must be taken seriously when we face new forms of exploitation of marine resources,” the organization said.
WWF Greenland says deep-sea mining can damage marine ecosystems and biodiversity.
Fishing is the main driver of Greenland’s economy, while hunting remains important to local communities.
The vote came one day after US President Donald Trump said oil, gas and mineral exploration was beginning in Greenland. Greenland’s government subsequently denied the claim. Trump did not mention deep-sea mining.
Greenland suspended new oil and gas exploration permits in 2021. Industrial oil drilling and gas extraction have never been conducted there, according to AFP.
Denmark considers lower temperature rule to allow electric cremation ovens
Denmark’s 20 crematoria could replace oil- and gas-powered ovens with electric models if authorities approve a lower minimum temperature requirement.
The Danish Environmental Protection Agency has proposed reducing the required temperature in cremation ovens’ post-combustion chambers from 800 to 750 degrees Celsius, engineering publication Ingeniøren reported.
The proposed change has been submitted for public consultation.
Electric ovens are expected to reduce both environmental effects and the financial cost of cremations.
Michael Smidemann, chair of the Danish Crematoria Association, said crematoria were interested in replacing their existing ovens.
“The background is a desire to sharpen the green profile, even though it is somewhat mixed how green the electricity we receive actually is,” he told Ingeniøren.
Electric cremation ovens can reach 750 degrees. Requiring them to reach 800 degrees would demand additional heating elements, increasing electricity use and causing heavy wear on the ovens’ brickwork, according to Ingeniøren.
Denmark recorded 58,185 deaths in 2025, according to the Danish Crematoria Association.
Of those who died, 51,252 were cremated, corresponding to 88.1 percent of all deaths.
A cremation typically takes about 90 minutes, according to information from the City of Copenhagen and other sources.
Specialized services received 61 percent of growth in municipal spending
Denmark’s specialized social and education services received 61 percent of the inflation-adjusted growth in municipal service spending from 2018 through 2025.
The finding comes from an analysis by Arbejderbevægelsens Erhvervsråd, or AE, an economic policy institute linked to the Danish labor movement, according to Dagbladet Information.
Specialized services include support for children, young people and adults with particular needs, along with special classes and special education.
Municipalities spent approximately 80 billion DKK on these areas in 2018. By 2025, spending had risen to 93 billion DKK.
Residential facilities accounted for 40 percent of the increase. Municipal spending on those facilities now totals about 27 billion DKK, according to AE.
“When expenditures in the specialized areas grow, there is less money for the general areas, which also need investments,” AE director Lars Andersen said.
However, the analysis does not establish that the increased specialized spending directly caused cuts elsewhere.
Municipal service funding also covers daycare centers, public schools and elderly care.
The government and Local Government Denmark, the association representing Denmark’s municipalities, have increased the overall spending limit annually since 2018. Their latest agreement raises it by 3.3 billion DKK for 2027.
Finance Minister Peter Hummelgaard of the Social Democrats has previously acknowledged that rapidly rising specialized social service costs continue to create financial difficulties for some municipalities.
Too Good To Go to sell surplus household and personal care products
The Danish-founded app is introducing five new product categories, allowing customers to buy discounted goods ranging from pet accessories to flowers and dietary supplements.
Too Good To Go announced Thursday that its platform will now offer surplus personal care products, pet accessories, flowers and plants, nutrition and dietary supplements, and household goods.
The expansion marks a shift for the company, which has focused on reducing food waste since its launch in 2016.
“Too Good To Go started with food because we saw how absurd it was that something so valuable could end up as waste. Ten years later, it is clear that the same principle applies outside the world of food,” CEO Mette Lykke said.
According to the company, more than 8,500 stores will offer products across the new categories.
Approximately one-third of those retailers already work with Too Good To Go to sell surplus food.
The app currently operates in 20 countries, with 150 million registered users and 200,000 active business partners.
Through its existing model, retailers sell unsold food in discounted surprise bags, with Too Good To Go receiving a percentage of each transaction.
The company says its expansion will help businesses recover value from unsold merchandise while giving customers access to a wider selection of discounted products.
“Our partners are increasingly approaching us with challenges regarding surplus goods that extend beyond food and asking if we can help. Surplus exists in all parts of the store,” Lykke said.
Surplus stock can include seasonal products, discontinued items, outdated packaging and gift sets that are no longer in demand.
Frederiksen warns Western alliance is weakening amid U.S.-Ukraine tensions
Denmark’s prime minister has expressed serious concern about Washington’s recent actions toward Ukraine, including a diesel agreement with Russia and reported disruptions to military support.
Speaking Thursday as she arrived at a European Union summit in Brussels, Mette Frederiksen said the developments had put further strain on relations between Western allies.
“I believe that the Western alliance is in a worse place now than we were a couple of days ago,” Frederiksen said.
Her comments followed reports of an energy ceasefire, gaps in U.S. intelligence sharing with Ukraine and restrictions affecting access to Starlink, the satellite internet network used by Ukrainian forces.
Washington has also reached an agreement to purchase Russian diesel, raising concerns about its approach to Moscow while Russia’s war against Ukraine continues.
Frederiksen, who leads Socialdemokratiet, the Social Democrats, described the overall situation as very serious.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy also expressed frustration Thursday, urging the United States not to side with Russia.
His remarks came after Ukraine was reportedly caught off guard by changes affecting American intelligence support and Starlink access.
“We need HONESTY from our partners about this war: It is important that everyone in America does not take the aggressor’s side, but supports our efforts to protect life, end this war and guarantee security,” Zelenskyy wrote on X.
The statements from Frederiksen and Zelenskyy reflect concerns about Washington’s recent decisions and their implications for cooperation with Ukraine.
Both leaders raised the issue as questions continued over American support for Ukraine and its relationship with Russia.
Crown Prince Christian receives Denmark’s highest Dannebrog honor
King Frederik has marked his eldest son’s 21st birthday with a royal decoration and the release of new official portraits, while celebrations remain private.
Crown Prince Christian was awarded the Grand Commander Cross of the Order of the Dannebrog on Thursday, according to a statement from the Danish Royal House.
The decoration is the highest rank within the Order of the Dannebrog and is reserved for members of royalty who already hold the Order of the Elephant.
Christian received the Order of the Elephant on his 18th birthday, making him eligible for the distinction.
With his appointment, Denmark now has seven Grand Commanders of the Order of the Dannebrog.
The cross currently bears the monogram of King Frederik IX, who last awarded it. It will be updated with King Frederik’s monogram during restoration.
The Royal House also released portraits showing Christian wearing the Royal Life Guards’ red ceremonial uniform.
The photographs were taken several weeks earlier at Christian VII’s Palace at Amalienborg.
Christian currently serves as a second lieutenant and platoon commander with the Royal Life Guards at Høvelte Barracks.
He completed his compulsory military service in August 2025 before beginning officer training and is expected to remain in service until summer 2027.
The crown prince receives neither a military training salary nor a royal allowance.
His father also trained as a lieutenant, later qualifying as a naval frogman and serving four months with Greenland’s Sirius Patrol in 2000.
In a recent interview with Politiken, Christian said he would consider deployment after completing his lieutenant training.
The Nordic region’s largest bank reported third-quarter earnings broadly in line with analysts’ expectations, but uncertainty surrounding regulatory assessments weighed on investor confidence Thursday.
Nordea shares fell 7.3 percent by 12:50 p.m., making the bank the worst performer in Denmark’s C25 stock index.
The decline followed the publication of Nordea’s quarterly financial results, which showed a profit of 1,181 billion euros and total income of 2,968 billion euros.
Both figures were broadly consistent with analysts’ forecasts.
However, the bank announced it would suspend a planned share buyback program while awaiting clarification from the European Central Bank (ECB) regarding its risk assessments.
The regulatory process is not expected to conclude until 2027.
Share buybacks allow companies to return money to shareholders by purchasing their own shares, often reducing the number available and potentially increasing the value of those remaining.
According to Danish financial newspaper Børsen, Nordea had planned to repurchase approximately 500 million euros worth of shares.
Martin Munk, senior equity adviser at Jyske Bank, said the market reaction reflected regulatory uncertainty rather than disappointing financial performance.
“It is not the financial statements that are creating noise. Rather, it is the uncertainty about where they land with the ECB,” Munk told MarketWire.
Nordea CEO Frank Vang-Jensen acknowledged that the regulatory review was taking longer than anticipated.
“It has proven to be a long process,” he told Børsen.
Vang-Jensen said the bank considered pausing repurchases appropriate while uncertainty remained over its future risk-weighted assets, a measure used to determine how much capital banks must hold against potential losses.
Tiny parasitic wasp discovered in Denmark for the first time
A nature enthusiast searching beneath ferns in a North Zealand forest has identified an insect species never previously recorded in the country.
The discovery was made in mid-September at Gribskov National Nature Park during a bioblitz, a 24-hour event in which participants search for and document wildlife.
Around 70 people took part in the event, organized in collaboration with the Vores Vilde Natur project and biodiversity platform Arter.dk.
Nature educator Lars Holm Hansen discovered the wasp, measuring just a few millimeters, while shaking bracken ferns to examine the insects hiding underneath.
He collected several specimens using an insect aspirator but could not immediately identify them.
After posting a photograph on Arter.dk, he received help from experts who identified the species as Hemiptarsenus ornatus.
“It shows that if you put in a little effort out in the field, you can get lucky, and it is simply worth the effort,” Hansen said.
The Natural History Museum of Denmark confirmed the finding in a press release.
Museum insect curator Lars Vilhelmsen explained that the species has previously been recorded in Germany, Sweden and Norway.
“It has probably been here all along. It is already known from several countries around us, but it is so small that you do not just easily spot it,” Vilhelmsen said.
He added that relatively few people in Denmark study parasitic wasps, meaning many species may remain undocumented.
Hansen, who had participated in six bioblitz events this year, also suggested the insect’s Danish name: smykket dværgsnyltehveps.
He believes Danish names make unfamiliar species easier to discuss and remember.
Red-Green Alliance demands guaranteed transport for students in rural areas
Free public transport for young people will have limited value without reliable bus and train connections, according to Enhedslisten, the Red-Green Alliance.
The left-wing party is calling for a transport guarantee ensuring that young people across Denmark can reach upper secondary schools and vocational education programs using public transport.
The proposal is among its demands in negotiations over the government’s next national budget.
“Unfortunately, there are places in Denmark where no buses run, and then you cannot use free public transport for very much,” party leader Pelle Dragsted said.
Enhedslisten has already secured a commitment in the government’s policy platform to provide free public transport for people younger than 22.
However, Dragsted argues that years of declining bus services in rural areas have discouraged passengers, contributing to further reductions in services.
The party wants additional funding to reverse that trend, although it has not specified the proposal’s total cost.
It suggests raising 1 billion DKK by taxing property companies’ profits from real estate transactions.
Dragsted acknowledged that budget negotiations alone might not resolve the broader problems facing public transport.
“But we hope that we can take a step. And we think that the idea of ensuring that young people have a right to transport should be a minimum.”
He compared the proposal with existing municipal obligations to provide transport for schoolchildren living sufficiently far from their schools.
Enhedslisten is also demanding the removal of public school fees, expanded free dental care and restrictions on profits from welfare services.
Dragsted argued that these measures would help balance the government’s planned tax cuts and benefit ordinary residents.
Auto group charged with exploiting 18 foreign mechanics in Denmark
A criminal case involving workers from India, Sri Lanka and other countries will be heard at the Court in Hillerød, following allegations of unpaid overtime, threats and restrictions on trade union membership.
According to TV 2 Kosmopol, prosecutors have brought charges against two men and two companies connected to a car group in North Zealand.
North Zealand Police allege that 18 foreign mechanics were subjected to human exploitation over a four-year period.
The indictment states that the workers were required to work overtime and weekends without additional pay.
They were also allegedly prohibited from joining a trade union, limiting their ability to seek collective representation over their employment conditions.
Prosecutors further allege that the mechanics were threatened with dismissal and deportation to their home countries if they complained about their working or living conditions.
TV 2 Kosmopol reported that although the mechanics’ stated monthly salaries were 38,000 DKK, they received only 7,517 DKK after tax.
The case will now be considered by the Court in Hillerød, which must determine whether the defendants are guilty of the charges.
The court will also decide whether approximately 4.1 million DKK should be confiscated from the defendants in connection with the alleged exploitation.
Denmark introduced a specific provision on human exploitation into its criminal code in June 2022.
The provision was designed to address serious cases of labor exploitation that do not meet the legal definition of human trafficking.
The charges in the North Zealand case have been brought under that provision, with the defendants’ criminal responsibility yet to be established.
Denmark faces 12.7 billion DKK increase in EU contributions under new budget proposal
The Danish government is preparing for difficult negotiations in Brussels over the European Union’s next budget, with disagreements emerging over spending priorities and national contributions.
According to estimates from Denmark’s Finance Ministry, a proposal presented by Ireland’s EU presidency could increase Denmark’s annual contribution by approximately 12.7 billion DKK compared with the current budget period.
The estimate remains uncertain but represents a reduction from the European Commission’s original proposal, which was initially expected to increase Denmark’s contribution by 16.6 billion DKK annually.
Updated calculations have since lowered that estimate to 15.7 billion DKK, based on 2027 prices.
