The proposed increase could affect the Danish government’s spending priorities.
For comparison, its plan to eliminate VAT on fruit and vegetables and halve VAT on other food products would cost approximately 17.4 billion DKK annually.
Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen, of Socialdemokratiet, the Social Democrats, is attending Thursday’s EU summit in Brussels, where budget negotiations are beginning.
Denmark has joined Germany, the Netherlands, Sweden, Finland and Austria in calling for tighter EU spending.
The six countries want greater emphasis on defense and economic competitiveness rather than agricultural subsidies and regional development funding.
France has also expressed opposition to higher national contributions, citing financial pressures.
However, several other EU members want to preserve existing agricultural and regional support programs.
Despite disagreements, no member state has rejected Ireland’s proposal as the basis for negotiations.
European Council President António Costa will oversee the discussions, with a possible agreement expected at December’s EU summit.
Border checks between Denmark and Germany extended for another six months
Travelers entering the country may continue to face inspections until May 17, 2027, as authorities maintain that security threats remain serious.
Justice Minister Nicolai Wammen, a member of Socialdemokratiet, the Social Democrats, informed the European Commission of the decision Wednesday, according to a statement from the Justice Ministry.
The temporary controls were previously scheduled to expire November 11, following a four-month extension announced in June.
Denmark’s decision comes despite the general principle of open borders under the Schengen Agreement, which allows people to travel between participating European countries without routine border checks.
However, regulations introduced in 2024 allow countries to extend existing border controls when the security threats that originally justified them remain in place.
Wammen said Denmark continues to face threats involving terrorism and sabotage.
“The security situation at home is serious, and we continue to see a terror and sabotage threat directed at Denmark,” he said in the ministry’s statement.
He also referred to recent developments in Ceuta, a Spanish territory in North Africa, as an example of how quickly movements of people across borders can change.
“The overall picture emphasizes how important it is for the security and safety of Danes to have control over the checks at the border,” Wammen said.
Under the extended measures, people crossing from Germany into Denmark may be stopped by authorities and asked to provide documentation confirming their right to enter or remain in the country.
Reports of AI-generated child abuse material rise sharply in Denmark
Save the Children received 4,069 reports of suspected artificial intelligence-generated sexual abuse material involving children and young people during the first six months of 2026, according to figures obtained by Kristeligt Dagblad.
The international children’s rights organization recorded 6,558 reports throughout 2025, compared with 2,770 in 2024, an increase of approximately 140 percent.
The figures reflect reports submitted by people who believe they have encountered such material online, rather than confirmed cases.
Lea Wermelin, justice spokesperson for Socialdemokratiet, the Social Democrats, expressed concern about the growing numbers.
“The technology makes it much easier to make, but we must never get used to it just being something encountered online,” she told Kristeligt Dagblad.
Pernille Spitz, Save the Children’s head of protection against abuse, warned that greater exposure to such content could make it appear more acceptable.
“The more of it there is, and the easier it is to come across, the more legitimate it may seem,” Spitz said.
Save the Children’s reporting service, AnmeldDet, reviews submissions from the public and assesses whether they should be forwarded to authorities.
During 2026, the service has referred 377 reports to police.
Denmark’s National Special Crime Unit, known as NSK, told Kristeligt Dagblad that it could not determine what proportion of child sexual abuse material involved artificial intelligence.
However, the agency said it believed AI was increasingly being used to produce such content.
Denmark amended its criminal code in 2025 to make realistic AI-generated child sexual abuse material punishable by law.
Denmark restricts land registry searches after 17 million queries in days
An unusually high volume of requests for publicly available property information has prompted authorities to introduce new safeguards following disruptions to a government database.
The Danish Court Administration said 17.2 million searches were recorded in the Digital Land Registration System over several days, compared with fewer than two million in a typical week.
The activity was discovered after the system experienced repeated disruptions during week 41.
Rikke Holler, president of the Land Registration Court, emphasized that the searches were legal and involved only information available without logging in through MitID, Denmark’s digital identification system.
“It is the number of lookups that gives cause for attention,” Holler said.
The system provides limited public information about properties, cooperative housing and vehicles.
Authorities have not identified what caused the surge in activity.
Justice Minister Nicolai Wammen, a member of Socialdemokratiet, the Social Democrats, said he had informed the Danish Parliament about the incident.
Although the searches were permitted, Wammen said their unusual volume warranted serious attention.
The Danish Court Administration warned that publicly available information could potentially be used to make fraud attempts appear more convincing.
It also referred to a recent leak involving 8.8 million CPR numbers, Denmark’s personal identification numbers.
Wammen urged people never to share passwords or confidential information through phone calls or emails, even when someone contacting them knows details they consider private.
The Land Registration Court has introduced additional limits on searches to maintain system stability.
Officials did not specify the measures but reported that the number of queries had decreased following their introduction.
Danish agriculture group threatens legal action over temporary pig farm permit freeze
A proposed one-year suspension of permits for new conventional pig farms and expansions of existing facilities has raised questions about the government’s legal authority and potential compensation claims.
Landbrug & Fødevarer, the Danish Agriculture and Food Council, warned in a consultation response that the measure could lead to lawsuits over financial losses.
“If the amendment to the executive order is implemented, a number of lawsuits regarding liability for compensation for economic losses as a result of the regulation must be expected,” the organization stated.
Christian Fink Hansen, the council’s pig sector director, called for an assessment of the proposal’s economic impact on businesses.
He warned that the industry could otherwise be forced to pursue compensation claims in court.
The suspension is scheduled to take effect October 26, but applications submitted since September 23 must already be assessed under the proposed rules.
Several legal experts have questioned whether Nature and Animal Welfare Minister Christian Rabjerg Madsen, of Socialdemokratiet, the Social Democrats, has authority to impose the restrictions.
Two experts cited by Dagbladet Information disputed the legal basis for an immediate suspension, while another supported the minister’s position.
Rabjerg Madsen has rejected those concerns, citing assessments by lawyers from his ministry and the Justice Ministry.
“I am completely at ease. I do not make an amendment to an executive order without an assessment of the legal basis having been carried out,” he said in September.
Although the government’s June platform proposed introducing the measure through legislation, Rabjerg Madsen instead used an executive order, which does not require parliamentary approval.
The government says the suspension will remain in place while it clarifies future production rules through negotiations involving the pig industry, which began September 30.
Full train service between Fredericia and Odense to resume Monday
Full train service between Fredericia and Odense will resume on Monday, Banedanmark announced on Wednesday.
Banedanmark, which operates, maintains and develops Denmark’s state-owned railway network, announced the resumption in a post on the social media platform X.
Earlier on Wednesday, railway operator DSB said in a preliminary announcement that fewer trains would run on the route through Sunday, October 18.
All regional trains on the section have been replaced by buses since Friday, when a fire broke out in a railway relay hut near Aarup, a town on western Funen.
International trains, InterCityLyn express services and InterCity trains have continued to run as normal, but at reduced speeds on parts of the route between Odense and Middelfart or Fredericia.
Signal fault disrupts trains between Copenhagen and Næstved until evening
A signal fault near Kildebrønde in eastern Zealand is disrupting train services between Copenhagen Central Station and Næstved via Køge.
On Wednesday morning, DSB said passengers should expect longer travel times until 1 p.m. But about an hour before that deadline, the railway operator announced that disruptions would continue until 7 p.m., according to its website.
Banedanmark, which operates and maintains Denmark’s state-owned railway network, told DSB that repair work would not take place until Wednesday night, leading into Thursday.
However, a solution has been found that will allow trains to run normally on the affected section after 7 p.m., even though the fault will not yet have been repaired.
Some trains that usually run via Køge Nord are being diverted through Roskilde instead. These services will not stop between Copenhagen Central Station and Ringsted.
Additional replacement buses were introduced between Køge and Næstved on Wednesday morning to ease pressure on train services. The buses stopped running at noon, and DSB is advising passengers to take the S-train from Copenhagen toward Køge. Trains between Køge and Næstved are running once an hour.
Banedanmark told the Danish news agency Ritzau that a severed cable caused the signal fault. DSB advises passengers to check Rejseplanen, Denmark’s public transport journey planner, before setting off.
Meanwhile, fewer trains are running between Odense and Fredericia through Sunday, October 18, according to DSB. The date is provisional, and services could return to normal earlier or later than expected.
All regional trains on the route have been replaced by buses since Friday, following a fire in a railway relay hut near Aarup in western Funen.
International trains, as well as InterCityLyn and InterCity services, are running as normal, but at reduced speeds on some sections of the route.
On Tuesday afternoon, all train traffic between Odense and Fredericia was also halted for a couple of hours after a cable fell onto the tracks and caused a short circuit in the overhead power system.

articles.title: Russian blitz kills 7 across Ukraine as Zelenskyy head for Oslo talks
articles.body:
Russian missile and drone blitz on Ukrainian civilian areas killed at least seven people Tuesday, officials said, as President Volodymyr Zelenskyy visited Norway to secure further U.S. and European aid.
U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff, who along with Jared Kushner unsuccessfully tried to steer Russia and Ukraine toward a settlement, was also expected in Oslo, the Norwegian government said. Kushner, President Donald Trump's son-in-law, will attend the meeting by videoconference, it said.
Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store and Finnish President Alexander Stubb were scheduled to meet with Zelenskyy in the capital, Oslo.
With further U.S. support for Ukraine in doubt as relations between Zelenskyy and President Trump strained again, the Ukrainian leader said he spoke with U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who is on a trip to Asia.
The conversation followed Zelenskyy's statement to a bipartisan group of U.S. lawmakers Monday that he believes "some political decision has been made to slow down ... support for us."
Ukraine has nearly run out of U.S.-made Patriot air defense interceptors needed to stop Russia's ballistic missiles, Zelenskyy said, and he urged Washington to send more. He also said the Pentagon is delaying the delivery of missiles other countries purchased for Ukraine.
Zelenskyy also said he sought Rubio's help to ensure the United States continues to share vital intelligence with Ukraine after Kyiv received none or belated warnings about Russian missile attacks in recent days.
Zelenskyy also said speed restrictions remained in place on Kyiv's use of the military-grade version of U.S. company SpaceX's satellite internet service, hampering battlefield operations.
President Trump has also waived sanctions on Russia, a move Zelenskyy criticized as helping Russian President Vladimir Putin continue Moscow's full-scale invasion, which reaches its five-year mark in February.
Zelenskyy said he had "a substantive conversation" with Rubio.
"I am grateful for his readiness to help and his clear position," Zelenskyy said on social media.
With the Russian army stalled on the front line, Putin is trying to bomb Ukraine into submission while depriving it of vital U.S. support, Western leaders and analysts say.
European countries, worried by Russia's plans on the continent and viewing Ukraine as a bulwark against Moscow's ambitions, are trying to compensate for any decline in U.S. supplies, but some key assets are U.S.-made.
European countries and EU institutions have allocated 237 billion euros (about $266 billion) to supporting Ukraine, compared with 115 billion euros from the U.S., according to Germany's Kiel Institute, a think tank that tracks assistance to Kyiv.
EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas Tuesday questioned whether U.S. negotiators were honest brokers in peace efforts. Ukrainian officials say the Trump administration encouraged Kyiv to surrender land to Russia in return for peace.
"Although American negotiators have been trying to push Ukraine into surrender for one and a half years, why Ukraine has not surrendered on Putin's terms is because Europe has supported Ukraine," Kallas said.
"Ukraine wants peace more than anybody because it has been under bombardment for four years," she told EU lawmakers in Strasbourg, France. "The only one who does not want peace is Russia."
Russian missile and drone attacks killed four people and wounded 27 others, including children, in Kyiv region over the past day, regional police said.
Police said three people were killed and six were wounded in the Obukhiv district, where warehouses were damaged. In the Bucha district, one woman was killed and 21 people were wounded, eight of them children, and hundreds of buildings were damaged, according to police.
A Russian attack on the Kyiv-Odesa highway killed three people and injured four when two vehicles caught fire Tuesday morning, Ukraine's State Emergency Service said. Among the dead was the driver of a shuttle bus hit in the attack. The bus transports passengers from Kyiv to the National Military Memorial Cemetery.
National grid operator Ukrenergo reported power outages in 12 Ukrainian regions following the Russian attacks.
The Russian Defense Ministry said its forces conducted drone strikes on logistics centers, port infrastructure and three cargo ships in the port of Reni in Odesa region. Its forces also hit another bulk carrier at sea on its way to Odesa.
Meanwhile, air defenses intercepted 136 Ukrainian drones over multiple Russian regions overnight, the ministry said.
A fire broke out at an unspecified industrial facility in the Tambov region following the attack, Gov. Yevgeny Pervyshov said.

articles.title: Zelensky’s feud with Trump endangers his plan to defend Ukraine
articles.body:
Zelensky’s feud with Trump endangers his plan to defend Ukraine
- Zelensky’s row with Trump is hurting Ukraine’s defence, with delays to Patriot missiles, possible limits on intelligence, and fears of weaker support before winter.
- NATO officials want Ukraine to calm tensions. They warn a broken US tie could force Kyiv into a painful deal with Russia and leave Europe exposed.
- Trump is putting more pressure on Kyiv while easing pressure on Moscow, including a diesel deal and softer sanctions. Zelensky will meet Steve Witkoff in Oslo for peace talks.
AI generated
KYIV – The feud between US President Donald Trump and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky is starting to compromise Ukraine’s ability to defend itself.
Strains that have lingered under the surface escalated dramatically over the past week when the Ukrainian president accused the US of throttling vital access to SpaceX’s Starshield satellite technology and delaying supplies of key Patriot interceptors to repel Russian ballistic missile strikes.
Senior NATO officials are concerned the relationship between Zelensky and the US president could be beyond repair and may lead to Ukraine being forced into accepting a painful settlement to the war with Russia, according to a person familiar with the matter.
Zelensky is set to meet Trump’s envoy Steve Witkoff in Oslo on Oct 20 for new peace talks that would also be attended remotely by the president’s son-in-law, Jared Kushner.
The breakdown in relations coincides with Trump fighting to salvage his majority in Nov 3 midterm elections.
The argument risks leaving Kyiv at its most vulnerable heading into another frigid winter and with civilian casualties already surging from constant Russian attacks.
“It’s going to be a long, dark, cold winter,” said Justin Logan, director of defence and foreign policy at the Cato Institute in Washington. “It’s almost November, their interceptor stockpiles are close to zero, the Europeans’ ability to replenish them is limited because inventories are limited.”
Secretary-General Mark Rutte is aware of the risks posed by the souring relationship and his main concern is to lower the temperature to make room for pragmatic solutions that ensure Ukraine has what it needs to stay in the fight, a NATO official said.
NATO officials have urged Ukraine to try and deescalate with the US, one of the people said.
If Zelensky won’t do that, then US arms supplies that are being financed mainly by the Europeans through the so-called PURL programme could eventually also be affected given Trump’s unpredictability, according to that person.
The person declined to be named because the talks are private.
The tensions between the US and Ukraine have never been so intense – or so personal – since Russia’s full-scale invasion began in 2022.
Speaking to Bloomberg News on Oct 18, Zelensky accused Trump of trying to pressure Kyiv into surrendering to Moscow.
He also said the US is delaying deliveries of crucial Patriot air defence interceptors used to defend Ukraine’s cities.
And Ukrainian officials now suspect the US is intermittently restricting intelligence sharing and early warning alerts about Russian ballistic missiles.
While Trump has denied ordering disruptions to the Starlink satellite service used by Ukraine to defend against Russian air attacks, the president and his administration have openly criticised Zelensky.
They’re ratcheting up pressure on Ukraine across a number of fronts, even as they lessen the leverage the US has over Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Trump said on Oct 19 that “somebody else” instead of Zelensky should negotiate on behalf of Ukraine, the day after he attacked him for the energy strikes on Russia in a lengthy post that justified his own policy toward Moscow.
“Russia frankly has been fine on Ukraine,” Trump told reporters. “They haven’t been doing much.”
Behind the scenes, Europeans are trying to help patch things up with the Trump administration, one of the people said.
But there’s no plan so far for a trip to Washington, another person said, something that officials have done during previous dust-ups between Zelensky and Trump, most famously following the their face-to-face confrontation in the Oval Office in February 2025.
The dispute is existential for Europe.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz warned on Oct 19 that Putin is seeking not only to defeat Ukraine, but to also undermine democracy in Europe.
“I’m trying to convince Donald Trump each time I’m meeting him that this should be in his own interest,” Merz told Bloomberg TV in an interview on Oct 19. “A stable Europe, European continent, European Union as a partner in the world is something which is worthwhile for the Americans as well.”
Trump, who has pushed European leaders to shoulder most aid for Ukraine in the conflict, is ratcheting up pressure on what most analysts and even a growing number of Republican congressional allies believe is the wrong side of the war – not only by holding back offensive military support for Ukraine but also by undermining core defensive capabilities such as air defence.
The fire under the latest conflict was lit by Trump’s unilateral decision to make a deal with Russia for diesel exports earlier in October and his waiving of congressionally mandated sanctions targeting Russian energy, a series of moves that are likely to help Moscow finance its war machine.
One obvious sore point for the US president is Ukraine’s successful campaign of long-range drone strikes on Russian refineries.
The administration has tried to divert blame for rising energy prices away from the war the US started in Iran and towards the fighting between Russia and Ukraine ahead of the midterms in which Republicans are expected to lose control of at least one chamber of Congress.
Zelensky said in Oct 19’s interview that the US is delaying Patriot interceptor deliveries that Kyiv has already paid for.
The US is now supplying Ukraine with only 12 Patriot missiles a month, approximately a quarter of the amount delivered under President Joe Biden.
The Trump administration is also selling the missiles to Ukraine, while Biden provided them for free.
“The US inventory of Patriot missiles is very low, about 800 by our estimate,” Mark Cancian, a former US defence budget expert now at the Centre for Strategic and International Studies in Washington.
The Pentagon is worried about what is still required for operations in the Middle East, as well as in a potential conflict with China, he said.
Asked on Oct 19 if the relationship between the two administrations is fundamentally broken, Secretary of State Marco Rubio avoided a direct answer, saying that Trump’s goal is to end the war.
“He’s willing to do whatever he can to try to bring it to an end, even if that means having to nudge both sides to get there,” Rubio said. BLOOMBERG

articles.title: Zelenskiy to meet Witkoff as Trump praises Russia and rebukes Ukraine
articles.body:
Zelenskiy to meet Witkoff as Trump praises Russia and rebukes Ukraine
OSLO/KYIV, Oct 20 - Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy was due on Tuesday in Oslo to meet US special envoy Steve Witkoff, trying to repair ties that have deteriorated this month as President Donald Trump courted Moscow.
Trump, who has waived sanctions on Russia in what he says is an effort to lower US fuel prices, has repeatedly rebuked Zelenskiy and called for him to be replaced.
Kyiv says Washington has lately failed to provide early warning of Russian missile launches, throttled SpaceX's Starshield satellite links that guide Ukrainian drones, and failed to deliver air defences paid for by European allies.
In the latest comments expressing warmth towards Moscow and coldness towards Kyiv, Trump said on Monday: "Russia, frankly, has been fine on Ukraine." Zelenskiy was "not helping matters much" and Kyiv should find "somebody else to negotiate".
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio acknowledged on Tuesday that a consignment of US air defence missiles bought by Europeans for Ukraine may not have been delivered, but played down the significance.
"I think the important takeaway for you is that there has not been some deliberate political directive to go out and harm Ukraine," he told journalists during a visit to India.
The Kremlin said it was hoping to set up a meeting soon between Witkoff and Russian President Vladimir Putin, an apparent indication that Witkoff could head to Russia after meeting Zelenskiy.
RUSSIA STEPS UP ATTACKS
As US ties with Ukraine have deteriorated, Russia has stepped up attacks on Ukrainian cities, particularly targeting power stations and fuel in apparent defiance of a call from Trump for both sides to spare each other's energy systems.
Ukraine held back for several days from hitting Russian oil refineries in deference to Trump's request but resumed strikes after no sign Russia was complying. Both sides have also struck data centres.
Trump has criticised the Ukrainian attacks on Russia while saying little about Russia's more severe attacks on Ukraine, which Kyiv says have become even more intense and deadlier because of the withdrawal of US technology to fend them off.
In the latest attacks, Ukrainian officials said a Russian drone struck near a petrol station on a highway heading south out of Kyiv, killing three people and setting cars ablaze.
Footage released by Ukraine's emergency services of a separate attack on a warehouse in the capital that also killed three people showed firefighters battling a huge blaze, surrounded by twisted wreckage.
Energy facilities were attacked in seven Ukrainian regions overnight, knocking out power, and the western Lviv region was struck again during the day. Three other people were reported killed in Kramatorsk in the east.
ZELENSKIY SPEAKS TO RUBIO
Zelenskiy said he had spoken with Rubio about ballistic missile interceptors, early warning of Russian attacks and "the situation with Starlink/Starshield, which needs to be restored".
"Of course, all of this comes against the backdrop of our diplomatic efforts to end this horrific war and the constant killing of people," Zelenskiy said in a post on X.
The deterioration of relations began 10 days ago when Trump lifted sanctions on Russian diesel in a deal agreed with Putin, which he said would help reduce prices. High fuel costs since Trump launched strikes on Iran have hurt his Republicans before legislative elections next month.
Trump has since repeatedly berated Zelenskiy over Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries, which Kyiv says are one of its few ways of fighting back after nearly five years of intensive Russian bombardment.
Trump later issued a broad waiver for tougher sanctions on Russia that were meant to have begun this week.
Washington denies withholding intelligence from Kyiv or imposing curbs on Starshield, the military-grade version of SpaceX's Starlink communications system.
Kyiv says the satellite receptors no longer work when mounted on fast-moving objects such as drones. SpaceX boss Elon Musk has said Starshield is controlled by the US government and any limits on its use are ultimately up to Trump.
Western European countries consider defending Ukraine from Russia's invasion to be an existential issue for European security and have strongly backed Zelenskiy, seeking to head off a deeper rupture between Washington and Kyiv.
The United States under Trump has largely stopped providing weapons to Ukraine but lets European countries buy them on Kyiv's behalf. It also provides intelligence and technology that Europe cannot match.
Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Stoere said the goal of hosting Tuesday's Oslo meetings was "to steer the diplomatic efforts onto a more constructive path".
Finland is co-hosting the talks. Finnish President Alexander Stubb said he would attend to discuss "Russia's illegal war of aggression against Ukraine and the overall security situation in Europe."
Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, who has led US negotiating efforts with Witkoff, was expected to attend meetings virtually, Norway said. Zelenskiy, Stubb and Stoere will hold a press conference on Tuesday. REUTERS

articles.title: US investigation, Kiev’s cooperation with drug cartels: SVR statements
articles.body:
MOSCOW, October 20. /TASS/. During an investigation into the illegal activities of Mexican drug cartels, US law enforcement agencies obtained information about their cooperation with representatives of the Kiev regime, the press bureau of the Russian Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR) said in a press release.
TASS has compiled the SVR’s key statements.
Investigation
While investigating the illegal activities of Mexican drug cartels, US law enforcement agencies have obtained information about their cooperation with the Kiev regime: "According to information coming to the SVR, there is a new reason to panic in Kiev. The Ukrainian presidential office has learned that, in the course of a probe into illegal activities of Mexican drug cartels, US law enforcement agencies obtained information about their cooperation with representatives of the Zelensky regime."
The US has found that Mexican criminal groups have been sending militants to Ukraine to receive training in the assembly and combat use of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs): "The Americans have uncovered that criminal groups have, for a long time, been sending their militants to Ukraine to train them in the assembly and combat use of drones. At least 80 individuals have been identified who underwent such training within the ranks of the Ukrainian armed forces."
"Payment for this 'education' was funneled to officials close to [Vladimir] Zelensky, using funds generated by drug traffickers from the sale of illicit substances in the US."
Kiev’s concerns
Kiev recognizes that the presence of trained drone operators within drug cartels poses risks to US officers involved in combating drug trafficking along the border with Mexico: "The Ukrainian presidential office is aware that the presence of trained FPV drone operators within the ranks of drug cartels poses risks to the lives of US security officers involved in anti-drug operations along the border with Mexico."
Risks for Zelensky
Zelensky’s cooperation with drug cartels "could become yet another ‘nail in the coffin’ of his political career."
The Kiev regime’s cooperation with drug cartels, combined with attacks on Russian oil refineries, could push the US past the breaking point and lead to a refusal to assist Zelensky: "This fact comes alongside the abysmal corruption of Ukraine’s gauleiter, his offensive behavior and his disregard for Washington’s more than obvious warnings against targeting Russian oil refineries, as well as his refusal to hold an election. All this, Zelensky’s team fears, may be the last straw for the White House and force it to cancel all support to Kiev’s bloody clown."
Situation with drug cartels
The Kiev regime is stepping up its cooperation with Mexico’s largest drug cartels and facilitating the growth of drug transit from Latin America to Europe, the Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR) reported on June 29.
According to its press release, Ukrainian ports in the Odessa region have become a key transshipment hub for drug trafficking from Latin America to Europe via Poland, Moldova, and Romania.
A video posted on social media earlier allegedly showed Latin American mercenaries from Mexico, Colombia, and Panama serving in the Ukrainian armed forces in a wooded area.
One of the mercenaries shouted a slogan in support of the Jalisco New Generation Cartel and the Los Chapitos group.
According to the Milenio newspaper, which cited national intelligence documents, drug cartels are sending their fighters to Ukraine, where they participate in combat operations under the guise of volunteers to learn how to operate FPV drones.
The newspaper emphasized that members of the Sinaloa and Jalisco New Generation cartels have begun using drones with fiber-optic cables, following the example of Ukrainian servicemen.
This control technology makes the drones immune to the radio signal jammers used by the Mexican security forces.
The Mexican authorities lack the necessary technology and an effective legal framework to combat the drones that drug cartels use to attack civilians, conduct espionage, and smuggle drugs, security experts interviewed by the El Universal newspaper reported.
According to a video released on September 14 by the Donetsk People’s Republic (DPR) branch of the Russian Federal Security Service (FSB), weapons and ammunition supplied by the West to Ukraine end up in the hands of Mexican drug cartels.

articles.title: Trump can strike Iran again. He cannot bomb Hormuz open
articles.body:
A navy can control water. It can’t make a merchant captain sail through it. Warships stop missiles, sure, but no admiral can promise a shipping company that its crew, its cargo and its insurance cover will all survive the next voyage. That gap is the real problem in the US-Iran war, and airstrikes alone won’t close it.
Look at what happened this month. Kpler data shows nearly 20.8 million barrels of oil passed through the strait on 8th October, but only 2.9 million on 11th October. A single day proves little, and Washington disputes independent tracking of the strait anyway. CENTCOM says about 97 percent of ships seeking to transit have done so without being hit. Still, the drop shows how fast a recovery falls apart once crews start to wonder whether passage could be fatal. AFP counted 23 attacks in the first two weeks of October, including six on a single day, the most since the war began, and the IMO says 24 seafarers have died in the area since February. On Saturday, Iran’s Revolutionary Guards said two loaded tankers caught fire after hitting mines, a claim that has not been independently confirmed.
President Donald Trump has said the US will not strike Iran before the 3rd November midterms, while insisting the blockade stays in force. Planners are reportedly readying options, including a massive ordnance air blast bomb, should he give the order. The diplomatic track is not dead, but it is stuck. Trump rejected Iran’s seven-day plan to reopen the strait last month and now speaks of “productive discussions.” On Sunday, Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said the offer is still on the table: if Washington accepts Tehran’s conditions, the strait would open within six days and talks would resume on the seventh. Tehran hasn’t paused in the meantime. Reuters reported that Iran has changed how it picks its targets, and UK maritime authorities have logged attack after attack on tankers and container ships this month. The election may delay the next American bombing run. It does nothing about the bill the world is already paying.
Asia pays the most. Before the war, US Energy Information Administration data showed that 89 percent of the crude oil and condensate passing through Hormuz in the first half of 2025 was bound for Asian markets. China, India, Japan and South Korea took nearly three-quarters of it. The strait also carried over a fifth of the world’s liquefied natural gas.
So when traffic stutters, the damage goes well beyond the oil price. Freight and insurance get dearer, and that lifts the cost of every barrel on arrival. Diesel runs short, which hurts trucking, farming and factories. Gas supplies lurch around, and anyone trying to plan electricity output is left guessing. The International Energy Agency’s October oil market report warned that renewed attacks were threatening the recovery in Gulf exports and that tight diesel markets were already cutting into incomes. And Reuters reported last month that marine fuel in Singapore was still more than 60 percent above prewar prices.
Gulf producers aren’t winning here either. The World Bank forecast this month that GCC economies will shrink by an average of 4.3 percent in 2026, with Qatar down 20.9 percent and Kuwait down 14.6 percent. Its rebound scenario for 2027 assumes the conflict eases by the end of this year, which is a big assumption. If it slips, the numbers get worse. Even Saudi Arabia’s workaround is under strain. Houthi attacks more than halved flows through Bab al-Mandeb in September, pushing Saudi crude back toward Hormuz, where it made up 43 percent of the strait’s oil traffic. Buyers and sellers are both being squeezed, and the Gulf partners Washington says it is defending are paying a good part of the cost.
The usual debate asks what options Trump has left. Keep the blockade and escort ships? Resume strikes? Take Kharg Island? Think about a wider ground war? That’s a list of tools, and a list of tools isn’t a strategy. The real question is whether any of them produces a waterway that commercial operators actually treat as open.
Naval escorts are the mildest option, and they do real work. They deter attacks and keep vital cargo moving. But Iran doesn’t have to beat the US Navy. A few surviving drones, missiles, small boats or mines will do, because they turn every voyage into a gamble. Guarding individual crossings for years isn’t the same as getting normal trade back.
READ: Iran’s IRGC Navy threatens to sink US warships approaching Strait of Hormuz
New air and missile strikes could wreck launch sites, command centres and coastal batteries, and things might go quiet for a while. They might also push Tehran to scatter what weapons it has left and hit softer targets around the Gulf. A Reuters investigation counted at least 135 strikes by Iran and allied forces on 84 infrastructure sites in seven Gulf countries since the war began in February. American force isn’t useless. But Iran can answer damage at home by causing trouble across a much wider regional economy.
Then there’s Kharg Island, which handles roughly 90% of Iran’s oil exports. It looks like a tempting prize, a possible bargaining chip. Yet the island sits only about 16 miles off Iran’s coast, well within reach of attack from the mainland. Take the island and you’ve signed up to defend and supply it, and that’s where the trouble starts. A full invasion would be a burden far out of proportion to the goal of keeping ships safe.
Escalation has a cost elsewhere, too. The Center for Strategic and International Studies estimates that replacing the Tomahawk missiles used in this war could take until late 2030. It doesn’t claim Washington is short of weapons for the Iranian fight. The concern is quieter: every high-end munition fired now is one that won’t be there in a Western Pacific crisis. A decision made in the Gulf ends up with a price tag in Asia.
I don’t think any of this means the United States should live with Iranian coercion of shipping. Attacks on civilian vessels have to stop. Seafarers aren’t bargaining chips. Washington and its partners have good reasons to protect navigation and keep up deterrence. But deterrence with no political way out turns into an expensive habit of managing danger without ever ending it.
So what would work? Something small and checkable, to begin with. Attacks on commercial ships would stop at once, and passage would be monitored and open to all vessels equally. Gulf states, shipowners and the relevant international maritime bodies would agree on how to report incidents and keep ships out of each other’s way. The blockade would ease in stages, each step by one side matched by a step from the other and tied to proof that commitments are being kept. Qatari-mediated exchanges show how far apart Washington and Tehran still are, which is exactly why verification and sequencing matter so much. Nuclear questions and wider regional disputes will still need negotiating. Merchant shipping shouldn’t have to wait for them.
Such a deal wouldn’t hand Iran a veto over Hormuz. It would test Tehran’s behaviour while leaving room to respond if attacks start again. And it wouldn’t guarantee peace. What it would offer is something another bombing campaign can’t: a way to tell whether the strait is getting safe enough for ordinary business to come back.
Asia and the Gulf shouldn’t sit and hope. China, India, Japan and South Korea deal with Washington and Tehran in very different ways, yet they share the same stake with the Gulf states that sit on the other side of the strait. They can press both sides in public for transit rules that can be checked, help with monitoring and incident reporting, and make clear to insurers and shipowners that the lanes will be trusted again only once the attacks end. The countries that take most of the strait’s cargo, and those that ship it, have the strongest claim to a say in how it reopens.
Trump can still order more strikes. He can turn up the pressure, grab territory or declare another tactical win. The harder test is whether he can turn military leverage into a lasting opening of the world’s most sensitive energy corridor. For Asia and the Gulf, that’s the difference between one more show of American firepower and a return to economic security.
Hormuz can’t be bombed back to normal. It has to be made safe enough for the world to trust again.
OPINION: Beyond oil: The Gulf crisis is becoming a food security crisis

articles.title: Houthi missile strike kills 53 Yemeni soldiers, wounds 200 as Saudi Arabia cancels major summit
articles.body:
At least 53 Yemeni soldiers were killed and 200 others wounded Monday when Iran-backed Houthi rebels launched ballistic missiles at a military training camp in southern Yemen, in one of the deadliest attacks since fighting intensified earlier this year, Yemeni military officials said. The strike came as Saudi Arabia canceled a major international investment conference following repeated Houthi attacks on its territory.
The missiles struck a camp in Shabwa province operated by forces loyal to Yemen's internationally recognized, Saudi-backed government. According to a Yemeni military official, the attack occurred as newly recruited soldiers were lining up for a training session. The provincial government warned that the death toll could rise as authorities assessed the casualties.
The Shabwa authorities condemned the strike as a major escalation, saying it had targeted recruits undergoing training and preparation. They called on Yemen's presidential leadership and the Saudi-led coalition to accelerate the deployment of air defense and early warning systems to protect the province against further attacks.
Rashad al-Alimi, chairman of Yemen's Presidential Leadership Council, promised a "firm response," accusing the Houthis of resorting to terrorist attacks when facing military pressure. The rebels acknowledged carrying out the strike, claiming that the camp was operated by Saudi officers and that some had been killed. They provided no evidence to support that assertion, and Saudi authorities did not immediately comment.
The attack marks another escalation in Yemen's civil war, which has intensified since the broader conflict involving Iran began in February. The renewed fighting shattered a ceasefire established in 2022 that had largely halted major hostilities between the Houthis and government forces.
The Houthis, who control Yemen's capital, Sanaa, and much of the country's north, have expanded their military operations in recent weeks, targeting Saudi airports, oil infrastructure and military facilities while also capturing territory along the Red Sea coast near the strategically important Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
On Monday, the rebels claimed to have conducted six additional attacks against Saudi Arabia, including strikes targeting oil facilities, military installations and Riyadh's international airport. They did not specify when the operations occurred. Saudi Civil Defense authorities issued danger alerts, although there were no immediate reports of casualties or damage from those latest claims.
The continuing attacks have begun disrupting major economic events in the kingdom. Saudi Arabia announced Monday that it was canceling an international investment conference scheduled for the following week, which had been expected to attract senior executives from Wall Street and other international financial institutions. The decision underscored the growing consequences of the Houthi campaign for Saudi Arabia's economy and international business activities.
The latest escalation follows a series of deadly incidents inside Yemen. On Sunday, the Houthi-run Health Ministry accused Saudi-led forces of carrying out an airstrike in the rebel-held northern province of Saada that killed at least nine people, including five children and two women. The rebels said additional strikes over the weekend had left more than 30 people dead or wounded. Saudi Arabia did not immediately respond to those allegations.
Saudi Arabia entered Yemen's civil war in 2015 after the Houthis seized Sanaa and large areas of northern Yemen. Riyadh has long viewed the movement's military capabilities and its ties to Iran as a threat to its security. According to U.N. experts, Iran and allied groups in Lebanon and Iraq have provided the Houthis with military expertise, training and advanced weapons, although Tehran denies supplying arms to the rebels.
The conflict has taken on renewed strategic importance as Houthi forces advance near Bab el-Mandeb, a vital maritime chokepoint connecting the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden. Earlier this month, the Saudi-led coalition launched a major offensive aimed at removing the rebels from recently captured territory along the coast.
Meanwhile, the U.S. State Department renewed its demand Monday for the release of more than 20 Yemeni employees of the American Embassy in Sanaa, marking five years since their detention by the Houthis. The embassy suspended operations in 2015, but local employees continued providing security and maintenance services. Washington called for their immediate and unconditional release.

articles.title: Trump 'open to summit with Xi and Putin'
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump said on Monday he is open to three-way arms-control talks with President Xi Jinping and Russian leader Vladimir Putin as soon as next month, raising the prospect of an unprecedented meeting.
"We would have it to talk about nuclear weapons and denuclearisation," Trump told reporters outside the White House. "If President Xi wants to have it, I'd have it. I'm sure we'd talk about other things like trade too."
The Kremlin said earlier that the Russian, Chinese and US leaders could meet at an Asia-Pacific summit in Shenzhen next month, following a Wall Street Journal report that Putin wanted the three-way talks to broker a peace deal favourable to Moscow.
The three leaders have met separately but never held formal talks together.
"I would do it, not so much for Ukraine, because Russia, frankly, has been fine on Ukraine. They haven't been doing much," Trump told reporters when asked if he would attend a meeting with Putin and Xi to discuss Ukraine.
Pressed on whether he would discuss Ukraine at any Xi-Putin summit, Trump replied that he would do "whatever I can do to end the war."
But Trump defended his recent diesel deal with Putin and decision to waive new sanctions on Moscow, which has opened a huge rift with Kyiv and prompted Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky to warn the US leader he is on the wrong side of history.
"Zelensky doesn't know what he's talking about," Trump said when asked about the Ukrainian's comments. "To be honest, I think it's time for somebody else to negotiate on behalf of Ukraine."
Moscow launched one of its broadest air assaults in months overnight, cutting power to more than half a million households and damaging energy infrastructure across Ukraine. Ten people were reported killed.
Kyiv has accused Washington of withholding vital intelligence and slowing speeds on a satellite system used to track incoming strikes.
Last week, Trump told reporters he thought a denuclearisation deal with Russia and China was possible, but that it "doesn't have to be this year." It's not clear how advanced any talks between the countries are.
Russia has the most stored nuclear warheads, followed by the United States and China, according to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute.
The Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty expired earlier this year. The New START treaty, signed in 2010, allowed a single extension, which Putin and former US President Joe Biden agreed to for five years. Any new extension would require an executive decision to voluntarily extend the limits of the treaty.
China's foreign ministry said last week that its "nuclear strength is by no means at the same level with that of the US and Russia" and that it would be "neither fair, reasonable nor realistic to ask China to join the so-called trilateral nuclear disarmament negotiations at this stage."
Trump has already agreed to attend the Apec summit in Shenzhen next month, marking his second trip to China this year and his third visit with Xi over the same period. (Agencies)
Edited by Cecil Wong

articles.title: Yemen forces advance in Taiz; Iran blames US for Hormuz crisis
articles.body:
Yemen forces advance in Taiz; Iran blames US for Hormuz crisis
Yemen’s conflict escalates as Houthi missile strikes kill over 50 in Shabwa, while government forces target rebel positions and Iran urges regional diplomacy.
Yemen's government forces have targeted Houthi positions, vehicles and weapons south of Taiz, as fighting continues to escalate across the country.
More than 50 people were killed and over 200 wounded in a Houthi ballistic missile attack on a military camp in Yemen's Shabwa province, marking the deadliest attack in weeks.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi has blamed the US for insecurity and tensions in the Strait of Hormuz, calling for regional disputes to be resolved through diplomacy.
Speaking alongside Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov, Araqchi also called for a regional security arrangement without the presence of foreign forces.
Hegseth meets Netanyahu in unannounced visit to Israel
US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth met with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu during an unannounced visit to Israel on Monday, Axios reported, citing two sources familiar with the matter.
The Pentagon and Israel's embassy in Washington did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
News of Hegseth's trip comes a day after US President Donald Trump endorsed Netanyahu in next week's parliamentary election in Israel - its first vote since the outbreak of its genocidal war.
Netanyahu's religious-nationalist coalition is projected to lose its governing majority, although the opposition may also struggle to form a government, opinion polls show.
Israel said on Monday it would resume allowing commercial goods shipments into Gaza after a days-long halt over a tax dispute involving Hamas and merchants, restoring a key route for food and other essentials to the aid-dependent enclave.
"The resumption of coordination is being carried out in accordance with Israel's commitment to the humanitarian provisions of the ceasefire agreement," COGAT said.
COGAT said the merchants' accounts had not been independently verified and shipments would resume gradually, with priority given to essential goods ahead of winter.
Israel announces reopening of Kerem Abu Salem crossing
The Israeli government announced the reopening of the Keram Abu Salem crossing, six days after it was closed and truck entry was suspended due to disputes between suppliers and the Ministry of Economy in Gaza over taxes and payment mechanisms.
The Israeli government stated that the resumption of goods imports would be gradual, focusing on essential equipment and materials needed to prepare for winter
Iran summons German ambassador in tit-for-tat move
Iran's foreign ministry on Monday summoned Germany's ambassador to Tehran, accusing Berlin of levelling "baseless political allegations" against the Islamic Republic.
The move to summon ambassador Axel Dittmann was in retaliation for Germany's own decision to summon the Iranian ambassador on Monday over accusations that Tehran was involved in a plot to assassinate pro-Israel public figures.
"Levelling security-related accusations against Iran has long been a tactic employed by the Zionist regime and certain Western nations," Iran's foreign ministry said, in a statement carried by official news agency IRNA.
Germany summoned the Iranian ambassador on Monday, the Foreign Ministry said in a post on X, after a German court sentenced two men for planning to kill the leader of a Jewish organisation in Germany.
The court said last week that one of the men had been steered by Iran's intelligence service.
Later on Monday, Germany's ambassador to Iran was summoned to the ministry of foreign affairs over "baseless accusations," Iranian media reported.
Tunnel discovery near Beirut sparks Hezbollah tensions
Lebanese security forces are investigating a tunnel discovered in a wooded area northeast of Beirut, prompting opposition lawmakers to accuse Hezbollah and demand a wider security crackdown.
However, a Lebanese military source told The New Arab that preliminary findings suggest the tunnel was small and not intended for military or security purposes.
The discovery comes amid heightened tensions over Hezbollah's weapons and continued Israeli attacks on Lebanon.
Pakistan's army chief, General Asim Munir, is due to arrive in Tehran on Tuesday, Iran's semi-official Tasnim news agency reported. There was no Pakistani confirmation of the visit.
Houthis claim attacks on Saudi Aramco site, airports
Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis said on Monday they carried out several attacks against Saudi energy, airport and military targets, including an Aramco site in Yanbu, the Shaybah oilfield, King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh and Abha airport.
Saudi Arabia did not immediately confirm the attacks, and Reuters could not verify the claims.
WFP cuts aid to 500,000 Palestinians in Gaza over funding
The UN World Food Programme has said funding shortages are forcing major cuts to its aid programme in Gaza, leaving about 500,000 people without monthly food support in a territory where two-thirds of the population struggle to get enough to eat.
The WFP said it was reducing the number of recipients of its monthly assistance to 1.1 million people from 1.6 million.
In addition, food rations have been halved, cash assistance has been cut for 75,000 families, and the number of daily hot meals for those unable to cook has fallen to 150,000 from 250,000, with some families in hard-to-reach areas now receiving a hot meal only every other day.
Saudi investment conference to be postponed after attacks
A major Saudi investment conference is set to be postponed, three sources briefed on the matter told AFP on Monday, as the kingdom comes under repeated attacks from Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis.
Saudi Arabia's annual Future Investment Initiative (FII) conference, nicknamed "Davos in the desert" and usually drawing foreign leaders and business titans, was scheduled for Riyadh from 26 to 29 October.
One source said the event "won't happen on time" and that organisers "won't announce a new date soon".
A second source, who confirmed the event would be postponed, added: "Who would be willing to risk flying to Riyadh these days?"
If officially confirmed, the postponement would deal a blow to the kingdom's ambitions to draw foreign capital, diversify its oil-reliant economy and push its reform agenda.
Israel announces arrests after West Bank settler attacks
Israeli police said Monday they had arrested 10 people in the occupied West Bank after settler attacks on an American photographer and a French mayor that drew international condemnation but mixed messages from the government.
In a rare action against rising settler violence, police said they raided several locations across the occupied territory and seized cars and potential evidence related to the attacks.
"Following the severe incidents of violence over the past weekend, including the assault of a media worker and the suspected attacks on foreign civilians, an arrest operation was conducted before dawn," said Major General Moshe Finchi, the Israeli police's West Bank commander.
"Suspects were arrested on suspicion of involvement in the violent incidents, violating a military commander's order concerning a closed military zone, and illegal construction," he said.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi said regional issues should be resolved through diplomacy and blamed the United States for insecurity and tensions in the Strait of Hormuz, speaking at a joint news conference with Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov on Monday.
Araqchi also called for regional countries to work toward a joint security arrangement.
"We welcome any initiative that leads to security from within without the presence of foreign forces, and consider it the right move," Araqchi said.
More than 50 people were killed and over 200 wounded when Yemen's Houthis hit a military camp in energy-rich Shabwa province with ballistic missiles, officials and military sources said on Monday.
It marked the deadliest attack in weeks as fighting between the Iran-backed Houthis and Yemen's internationally recognised, Saudi-supported government escalates after the collapse of a years-long truce.
"More than 53 recruits" were killed and over 200 injured, all new members of the internal security forces who were undergoing training, Shabwa authorities said in a statement.

articles.title: Houthi ballistic missile strike kills at least 53 Yemen govt troops
articles.body:
Houthi rebels killed at least 53 Yemeni government soldiers in a ballistic missile strike on a military camp Monday, one of the deadliest attacks since fighting surged this summer, military officials said.
The attack wounded an additional 200 recruits at the military camp in the southern province of Shabwa, the provincial government there said. The rebels acknowledged targeting the camp.
The fighting between the Houthis and Yemen’s Saudi-backed government forces is a widening front in the Iran war that began in February. The escalation shattered a 2022 cease-fire deal that largely stopped fighting in Yemen’s civil war.
The Houthis have put their growing military capabilities on display on multiple fronts in recent weeks, repeatedly striking Saudi Arabia’s main international airport hundreds of kilometers away and seizing territory inside Yemen near a key shipping chokepoint.
Iran and its allies in Lebanon and Iraq provide expertise, training and sophisticated weapons to the Houthis, according to U.N. and other experts. Iran denies arming the Houthis, which would violate a U.N. embargo.
The provincial government in Shabwa said in a statement that the death toll is preliminary and may rise. It said the recruits were receiving training to be part of internal security forces.
"This bloody, treacherous attack targeted new recruits in the training and preparation phase and is considered an extremely critical military escalation and a blatant aggression on the security and stability of Shabwa province," the statement said.
It called on Yemen’s president, the Saudi-led coalition and the government to expedite air defense and early warning systems to reinforce Shabwa’s capabilities.
The head of Yemen's ruling Presidential Leadership Council, Rashad al-Alimi, promised a "firm response" and said the attack reflects the Houthis' "approach of resorting to cowardly terrorist attacks whenever they face pressures or their Iranian-backed sabotage plots falter."
One Yemeni military official said the missiles struck while recruits were lining up in formation for a training session. The official spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to talk to the media.
On Sunday, an airstrike blamed on Saudi-led forces killed at least nine people in Yemen’s rebel-held northern province of Saada, the Houthi-run Health Ministry said. Five children and two women were killed in the attack, one of several that killed or wounded more than 30 people over the weekend, according to the rebels.
There was no immediate comment from Saudi Arabia.
The Houthis, a Shiite religious and political movement rooted in northern Yemen, are increasingly attacking Saudi Arabia because it supports Yemen’s internationally recognized government in the civil war. The Sunni kingdom, which has long feared the emergence of a well-armed ally of Shiite Iran on its border, joined the war in 2015 after the rebels seized much of northern Yemen, including the capital, Sanaa.
The rebels have been targeting Saudi airports and oil and military facilities. The headquarters of Saudi oil giant Aramco has been struck as well in a blow to the world’s top oil exporter.
The rebels also recently seized more territory along Yemen’s Red Sea coast and near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a crucial shipping alternative to the Strait of Hormuz.
The Saudi-led coalition this month launched a major military offensive to dislodge the rebels from that strategic perch and retake the territory.

articles.title: Zelensky lobbies US senators to pressure Trump – Axios
articles.body:
Zelensky lobbies US senators to pressure Trump – Axios
Vladimir Zelensky has appealed to a bipartisan group of US senators to pressure President Donald Trump into lifting alleged restrictions on US military assistance and intelligence sharing, Axios reported on Monday.
During a virtual meeting with lawmakers led by Republican Senator Thom Tillis and Democrat Richard Blumenthal on Monday, Zelensky complained about alleged disruptions to weapons deliveries, satellite communications, and early warnings of Russian missile attacks, according to a transcript obtained by Axios from Ukrainian officials.
The Ukrainian leader suggested that the Trump administration deliberately “slowed down support” to force Kiev into accepting a negotiated settlement with Moscow.
The lobbying effort comes as Trump has grown increasingly frustrated with Kiev’s refusal to halt attacks on Russian oil refineries, which he blamed for worsening the global diesel shortage and driving up fuel prices for US consumers.
The dispute escalated earlier this month after Trump struck a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to ease restrictions on Russian diesel exports and increase supplies to the global market. Kiev condemned the agreement, accusing Washington of making concessions to Moscow behind Ukraine’s back.
US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner reportedly reminded Ukrainian negotiators during talks in Miami that Washington is supplying Kiev with weapons and intelligence and that Ukraine should not pursue attacks that hurt American consumers. Ukrainian officials interpreted the remarks as a threat to suspend the assistance unless the refinery strikes stop.
The Trump administration has denied issuing any ultimatums. Secretary of State Marco Rubio has rejected claims that the administration deliberately restricted intelligence sharing or Starlink access. The Pentagon has likewise denied changing its intelligence-sharing policy.
Yet Zelensky continued to challenge the administration, telling senators that SpaceX’s Starlink and the US military’s Starshield satellite systems remain partially restricted and that Ukraine missed US early warnings about Russian ballistic missile attacks on three occasions over the past week.
He also accused Secretary of War Pete Hegseth of holding up Patriot interceptor missiles and AIM-9X missiles that NATO countries already purchased for Kiev.
The Washington Post reported that the Pentagon has yet to authorize certain transfers of Patriot missiles from third countries.
Following the meeting, Blumenthal pledged further congressional action, saying bipartisan support for Kiev remains “clear and unequivocal.”
Trump lashed out at Zelensky on Monday, accusing him of obstructing efforts to end the conflict and suggesting that someone else should negotiate on Ukraine’s behalf.
“Zelensky doesn’t know what he’s talking about,” Trump told reporters. “Maybe it’s time for Zelensky to get someone else to negotiate… We’ve given a lot to Ukraine, they’ve given nothing to us.”

articles.title: “Give Us Interceptor Missiles”: Zelenskyy Backs Energy Ceasefire With Russia if US Helps Ukraine
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
“Give Us Interceptor Missiles”: Zelenskyy Backs Energy Ceasefire With Russia if US Helps Ukraine
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has reaffirmed Ukraine’s commitment to maintaining open and transparent relations with the United States, while expressing support for a mutual energy ceasefire with Russia, provided Washington supplies sufficient interceptor missiles to protect Ukrainian energy infrastructure.
In an interview with Corriere della Sera on October 20, Zelenskyy emphasized the importance of honesty and cooperation in Ukraine’s relationship with the United States, according to remarks published on his official Telegram channel.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
“I have always wanted to hide nothing and never lie to the President of the United States. In any case, we have more in common than America does with Russia. Most people in Ukraine and the United States understand this. We would like to continue having the same open, honest, and pragmatic relations with America that we have today,” Zelenskyy said.
The Ukrainian president noted that Kyiv and Washington have maintained strong strategic ties, which have developed particularly actively since the beginning of Russia’s full-scale invasion.
He also expressed gratitude for US assistance, stressing that Ukraine has consistently sought to build its relationship with Washington on honesty, fairness, and transparency.
Addressing the possibility of an energy ceasefire with Russia, Zelenskyy reiterated that Ukraine supports a reciprocal agreement under which both sides would refrain from targeting each other’s energy infrastructure.
However, he stressed that Ukraine must retain the ability to defend itself against Russian attacks, arguing that any restrictions on Ukrainian retaliatory strikes should be accompanied by additional air defense assistance from the United States.
“Our position is very simple. We support a mutual energy ceasefire. If we are talking about not responding against Russian energy facilities after they strike our gas, electricity, oil—everything. The Russians strike. America cannot stop them. Let us believe that America really wants to, but cannot,” Zelenskyy said.
The Ukrainian president added that he was prepared to accommodate US President Donald Trump’s position on limiting attacks against energy infrastructure, but insisted that Ukraine should not be left defenseless.
“Then, as a partner, I am willing to meet President Trump halfway: if they strike us and we cannot respond, that is neither honest nor fair. But if that is what you need, and you cannot restrain Putin, then give us interceptor missiles so I can protect our energy infrastructure. If you could not stop Putin, you helped Ukraine instead,” he stated.
Zelenskyy’s remarks come amid continued Russian strikes on Ukraine’s energy system, highlighting the importance of additional air defense capabilities as Kyiv seeks to protect critical infrastructure.
On October 14, Russian forces struck all three of Kyiv’s combined heat and power plants during a large-scale missile attack that also targeted key energy facilities in Kharkiv and the surrounding region, according to Ukrainian Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi.
Koretskyi said Russian ballistic missiles specifically targeted energy infrastructure in Kyiv, Kharkiv, and the Kharkiv region. Additional strikes hit critical facilities in the Kyiv region responsible for supplying electricity to the capital and central parts of Ukraine.
At the same time, Ukraine’s efforts to strengthen its air defenses have reportedly faced delays in the delivery of US-made interceptor missiles.
According to The Kyiv Independent on October 19, citing a senior Ukrainian official and two military officials familiar with the matter, US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has yet to authorize a substantial shipment of Patriot interceptor missiles to Ukraine.
The reported delay has raised concerns among Ukrainian officials that Washington may be withholding the weapons to exert political pressure on Kyiv, despite Ukraine’s continued reliance on Patriot systems to defend against Russian ballistic missile attacks.
Discuss this article:

articles.title: Rubio assured Zelenskyy: Trump did not issue orders to harm Ukraine - Axios
articles.body:
Rubio assured Zelenskyy: Trump did not issue orders to harm Ukraine - Axios
Kyiv • UNN
Marco Rubio told Zelenskyy that the US had not restricted intelligence, weapons, or Starshield for Ukraine. He explained the delay in Patriot systems by the Pentagon's needs.
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio told Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy during a phone call on Tuesday, October 20, that U.S. President Donald Trump hasn't issued any kind of order to harm Ukraine. Axios reported this, UNN writes.
Details
The conversation, according to the publication, was an attempt to prevent further escalation of the "crisis" between the United States and Ukraine, as well as to refute Ukraine's accusations that Trump is trying to force Zelenskyy to make concessions to russia.
The 45-minute conversation took place several hours before a new round of peace talks with White House envoy Steve Witkoff, aimed at reaching a unified position with European allies on an updated peace proposal to be presented to kremlin head vladimir putin, the publication writes.
The "crisis," the publication writes, erupted 10 days ago when Trump announced a deal with russia on diesel fuel, while his envoys were holding talks with Ukrainian officials in Miami.
On Monday, Zelenskyy, the publication notes, "lobbied a bipartisan group of senators to pressure the Trump administration to reverse what he described as restrictions on intelligence sharing and arms supplies."
Rubio told reporters on Tuesday, October 20, that he "explained to Zelenskyy that the Pentagon had not changed anything regarding intelligence sharing with Ukraine, arms sales, or restrictions on the use of the Starshield satellite system."
"No change was ordered. It is not true that we restricted it," Rubio said.
Rubio, it is noted, "acknowledged to Zelenskyy that there could be a delay in sending Patriot interceptor missiles that have already been paid for by NATO countries." But the reason, he said, "is that the United States must ensure that it has sufficient resources to protect its own military bases around the world."
"Nothing is being deliberately denied. We balance between our obligations to partners and our own needs," he said. "There hasn't been a deliberate political directive to harm Ukraine."
Rubio also claimed that several instances in which Ukraine did not receive advance warning of Russian ballistic missile attacks were the result of technical failures, not a U.S. order.
"No doubt there are tensions," he said. "That is why we had the call. The president is frustrated. The president is responding to the insinuation that he is doing things to deliberately harm Ukraine, which is not fair and not true."
Rubio said that Trump was "angry and frustrated" by the lack of progress in peace talks between russia and Ukraine after two years of efforts.
Meanwhile, Witkoff had already arrived in Oslo on Tuesday for talks with Zelenskyy and European leaders.
Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre, Finnish President Alexander Stubb, representatives of the E4 countries (the United Kingdom, France, Germany, and Poland), and EU and NATO officials are expected to participate in the talks.
After Oslo, Witkoff plans to travel to russia to meet with putin and present ideas developed during consultations with Ukrainian and European leaders.
