He emphasized that achieving this requires the countries of the region to begin a process of building trust with one another.
Use of territory of regional countries against Iran hinders building of trust.
In response to remarks by Qatari officials regarding ensuring regional security and addressing concerns, Baghaei stated that Iran’s expectation of countries in the region is precisely that they take the establishment of a regional mechanism seriously and prevent their territory from being exploited to pose threats against other nations.
Regarding the final statement of the Persian Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) summit and the allegations made against Iran, he stated, "We expect officials from the Persian Gulf littoral states to exercise greater reflection when expressing certain views and positions. We have had bitter experiences, and the repetition of claims—which they themselves know to be untrue—is not a sign of good faith and does nothing to foster trust."
Iran is prepared for any potential action by aggressors.
In response to a question regarding meetings between US officials and regional parties, the Foreign Ministry spokesperson stated that Iran is not currently in a state of peace. Given the existence of a naval blockade against Iran, the country is duty-bound to consider every possibility at any given moment.
He reiterated, "Drawing lessons from past experiences, the defenders of Iran stand ready to repel any act of malice by aggressors."
'Regional security without foreign intervention'
Baghaei rejected allegations that Iran sought dominance over the Strait of Hormuz, saying its approach was oriented towards peace rather than regional hegemony.
Addressing tensions surrounding the strategic waterway, he said the fundamental problem was military aggression by the United States and the Israeli regime against Iran.
He also urged Persian Gulf countries to prevent their territories from being used for staging military aggression against the Islamic Republic, arguing that hosting forces involved in such aggression undermined good-neighborly relations.
“Regional countries have witnessed that the US military presence does not create security. On the contrary, it creates insecurity,” he said, and reiterated Tehran’s support for dialogue among regional countries.
MNA/6983708

articles.title: Zelensky should get ‘somebody else’ to negotiate to end Ukraine war, Trump says
articles.body:
Zelensky accuses US of delaying missiles as Trump calls for new Ukraine negotiator
Public clash deepens after US president defends Russian diesel deal and says wartime leader ‘doesn’t know what he’s talking about’
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky accused the United States on Monday of deliberately delaying the delivery of interceptor missiles to his country, as tensions between Kyiv and Washington escalated over military aid and intelligence sharing.
Kyiv said it had no early warning of powerful Russian missile strikes, echoing similar claims made last week.
Speaking to US senators on Monday, Zelensky said “the Pentagon is delaying the delivery of missiles” already paid for by European countries and that the shipment was waiting for US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth’s signature.
He also said several European countries were ready to transfer Patriot interceptor missiles from their own stockpiles but were still awaiting US approval.

articles.title: Pezeshkian calls for stronger Iran-Russia cooperation to advance peace and multilateralism
articles.body:
Pezeshkian calls for stronger Iran-Russia cooperation to advance peace and multilateralism
TEHRAN – Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian has called for faster implementation of agreements between Tehran and Moscow, citing energy, transport, trade and power generation as priority areas for expanding bilateral cooperation.
Pezeshkian made the remarks on Monday during a meeting with Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov in Tehran, where the two sides discussed the strategic partnership between the countries, the implementation of existing agreements and developments in the region and beyond.
The president said the two countries could play an effective role in strengthening peace, sustainable security and a multilateral international order by drawing on their shared capabilities and regional and international mechanisms.
The Iranian president welcomed the continued expansion of relations between Tehran and Moscow, stressing the need to deepen bilateral cooperation, strengthen political and diplomatic coordination, and ensure that previously reached agreements translate into practical results.
Referring to his recent meetings and telephone conversations with Russian President Vladimir Putin, Pezeshkian said the two leaders had been following up on bilateral understandings, implementation plans and joint projects through ongoing consultations. He expressed hope that his upcoming visit to Moscow would help advance the agreements and produce tangible outcomes in areas of mutual interest.
He also thanked the Russian president, government and people for their support and solidarity during the recent war against Iran, emphasizing the importance of continued mutual support and closer political and diplomatic cooperation in pursuit of the two countries’ shared interests.
Turning agreements into practical projects
Pezeshkian also highlighted understandings reached on the Caspian Sea and trade as a foundation for expanding economic and regional engagement. He said agreements in energy, transport and power generation should move towards implementation through clearly defined operational arrangements, practical mechanisms and specific timelines.
The president’s remarks underscored Tehran’s emphasis on translating the strategic partnership into concrete projects rather than allowing bilateral understandings to remain at the level of political commitments. He said the upcoming visit to Russia would provide an opportunity to pursue this objective.
Energy cooperation, transport links, trade and power generation were identified as key priorities, alongside broader coordination through regional and international organizations. Pezeshkian argued that stronger economic ties between Iran and Russia could serve the interests of both countries while creating wider opportunities for regional cooperation.
Iran calls for a regional approach to peace and security
Pezeshkian also condemned the recent US-Israeli military aggression against Iran, saying the killing of the Leader of the Islamic Revolution, military commanders, scientists and schoolchildren, as well as attacks on the country’s infrastructure, had no justification under legal or international standards. He stressed that the attacks took place while Iran was pursuing dialogue and diplomatic engagement.
The president said Iran would not accept a situation in which a country used its military power and instruments of pressure to impose its will on other nations. Tehran, he said, sought an international order founded on mutual respect, the rights of nations, constructive cooperation and multilateralism. He added that Iran and Russia shared common ground on these principles.
Pezeshkian also stressed that Iran had no fundamental disagreements with countries in the region, pointing to the historical, cultural and religious ties linking Iran with its neighbors and other Muslim nations. He said Tehran remained committed to developing relations through dialogue, fraternity and mutual cooperation, and was ready to address existing challenges through understanding and regional mechanisms.
He said US intervention and divisive policies have contributed to tensions in the region. The president also criticized the presence of US military bases in regional countries, arguing that they had brought greater tension, division and insecurity rather than lasting stability.
Pezeshkian said sustainable regional security should be based on mutual trust, the participation of regional countries and respect for the legitimate interests of all parties. Iran, he added, welcomed joint initiatives with neighboring states in peace and security, economic development, cultural and scientific cooperation, and people-to-people exchanges.
His remarks placed regional diplomacy and cooperation among neighboring countries at the center of Tehran’s approach to security, rather than reliance on external military deployments.
Multilateral institutions as platforms for cooperation
Elsewhere in his remarks, Pezeshkian said developments in the international system had made it increasingly necessary to move beyond unilateral approaches and strengthen inclusive mechanisms for cooperation. Iran, he stressed, was determined to play an active role in building a fairer multilateral order based on mutual respect.
He pointed to Russia, China and other members of the BRICS group, the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) and the Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU) as having considerable potential to expand economic, political and security cooperation and strengthen the role of multilateral institutions in international affairs.
The president called for making fuller use of these platforms to expand economic engagement, facilitate trade, develop transport and transit infrastructure, and deepen regional cooperation. He said closer Iran-Russia relations, combined with the effective implementation of bilateral agreements and the use of regional and international mechanisms, could advance shared interests and strengthen cooperation at both regional and global levels.
Lavrov reaffirms Moscow’s commitment to the partnership
Lavrov, for his part, briefed Pezeshkian on his meetings with senior Iranian officials and said the discussions had covered political, economic, commercial and cultural ties. He reaffirmed Moscow’s intention to expand cooperation in oil and gas, energy, transport, communications, media, culture, science and higher education.
The Russian foreign minister also emphasized the alignment of Iranian and Russian views on international issues and the importance of continued diplomatic consultations to promote peace and security. Referring to agreements concerning the Caspian Sea, he called for closer coordination to protect the two countries’ interests and strengthen regional cooperation.
Araghchi calls talks with Lavrov ‘intensive’ and ‘productive’
Earlier on Monday, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi held talks with Lavrov, describing the discussions as “intensive” and “productive”. The two diplomats reviewed bilateral relations under the Comprehensive Strategic Partnership Treaty, as well as developments in the Persian Gulf, the Caucasus, Ukraine and West Asia.
Araghchi said Tehran and Moscow agreed that regional disputes required political solutions rather than military action. They also discussed Palestine, Lebanon, Yemen, security in the Strait of Hormuz and recent incidents involving commercial vessels and port infrastructure in the Caspian Sea.
Both sides reaffirmed their opposition to unilateralism and their commitment to multilateral cooperation through international institutions, including BRICS and the SCO. Lavrov reiterated Russia’s commitment to its agreements with Iran, citing humanitarian assistance and the gradual return of Russian specialists to the Bushehr nuclear power plant. He also said Moscow intended to continue implementing its economic and investment commitments to Tehran.
Lavrov expressed hope that Pezeshkian would visit Russia in the coming days to attend a summit of the Gas Exporting Countries Forum in Moscow, providing another opportunity to advance bilateral cooperation.

articles.title: Chemical brother: Russia’s production of explosives and ammunition is heavily dependent on Chinese chemicals
articles.body:
Russia’s explosives production relies heavily on imported chemicals from China. The Insider identified the key reagents used by Russia’s defense industry, the foreign companies supplying them, and the chemicals most critical to explosives production — including plasticizers, binders, acids, and stabilizers.
The Insider has previously reported that Russia’s chemical industry remains heavily dependent on foreign equipment, technology, and catalysts. That reliance is especially pronounced in the defense sector, where ammunition production depends on imported auxiliary components.
According to the available data, Russia imported more than $1 billion worth of chemical products in the first quarter of 2025, totaling 347,000 metric tons. China accounted for 87% of those imports, followed by Indonesia and India. The statistic accounts for imported chemicals but does not make a distinction between shipments that were intended for civilian or military use; however, many of the chemicals imported have clear military uses.
Components for explosives
Plasticizer
Explosives are central to modern warfare, and producing plastic explosives from RDX or HMX requires a binder, or plasticizer. One such plasticizer is dioctyl sebacate, which Russian manufacturers produce using imported sebacic acid.
In 2025, the Roshal Plasticizer Plant bought sebacic acid from Chinese supplier Farmasino Co., Ltd. As customs records show, the plant specified that the chemical was intended for production of dioctyl sebacate rather than for pharmaceutical use.
Binders
One binder used in explosives and imported by Russia is polyisobutylene. It is brought into the country in a form that is ready for use in explosives production.
In 2025, the Azot-Vzryv group purchased polyisobutylene in China from Nanjing E-Strong Technical Co., Ltd., through a Kazakh intermediary, Nartas LLP of Almaty. Azot-Vzryv has long supplied the Sverdlov Plant, a major Russian defense chemical enterprise in Dzerzhinsk, Nizhny Novgorod region. As far as is known, the plant is virtually the only Russian producer of military high explosives based on RDX.
Additionally, a polymer made from butadiene and acrylonitrile is used as a binder in solid rocket propellant. The Perm Gunpowder Plant consumes about 1,600 metric tons of acrylonitrile every six months. Of that amount, 600 tons reach Russia from Belarus, from a plant in Novopolotsk.
Acetic acid
Acetic acid is also needed to synthesize RDX. In Russia, it is produced in Nevinnomyssk. Since Nevinnomyssky Azot is the only Russian producer of high-purity synthetic acetic acid, it is regularly targeted by Ukrainian drones. Chinese supplies help fill the gap, accounting for about 20% of deliveries.
Dozens of tons of nonfood-grade acetic acid were ordered by the Altai Region’s Pioneer Trade LLC (which has taken part in tenders to supply the Perm Gunpowder Plant) and by Bina Group LLC (a regular supplier to the Perm Gunpowder Plant and NMZ Iskra, which manufactures fuzes). The acid was supplied by Chinese companies Eli-X (Qingdao) Chem Co. and Taizhou Ruibai Chemical Co.
Stabilizers
Diphenylamine is needed to prevent nitrocellulose propellant from degrading. It is used as a stabilizer and is produced from aniline. China supplies a significant share of Russia’s needs for the substance.
As The Insider reported last year, Chinese chemical producer Jiangsu Feiya Chemical Industry was among the companies supplying diphenylamine to Russia, with buyers including firms in St. Petersburg and Bashkortostan.
Fibers and composites
Composite materials are widely used in modern weapons. Their production requires aniline, which is then used to make aramid fibers.
One major Russian recipient of aniline is SPG-Kompozit. The company makes composite shelters for radar and navigation systems, polymer ammunition containers, and modular military structures.
Aramid fibers are also needed for missile bodies. For environmental and economic reasons, aniline production in Russia virtually ceased after 2016, but the authorities are trying to restart it. For example, Alfa-Bank has allocated 11.9 billion rubles ($143.8 million) to launch an innovative aniline plant based at Chapaevsk Aniline Plant JSC.
For now, however, Russia continues to import aniline and aniline derivatives from China. The main suppliers are Jilin Kangxin Chemical Industry Trade, Shandong S-Sailing Chemical, and Shandong Near Chemical. Buyers include SPG-Kompozit LLC, SZ HK AK Bars-Development LLC, and Albatros LLC.
Other chemicals important to the military industry
Among the main imported reagents used in Russia’s chemical and related industries (including both civilian and military production) are raw materials and additives for polymers, synthetic fibers, plastics, and rubber.
Antioxidants and flame retardants are particularly important in this sector because they are generally among the most difficult products to manufacture domestically.
Russia also imports large quantities of alcohols, including propyl alcohol and methallyl alcohol, as well as other substances such as butyl glycol, methyl ethyl ketone, perchloroethylene, and dimethyl sulfoxide. They are generally used without chemical modification — either in pure form or as ingredients in more complex products.
Surfactants and flotation agents used in mining and oil production are also important for export-oriented industries.
Who supplies the chemicals
Chinese companies supply virtually all of these chemicals to Russia. In most cases, they also manufacture the products themselves.
Despite repeated calls for developing domestic production capabilities, Russia’s chemical industry remains heavily dependent on foreign suppliers, particularly for medium- and small-volume specialty chemicals. As a result, the more effectively Ukrainian drones are able to strike chemical production facilities inside Russia, the greater the dependence on imports becomes.
China’s role is critical, particularly when it comes to Russia’s access to plasticizers, antioxidants, flame retardants, and other polymer additives.

articles.title: Iran prolongs talks in stalemate to influence US midterms, officials say
articles.body:
Iran prolongs talks in stalemate to influence US midterms, officials say
DUBAI, Oct 20 - Iran has deliberately prolonged talks with the US to try to weaken Donald Trump politically ahead of November's US midterm elections, senior officials say, while fears of renewed military action and deep distrust of Washington have reinforced Tehran's reluctance to strike a quick deal to end the war.
Three senior Iranian officials and an Iranian insider, speaking on condition of anonymity, said Tehran was convinced the US president was ready to resort to renewed attacks to try to break the stalemate in the eight-month-old war.
"Iran is preparing for renewed Israeli and US attacks, not for a deal with America to end the war," one of the officials said. "The clerical establishment is determined not to give Trump a political victory."
Tehran analyst Saeed Leylaz said that, by prolonging the talks, "Iran is influencing the US election without taking any unlawful action".
IRAN CAN EXPLOIT TRUMP'S POLITICAL PROBLEMS
The war, which began in February when the US and its ally Israel launched strikes on Iran, has helped drive Trump’s approval rating to a record low as polls suggest that Americans worried about high gasoline prices will punish his Republican Party in the November 3 congressional elections.
Trump has repeatedly said he expects oil prices to drop after the elections, but has not offered a detailed plan to end the war and reopen the Strait of Hormuz, a vital global energy shipping route effectively closed by Iran since the war began.
Iranian attacks both threatened and real have kept ship traffic through the strait to a trickle, while a US maritime blockade and trade sanctions have cut off Iran's oil export revenues and exacerbated growing domestic economic woes.
With Tehran refusing to make concessions it believes could benefit Trump politically, there is little chance of a breakthrough before the elections, the officials said.
Under pressure from Israel, Washington wants Iran’s decades-long nuclear programme - which Iran says is purely peaceful and Western powers allege has military dimensions - on the table from the outset.
For its part, Tehran insists that its conditions under a "seven-day plan" must be met before nuclear negotiations begin. And it offers no prospect of giving up the leverage over the Strait of Hormuz that the conflict prompted it to seize.
Iran's Foreign Ministry and the US White House did not respond to Reuters requests for comment.
IRAN CANNOT TRUST WASHINGTON, OFFICIALS SAY
Iran’s proposal, conveyed through Qatari mediators, offered to reopen the strait within seven days, albeit under Iranian control, provided that Washington lifted its maritime blockade, eased restrictions on Iranian oil exports, released frozen assets and ended hostilities on all fronts.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi said on Sunday that the offer remained on the table, with messages being exchanged through mediators.
Tehran's view that Washington cannot be trusted to commit to diplomacy stems from the attacks on Iran that have derailed previous negotiations, one Iranian official said.
In June 2025, an Israeli attack wrecked plans for a sixth round of US-Iran nuclear talks in Oman. And last February, the US and Israel launched their war just after another round of talks ended, with further technical discussions scheduled.
Maintaining a state somewhere between war and peace through the US midterms allows Iran to sustain pressure on Washington while reiterating its commitment to diplomacy.
Trump has said the US will not bomb Iran again before November 3. However, the officials said Tehran continues to expect that bombing will resume, sooner or later.
Alex Vatanka, director of the Iran program at the Middle East Institute in Washington, said the clerical establishment clearly wanted to hurt Trump politically.
"But the fundamental issue is that Tehran believes that Trump is interested in regime change ... and following Israeli Prime Minister (Benjamin) Netanyahu’s policy of seeking to bring down Iran’s ruling establishment," he said.
US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth discussed Iran with Netanyahu on Monday, three Israeli officials said, in an unannounced visit to Israel a week before a parliamentary election in which Netanyahu's position is at risk.
RETURN TO PREWAR STATUS IMPOSSIBLE FOR IRAN, SAYS ANALYST
Iran’s strategy of keeping negotiations alive without rushing towards agreement comes at a cost.
Prolonged uncertainty is weighing on Iran’s already crippled economy and wearing down public patience. Thousands were killed at the turn of the year when the security forces crushed spiralling anti-government protests.
Annual inflation hit 73.6% in September, according to the Statistical Centre of Iran, and the rial currency has fallen nearly 35% against the dollar since Washington reapplied its naval blockade in July.
Iran’s seaborne crude exports fell to zero in the second week of September from a 14-day average of 230,000 barrels per day at the start of the month, and remained there as of October 5, according to energy intelligence platform Vortexa.
But the leadership's distrust of Washington extends beyond the current conflict to existential concerns. Iran believes the US has repeatedly broken agreements even when Tehran honoured its commitments, Leylaz said, leaving little confidence that any comprehensive deal would endure.
“Reaching a sustainable deal with the US, even after the Trump administration, is no longer possible because of the deepened distrust,” Leylaz said. "Nothing will go back to the pre-war status quo." REUTERS

articles.title: Kremlin hawks savour Trump-Zelenskiy rift — if it lasts
articles.body:
Kremlin hawks savour Trump-Zelenskiy rift — if it lasts
MOSCOW, Oct 19 - Kremlin hawks are savouring a public rift between Donald Trump and Volodymyr Zelenskiy after a damaging week for Ukraine's president and a beneficial one for Russia, but the champagne is still on ice in Moscow.
While welcoming strains in Kyiv's relationship with its most important ally, Moscow regards the US president's behaviour as unpredictable and European leaders rallied behind Zelenskiy at a summit last week.
There has also been no end to Ukrainian drone attacks on Russia, most US sanctions remain in place on Moscow over Ukraine and Trump's actions can be seen in the light of November's midterm elections to Congress.
On the surface, there was plenty for Russian hawks to revel in after Trump repeatedly criticised the Ukrainian leader, who hit back at him, prompting the US president to say "it's time for Ukraine to get a new president".
"The ‘Man of the Year’ and the ‘new Churchill’ has been branded by his former master as a hindrance to peace and to US interests. After all, he bit the hand that fed him until it bled," former President Dmitry Medvedev, now deputy chairman of Russia's Security Council, wrote sarcastically on Telegram.
Kirill Dmitriev, President Vladimir Putin's point man for economic deals with Washington, reposted an image showing a bear symbolising Russia alongside an eagle representing the US and both creatures confronting Britain — in the form of a lion — and the European Union.
The image was captioned "Things Have Changed."
Dmitriev said he believed Zelenskiy's decision to criticise Trump had backfired, adding on X: "Zelensky overplayed his hand, and his hubris and attacks on President Trump will have significant consequences."
SCEPTICISM
Trump said on October 9 he had reached a deal with Putin to temporarily lift sanctions on Russian fuel and import Russian diesel and last week skipped new sanctions on Russia's oil buyers. In Kyiv, Ukrainian complaints about disruption to US intelligence sharing prompted talk of US betrayal.
But there appears to be a consensus in Moscow that the Trump-Zelenskiy rift has not yet delivered significant benefits.
Sergei Mironov, parliamentary leader of the pro-Kremlin Just Russia party, saw the rift as an attempt to "play to a domestic audience ahead of the Congressional elections."
"The US President needs cheap fuel prices for his voters. He also needs a scapegoat – someone onto whom he can shift the blame for price rises," he said. "But the point is that all this has little to do with Russia’s interests.”
Some Russians are also wary of what they see as frequent U-turns by Trump.
Moscow initially saw Trump's hosting of Putin in Alaska last year as a breakthrough that might lead to a peace deal in Ukraine on Russia's terms. But, like Trump's first term in office, the summit is increasingly seen as a disappointment.
The impact of the diesel deal may also be limited, as the export volumes — at least initially — are relatively small and Moscow taxes fuel production rather than exports, limiting the uplift for Russia's budget.
Trump’s decision to skip sanctions on Russian oil buyers — primarily China and India — is also not seen in Russia as a great gift, or as surprising, as such a move would increase oil prices at the very moment he wants to lower them.
A more tangible benefit to Russia may be Kyiv's complaints that it has not received recent warnings of Russian missile strikes and that there have been limits on the US Starshield system, which Ukraine uses for battlefield communications.
Writing for state media outlet RT, commentator Sergey Poletaev said Russia must be patient.
"For Russia, the task is to recognise this developing reality without mistaking it for an immediate victory," he said. "Zelenskiy has made his choice, the only question left is how long Washington will tolerate the consequences." REUTERS

articles.title: U.S. Defense Secretary Hegseth meets Netanyahu, Katz in unannounced Israel visit
articles.body:
U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth made an unannounced visit to Israel on Monday and met with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Defense Minister Israel Katz as the two countries discuss the possibility of renewing their war against Iran, an Israeli official told Haaretz.
The Pentagon did not announce Hegseth's visit in advance, and two sources familiar with the matter and a U.S. official told CNN that it had not been planned. Hegseth's office declined to comment on the report, while Netanyahu's office did not respond to a request for comment.
The visit comes after a report on CNN last week that the U.S. military has developed new strike plans against Iran that include the possible use of the GBU-43/B, known as the "mother of all bombs," to target the country's energy infrastructure and nuclear sites.
Hegseth said in a social media post that he had visited U.S. service members in the Central Command area of responsibility, which covers the Middle East, northeast Africa and parts of Asia.
News of Hegseth's trip also comes a day after U.S. President Donald Trump endorsed Netanyahu in next week's parliamentary election in Israel - its first vote since the Hamas attack on October 7, 2023, that shook the country and plunged the Middle East into turmoil, as Israel went to war in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran.
The president said it was only "a matter of time" before Iran acted on its promise to attack Israel and the United States. "If they don't change their ways, and fast, we will finish the job," he added. "If Israel had the wrong leader, anyone other than Bibi, the U.S. would have to do the job itself, and I don't want to do that."
U.S. Vice President JD Vance, however, declined to endorse Netanyahu in an interview earlier on Monday, saying he was not getting involved in Israeli elections.
"I endorse American candidates, and that's where I'm focused on is the midterms," Vance, who traveled to Budapest and endorsed Viktor Orban in Hungarian election earlier this year, said in an interview with digital media outlet 2WAY.
"I'm not anti-endorsing him, but I'm not pro-endorsing him, I'm not getting involved in Israeli elections." Vance said.
Q: Trump endorsed Netanyahu. Do you endorse Netanyahu? JD Vance: I endorse American candidates. I'm not getting involved in Israeli elections.

articles.title: Ukraine Seeks Insider Tips on Networks Supplying Western Electronics to Russia’s Weapons Factories
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine Seeks Insider Tips on Networks Supplying Western Electronics to Russia’s Weapons Factories
Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence (HUR) is seeking information about networks that help Russian defense manufacturers obtain foreign-made electronics and dual-use technologies despite international sanctions.
The agency has appealed to employees of manufacturing, logistics, and trading companies, as well as individuals familiar with illicit procurement schemes, to provide information that could help identify supply chains supporting Russia’s weapons production.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to HUR, Russian military-industrial enterprises continue to acquire Western electronic components and technologies necessary for manufacturing modern weapons, despite restrictions imposed on Moscow.
To circumvent sanctions, Russian companies reportedly rely on intermediaries, shell companies, and complex supply routes passing through third countries.
Ukrainian intelligence is particularly interested in identifying foreign suppliers of microelectronics and dual-use goods, companies acting as intermediaries, and Russian manufacturers purchasing these products for weapons production.
The agency is also seeking details about transportation routes and transit countries used to deliver restricted components to Russia.
The appeal comes amid continued Russian attacks on Ukrainian cities. According to HUR, more than 100 Ukrainian civilians have been killed and over 400 others, including children, injured in Russian strikes over the past week.
The attacks have affected residential buildings, passenger buses, shopping and business centers, and schools, the agency reported.
HUR said information about individual suppliers, intermediaries, or transportation routes could help identify broader procurement networks and expose companies involved in circumventing international sanctions.
The agency has encouraged individuals with relevant information to submit it confidentially through its secure Main Intelligence Bot, emphasizing that even isolated details could help trace supply chains used to obtain foreign technologies for Russian weapons manufacturing.
Ukraine’s military intelligence has also previously documented the presence of foreign-made components in Russian weapons systems, including the Kometa anti-jamming navigation modules installed in missiles, attack drones, and guided aerial bombs.
According to HUR, these modules are designed to protect onboard navigation equipment from electronic warfare interference, enabling Russian weapons to maintain navigation capabilities even in environments affected by electronic countermeasures.

articles.title: Reuters: Kushner and Witkoff to travel to Norway for Ukraine talks
articles.body:
Reuters: Kushner and Witkoff to travel to Norway for Ukraine talks
Jared Kushner, US President Donald Trump's son-in-law, and Steve Witkoff, US Special Envoy for the Middle East, are expected to take part in the next round of talks on ending the war in Ukraine,to be held in Norway this week.
Source: Reuters, citing people familiar with the matter
Details: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy is expected to take part in the meetings.
The talks will take place amid rising tensions between Washington and Kyiv over restrictions on Starshield and intelligence sharing.
In addition, one person familiar with the matter said US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has still not authorised the delivery of the latest package of US weapons purchased by NATO allies under the PURL programme The Prioritised Ukraine Requirements List (PURL) programme allows NATO allies to finance purchases of US-made weapons for Ukraine. .
However, the source could not confirm whether the package included missiles for Patriot air defence systems.
The White House has not yet officially commented on the information.
Background:
- On 18 October, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy accused US President Donald Trump of trying to pressure Ukraine into capitulating to Russia and delaying deliveries of interceptor missiles for Patriot air defence systems.
- On 19 October, Trump accused Zelenskyy of supposedly never having wanted to end Russia's war against Ukraine.

articles.title: Congressman from Trump's party threatens administration with consequences over Starshield restrictions for Ukrainian Armed Forces
articles.body:
Congressman from Trump's party threatens administration with consequences over Starshield restrictions for Ukrainian Armed Forces
US Representative Brian Fitzpatrick (Republican) has warned that those involved in restricting Ukraine's use of the Starshield program will be held fully accountable.
Source: European Pravda, citing Fitzpatrick on X (Twitter)
Details: The congressman announced talks with President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and his team this week to discuss the Starshield program, sanctions, and other matters pertaining to the defence of Ukraine.
Fitzpatrick noted that during the conversation, he will assure Zelenskyy that US officials involved in restricting the program for Ukraine will face consequences from Congress.
Quote from Fitzpatrick: "I will be assuring President Zelenskyy that anyone who attempts to limit the use of Starshield for Ukraine will be fully investigated and will be held fully accountable, to include public congressional oversight hearings, and immediate harsh and punitive budget cuts to any responsible agency or agency head."
Details: Fitzpatrick mentioned his bill, the Ronald Reagan Peace Through Strength Act, which aims to prevent US President Donald Trump from unilaterally lifting sanctions on Russian oil. He expressed confidence that the House of Representatives will approve this initiative.
Quote from Fitzpatrick: "The United States must provide any and all defensive equipment that Ukraine needs to defend itself. The United States must not import a single drop of Russian oil. Sanctions against the Russian regime must be harsher and stronger than they've ever been before. Each and every one of these items will be brought to the House Floor – and each and every one of these items will pass on the House Floor by an overwhelming margin.
This is, after all, what Ronald Reagan would do. And this is what we will do now. Ukraine can, and will, defeat Russia."
Details: Fitzpatrick reiterated that Ukraine is an indispensable ally of the US, while Russia is an enemy of Washington, and assured Kyiv of continued support.
Background:
- Following the US-Russia "diesel deal", Congressman Brian Fitzpatrick introduced a bipartisan bill that he says will prevent Trump from lifting sanctions; it was named the Ronald Reagan Peace Through Strength Act.
- US Republican Senator Thom Tillis is seeking an investigation into the Pentagon's actions with regard to problems with Starlink satellite communications systems encountered by the Ukrainian Armed Forces.
- Meanwhile, US President Donald Trump claims he did not give an order to restrict Ukraine's access to SpaceX's Starshield satellite technology.

articles.title: Chinese military vessels and spy drones track Keen Sword war games off Japan
articles.body:
Chinese military vessels and spy drones track Keen Sword war games off Japan
Surveillance coincides with US anti-ship missiles and Japanese long-range weapons deploying near Taiwan during exercises
Three People’s Liberation Army military aircraft – two drones and a reconnaissance plane – flew through international airspace between Japanese islands into the Pacific before heading back towards mainland China on Monday, prompting Japan to scramble fighter jets, the Joint Staff Office of Japan’s defence ministry reported the same day.
In addition, a TB-001 reconnaissance and attack drone passed between Yonaguni Island and Taiwan, flew northeast as far as waters off Amami Oshima, then turned back and passed through the Miyako Strait towards mainland China, the post said.
The aircraft movements coincided with Monday’s start of “Keen Sword”, a biennial joint military exercise between Japan and the United States running until October 29 across multiple locations in Japan. The exercise will involve about 45,000 Japanese Self-Defence Forces personnel and 12,000 US troops, making it one of the biggest drills ever conducted by the two allies.

articles.title: The very stable genius, nine years later
articles.body:
In January 2018, after a book questioned his mental fitness, the president of the United States sat down and wrote his own diagnosis.
“My two greatest assets have been mental stability and being, like, really smart,” he tweeted. “I think that would qualify as not smart, but genius. And a very stable genius at that!”
He was 71 years old.
Nearly nine years and one reelection later, the self-assessment has not moved an inch. The facts around it have.
Start with the war he promised would never happen.
Trump campaigned twice on ending American wars, not starting them. In January, the US military struck targets across Venezuela and extracted President Nicolás Maduro, who now sits in a New York jail awaiting trial on narco-terrorism charges.
The operation followed months of strikes on small boats in the Caribbean. Well over 100 people were killed on suspicion, never proof, of drug trafficking.
Months later came Iran, a war the administration still calls “Operation Epic Fury.”
Trump recently told a rally crowd that the United States had lost “18 incredible people” in that war. Reporting by The Washington Post placed the true figure at 22 or higher.
Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth called the Post’s reporting “a complete LIE.”
The two numbers have never been reconciled.
Then there is the money.
Qatar gave Trump’s government a $400 million Boeing 747 to use as Air Force One. The aircraft was painted navy and gold to suit his taste. Trump has said it will eventually go to his presidential library when he leaves office.
READ: Lavrov says Trump’s Gaza plan remains ‘ink on paper,’ calls for Palestinian statehood
At home, he gutted the East Wing of the White House to make room for a gold-leafed ballroom costing $300 million. He covered the Oval Office in gilt cherubs and molding, creating what his own press secretary called “a golden office for the golden age.”
Critics have used different words: tacky, gaudy, a monument to ego.
On the campaign trail this fall, Trump has promised every American adult a $5,000 “dividend” if Republicans retain control of Congress in November.
It echoes two earlier promises. One offered Americans $2,000 from tariff revenue. The other promised an unspecified share of “DOGE savings.” Both were announced with fanfare. Neither was paid.
Polling suggests that most Americans do not believe this dividend will be paid either. In one recent survey, only 17 percent of adults said Trump generally keeps his promises.
His relationship with the truth is not incidental to his politics. It is the engine of it.
For decades, Trump has told audiences that he graduated first in his class at the Wharton School. The university’s own records from 1968 show that he made neither the Dean’s List nor any honors roll.
He has also said repeatedly, including as recently as this March during a meeting with Germany’s chancellor, that his father was born in “a very wonderful place in Germany.”
Fred Trump was born in the Bronx. It was Trump’s grandfather who emigrated from Germany.
These are not policy disagreements or competing interpretations of history. They are verifiable facts about his own life. He has overwritten them in public, repeatedly, at no apparent cost.
The self-praise runs in a straight line from that 2018 tweet to the present.
Trump has told voters for years, in one formulation after another, that he knows more than America’s generals, more than its diplomats, more than its intelligence agencies.
In 2018, standing beside Vladimir Putin in Helsinki, Trump was asked whether he believed the conclusion of his own intelligence community that Russia had interfered in the 2016 election, or Putin’s denial.
“I don’t see any reason why it would be,” Russia, he replied.
He spent the following week trying, unconvincingly, to recast the remark as a simple misstatement.
The pattern recurs across his biography and in matters of war and peace: a confident assertion, a contradiction from the record, and no meaningful reckoning with the distance between them.
Three wars into a presidency that promised none, Trump’s instinct to trust his own judgment over everyone else’s has survived every piece of evidence that might have revised it.
That pattern is what a group of mental health professionals has spent nine years trying to name.
In 2017, Yale psychiatrist Bandy Lee assembled 27 colleagues for “The Dangerous Case of Donald Trump.” They argued that they had a “duty to warn” the public, despite professional norms against diagnosing public figures from a distance.
OPINION: Trump could lose Congress and still expand the US war on Iran
Psychologist John Gartner, one of the contributors, has been more direct. For years, he has described Trump as a “malignant narcissist,” a term coined by psychoanalyst Erich Fromm to describe leaders who are grandiose, paranoid, and remorseless.
In 2024, more than 230 mental health professionals signed a public letter repeating the warning ahead of the election.
None of this constitutes a formal diagnosis. The signatories are explicit that it cannot. Trump has never submitted to an evaluation.
Yet the consistency of the assessment, sustained across nine years and echoed by dozens of credentialed observers, is itself a kind of data point.
So is the legal record.
Trump was indicted four times in 2023 on a combined 88 felony counts. He became the first former American president ever charged with a crime.
In New York, he was convicted on all 34 counts in the hush-money case.
He did not go to prison.
Having won reelection in the meantime, Trump received an unconditional discharge: no fine, no probation, no punishment beyond the conviction itself. The judge said it was the only sentence available for a sitting president.
The two federal cases were dropped after Trump’s victory. The Georgia case was dismissed last November.
He did not defeat the charges.
He outlasted the clock.
None of it cost him the presidency.
Trump won the Electoral College in 2024 by 312 votes to 226. He also won the popular vote by 1.5 points. It was a real victory, if a modest one by historical standards, and the second-narrowest popular-vote margin since 1960.
Enough Americans, in other words, looked at all of it: the boasting, the contradicted facts, the criminal indictments, the wars he promised never to fight. Then they voted for him anyway.
That may be the harder question, more troubling than any diagnosis.
Presidential falsehoods are not new in American life. What is new is a public that increasingly treats them as beside the point.
There was once an expectation that a president’s word could be taken to the bank.
Whether that was ever entirely true, the pretense itself is now gone.

articles.title: From Tehran, Lavrov urges return to pre-war conditions in Hormuz
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Lavrov urges return to pre-war conditions in Hormuz during Iran visit
Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov has called for conditions in the Strait of Hormuz and the wider region to return to what they were before the US-Israeli war on Iran, following talks with his Iranian counterpart Abbas Araghchi in Tehran on Monday.
Speaking at a joint press conference, Lavrov reaffirmed Moscow's strategic partnership with Tehran and said Russia remained committed to its comprehensive cooperation agreement with Iran.
He described the talks as "productive" and said the two countries shared similar positions on regional developments, while pledging to continue cooperation through international organisations including BRICS, the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation and the Eurasian Economic Union.
Lavrov also announced that Russian personnel would gradually return to Iran's Bushehr nuclear power plant.
The developments come as diplomatic efforts to avert another confrontation intensify, with The New Arab reporting on Monday that a breakthrough in US-Iran mediation efforts could be announced this week.
Senior sources familiar with negotiations told TNA that Qatar and Pakistan were working to narrow differences between Washington and Tehran and secure mutual concessions, while ruling out an immediate military escalation.
Lavrov's visit, his first to Iran since the US-Israeli war began on 28 February, follows Moscow's recent involvement in exchanging messages between the two countries.
It also comes ahead of a possible visit to Tehran by Pakistan's army chief, General Asim Munir, who has been involved in mediation efforts between Washington and Tehran.
Iran and Russia blame US-Israeli attacks for regional instability
Araghchi described Iran's relationship with Russia as "strategic", saying it had taken on new dimensions since the implementation of their comprehensive cooperation agreement nearly two years ago.
He said Monday's discussions had been "extremely productive", covering regional and international developments alongside practical plans to expand political, cultural and commercial cooperation.
The Iranian foreign minister said economic ties between the two countries were developing significantly and that no major obstacles stood in the way of expanding bilateral trade.
On regional security, Araghchi blamed US and Israeli military attacks for instability in the Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz, as well as recent security incidents in the Caspian Sea involving attacks on Iranian and Russian vessels and port infrastructure.
He warned that the situation posed serious consequences for regional peace, security and the environment.
Araghchi also called for an immediate end to the genocide in Palestine, Israeli expansion in Lebanon and the war in Yemen.
The two ministers discussed tensions between Afghanistan and Pakistan, including the need to reduce tensions between Kabul and Islamabad and address threats from armed groups operating in Afghanistan.
Araghchi stressed that regional disputes could not be resolved through military means and required diplomacy and political solutions.
Lavrov, meanwhile, said opposition to US unilateralism remained a shared priority for Moscow and Tehran, with both countries seeking to strengthen multilateral institutions and uphold international law.
He also reaffirmed Russia's commitment to its comprehensive cooperation agreement with Iran.
Can Russia mediate between Iran and the US?
Despite the emphasis on regional diplomacy, neither minister publicly announced a new Russian mediation initiative between Washington and Tehran following Monday's talks.
Russia's potential mediation role began taking shape earlier this month, amid growing contacts between Moscow and Washington over the war in Ukraine.
On 10 October, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov revealed that Russian President Vladimir Putin had informed his Iranian counterpart Masoud Pezeshkian of an upcoming telephone conversation with US President Donald Trump.
The exchange followed a meeting between Putin and Pezeshkian in Turkmenistan on 9 October.
The Kremlin subsequently announced that Putin had conveyed Iran's position on a possible settlement to Trump, raising expectations that Moscow could become another diplomatic channel between Washington and Tehran.
However, Iranian officials have stopped short of recognising Russia as a formal mediator.
Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmail Baghaei said last week that, "technically, in the strict sense of the word", Pakistan and Qatar remained the actual mediators between Iran and the United States.
He added that consultations between Tehran and Moscow, particularly on the nuclear issue, were nothing new.
Ahead of his arrival in Tehran, Lavrov criticised Trump's approach towards Iran as "wrong", arguing that it would not help achieve an agreement based on mutual respect and international law.
His visit followed a stop in Bahrain, prompting speculation that he could also be carrying messages from Gulf states amid heightened regional tensions.
Experts question prospects of Russian mediation
Iranian analyst Hadi Mohammadi told The New Arab that Lavrov's visit reflected growing Russian concerns about developments in the Gulf and the possibility of further escalation.
He said Moscow appeared to be intensifying its diplomatic activities in an attempt to contain tensions, noting that the US-Iran confrontation had become closely linked to the war in Ukraine amid renewed contacts between Washington and Moscow.
Mohammadi suggested that Lavrov could be carrying messages from Washington or Israel during what he described as an extremely sensitive period.
He recalled that Putin had previously conveyed messages between Tehran and Israel, including an Israeli assurance before the latest war that it did not intend to attack Iran.
However, Mohammadi expressed limited confidence in Russia's ability to secure a breakthrough.
He argued that some international actors were making a fundamental mistake by pressuring Iran alone to accept the other side's conditions, while overlooking Tehran's position that it had been attacked and had complied with the Islamabad memorandum of understanding reached in June, which Iran accuses Washington of violating.
Mohammadi said Lavrov's visit could help reduce regional tensions but was unlikely to resolve the crisis on its own.
At best, he suggested, it could mark the beginning of further diplomatic exchanges, although he did not rule out the possibility that it represented a final attempt to avert another war.
Iranian analyst Abbas Aslani similarly told The New Arab that Lavrov's visit reflected the depth of cooperation between Tehran and Moscow in confronting Western pressure.
He said shared economic, political and military challenges had strengthened the importance of bilateral and regional coordination.
Aslani considered it possible that Lavrov was carrying a response or message from Washington, although he cautioned against drawing conclusions before the talks took place.
He also suggested that Moscow could use the visit to assess the Trump administration's position ahead of the US midterm elections on 3 November.
According to Aslani, Russia was already familiar with Iran's strategic red lines, including the conditions outlined in Tehran's seven-day proposal, and was unlikely to persuade Iranian officials to make substantial changes.
He described the visit as a potential opportunity to exchange "hard truths", but argued that any genuine breakthrough would depend on Washington accepting what he described as the new balance of power and security in the Gulf.

articles.title: Europe Needs to Follow Zelensky’s Lead in Challenging Washington’s Appeasement
articles.body:
The latest big news is of a possible trilateral meeting between Presidents Trump, Xi, and Putin to conclude a potential Ukraine “peace” deal. Seemingly, according to a WSJ article, Putin offered Trump such a mini summit in their call on Oct. 9 - that’s the call at which a Russia-US diesel deal was thrashed out. The idea is that the three leaders meet on the sidelines of the scheduled APEC summit slated for 18-19 Nov. in the Chinese city of Shenzhen.
The Trump administration has yet to confirm whether Trump has agreed to take up Putin’s offer of a summit meeting. But the signs are ominous, as it’s on the back of a long list now of actions by Trump that smack of appeasement of Russia – from bringing Putin out of the Western freeze and inviting him to the Anchorage summit, the diesel deal as above, and this week also announcing a delay in the rollout of the Lindsay Graham sanctions bill. It also comes after the U.S. seems to have limited intelligence sharing with Ukraine that has hampered Ukraine’s defense and cost lives.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Trump has tried to explain all this away as not wanting to do anything that risked Putin pulling away from peace talks on Ukraine.
The harsh reality, though, is that Trump has now established a clear track record of pulling punches on President Putin – from his entire second term in office, and indeed before. And yet, this seems to have achieved very little, despite numerous rounds of peace talks, including those run by Messrs. Witkoff and Kushner.
CARTOON: The Ghost of True Republicanism Haunts Today’s Imposter
Remember here that Trump suggested that cutting a Ukraine peace plan would be easy, and he could get the two sides to agree within weeks of taking office for his second term, then by Easter 2025, then by year-end 2026, and here we now are close to the end of 2026, and Trump’s appeasement of Putin seems to have achieved absolutely nothing.
Worse than that, I think it has emboldened Putin to prolong the war, as he thinks that with Trump in office, the Western alliance in defense of Ukraine will inevitably collapse, offering him up the whole of Ukraine on a plate. And the latter has always been Putin’s ambition.
It gets more war, and unfortunately Ukraine has ended up paying the price in more blood and lives lost. Now Trump seems to just be repeating the prior mistakes of Schroeder, Hollande, Merkel, Macron et al.
And the latest gift to Putin is a wet dream for Putin, a great power summit, as he will see it, where Russia, China, and the US can do what great powers do – divide up the world into spheres of influence. This would be Putin’s Yalta II.
Trump is either ignorant of history or uncaring of the fate of Ukraine and Europe. For Trump, the win is just appearing on the same stage as Xi and Putin, and a place in summit history, albeit I would add ignominy, rather as was the case for Chamberlain in 1938 over Czechoslovakia.
The only problem for Trump with this Yalta 2 is that, with no Ukraine or Europe represented, I don’t see how it can deliver a meaningful peace in the war in Ukraine.
Trump might agree to Putin’s terms that Ukraine needs to deliver the rest of Donbas to Ukraine, but I cannot see Zelensky agreeing to that unless Trump is willing to offer, in exchange, cast-iron security guarantees that if Putin breaks any such agreement the US will then go to war with Russia to defend the rest of Ukraine.
Trump is never going to offer any such security assurance, and even if he did, I don’t think the Ukrainians would trust it, since they don’t trust Trump and don’t really trust such an assurance after being let down over the Budapest Memorandum in 1994.
The Ukrainians also don’t trust Putin, as they assume, quite rightly, that this war was never about Donbas, but Putin’s desires for the whole of Ukraine. So they assume that once they surrender their fortress defense in Donbas – defended valiantly over 12 years now – Putin would take them and just drive on further into Ukraine.
Politically, also, for Zelensky, surrendering Donbas, with no serious security guarantees – and likely not NATO or EU membership – would be political suicide at home. It would likely provoke a social and political revolution (remember the Orange Revolution and then Euromaidan, so Ukraine has formed here), or even a coup, destabilizing Ukraine to Russia’s advantage. And that is why Putin continues to demand something – the surrender of Donbas – which he knows that Zelensky cannot seriously agree to.
The onus will then be on Putin to secure delivery on that agreement. But there, I don’t think his military is in much of a position to then take what Trump has gifted him. If they have failed to take the Donbas in 12 years of bitter fighting, why would we assume anything different from a mere sharpie signature from Trump?
And the downside for Putin is that any constraint on Ukraine in this war will be removed. Ukraine will surely then have an interest in maximum escalation – taking the war fully to Russia and hence launching all-out deep-strike drone attacks on Russian energy infrastructure. That is hardly likely to suit Trump or Xi, as it will have severe global market impact.
Unfortunately, the outlook for Ukraine in most likely scenarios now is grim – and I would argue because Trump has mismanaged the whole Ukraine peace process. It suggests a scenario either where Putin still thinks that he can take whatever Trump offers in China and demands more, plays the long war through to the French presidential election and the assumption European support for Ukraine caves after a Le Pen win, or Ukraine is left to reject any peace deal signed by Trump, Xi and Putin in Shenzhen but is then forced to battle on with no US support and likely strained European support.
Xi and Europe, to the rescue?
Trump and Putin likely want to exclude Europe from any such Ukraine peace talks. Xi may well too, albeit in the bigger scheme of things: does Xi want to risk signing up to a peace deal that neither Trump nor Putin can easily or quickly deliver on the ground, and that could see Ukrainian escalation to global markets, while also risking annoying European trade partners? Perhaps not.
Europe should remember here that it has agency and should impress this on both Trump and Xi. Whatever is agreed at Shenzhen, Europe has an interest in continuing to back Ukraine, given the existential threat from Russia and the US. under Trump AWOL in defending Europe; Ukraine now represents Europe’s best chance of buying time until it develops its own autonomous defense capability.
Indeed, I would have thought that Xi would not view any Trump-Putin deal over Ukraine that favorably if it opened the way then for a new special relationship between the US and Russia, a reverse Nixonian ultimately to screw over China. I would then have thought China and Europe have common interests in working together to forestall any Trump-Putin bromance consummated over Ukraine.
While playing China towards its interests over Ukraine, I think that Ukraine is such an existential interest for Europe that the latter needs to follow Zelensky in spelling out to Trump what his surrender of Ukraine to Putin would mean for the Transatlantic relationship.
They need to spell out that this would mean the end of NATO, and that Europe would be forced to fast-track efforts to develop a defense capability separate from the US. American companies would risk losing the milking-cow defense deals they have grown accustomed to.
It would also mean that Europe would not be a natural ally for the US in its ongoing hegemonic battle with China, and indeed, European defense companies would begin to compete more aggressively with their US counterparts. Net, net, this would mean a loss of US jobs and long-term damage to the US economy and ultimately its security.
Zelensky has confronted US appeasement; maybe Europe needs to do that too.
See the original in the author’s @tashecon blog here.
The views expressed in this opinion article are the author’s and not necessarily those of Kyiv Post.

articles.title: Russian drone kills six in Kharkiv Oblast park, including mother and her 14-month-old in a stroller. Hours later, Ukraine shows photos to US senators
articles.body:
Six people were killed in a Russian strike in the settlement of Nova Vodolaha in Kharkiv Oblast, including girls aged 1 and 11. Another 15 people were injured, including seven children, Kharkiv Oblast Governor Oleh Syniehubov said on 20 October. Russian forces struck a park with a drone while families with children were there, Ukraine’s Minister of Internal Affairs Ivan Vyhivskyi said.
Russian forces continue to attack Ukrainian cities, killing civilians and destroying civilian infrastructure. The Kharkiv Oblast Prosecutor’s Office has opened a war-crime investigation into the strike. The strike was aimed at people, Yurii Yurchenko, head of a police department in Kharkiv Oblast, said in a comment to Suspilne.
The 14-month-old girl was named Anhelina
The Russian drone circled the park several times before crashing, Yurchenko said. He said the drone struck a tree near a café, and the blast wave and shrapnel hit people at the establishment. The attack came at around 16:30, the prosecutor’s office said, adding that Russian forces had preliminarily used a Geran-3 drone.
The Russian strike killed three women, aged 28, 34 and 36, a man around 40 years old, and two girls, aged 14 months and 11 years, Syniehubov said in his statement.
The youngest girl, named Anhelina, was born in August 2025, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said. Her mother, Inna, died in the hospital, he added.
Zelenskyy shows US senators photos of the aftermath the same day
Zelenskyy met with US Senators Richard Blumenthal and Thom Tillis, along with their colleagues from both parties and both chambers of Congress, according to a 19 October post on his social media accounts. During the meeting, he discussed the Russian attack in Kharkiv Oblast and showed lawmakers photographs from the scene, including one of the infant who was killed in a stroller.
“This is how Russia responds to the lifting of sanctions and the easing of pressure,” he said in the post.
Zelenskyy said Ukraine needs air defense and that no one should think about making money with Russia while it continues its war. He asked that sanctions on Russia stay in place until the killing stops, urged the US to “be strong” and apply Lindsey Graham’s law, and called on Europe to keep supporting Ukraine.
Read also
- Russia hit Ukraine’s energy 76 times during a US-declared truce—and tens of thousands lost power overnight. Civilians killed and injured
- Trump defends Russia sanctions waiver, says he does not want to drive Moscow from talks
- Kyiv gets no warning of the first of two Russian ballistic waves, hours after Zelenskyy said US alerts were back

articles.title: Ukrainians in U.S. protest easing of sanctions on Russian diesel fuel
articles.body:
Ukrainians in U.S. protest easing of sanctions on Russian diesel fuel
The protests were reported by Vilni Media, Ukrinform says.
Participants called on the U.S. government not to ease economic pressure on Moscow, to preserve military communications and intelligence support critical to Ukraine, and to strengthen congressional oversight of decisions that could affect Ukraine’s defense capabilities.
In California, rallies took place in two cities: outside the federal building in Los Angeles and at Balboa Park in San Diego.
In Los Angeles, Ukrainian activists gathered outside the Federal Building on Wilshire Boulevard. The rally was part of a campaign organized under the slogans “Stop the Betrayal. Stand with Ukraine” and “Defend Ukraine – Not Putin.” Participants brought Ukrainian and American flags and signs urging Washington to increase pressure on Russia. One of their central demands was a review of the decision concerning Russian diesel fuel, which the activists view as an economic concession to Moscow.
The protesters argued that increased Russian energy exports would generate additional revenue for Russia that could be used to continue the war.
Another key issue was defense assistance to Ukraine. Globe4Ukraine cited reports of restrictions on Starshield military communications and problems with Ukraine receiving U.S. early-warning information about missile attacks. Activists said these reports warranted the attention of Congress because such capabilities could be critical to Ukraine’s defense.
Activists urged lawmakers to work to preserve critical defense assistance to Ukraine, investigate reports of restrictions on communications and intelligence capabilities, oppose sanctions exemptions for Russian diesel fuel, and ensure enforcement of U.S. sanctions laws.
“Supporting Ukraine protects America’s security, democracy, and the principle that borders cannot be altered by force,” the activists said.
Protests against the change in sanctions policy also took place on the other coast of the United States. In Seattle, representatives of Ukraine Defense Support and Voliy Fond organized a rally at Waterfront Park. Its main slogan was “Say No to Russian Diesel.”
The activists opposed a decision by the U.S. administration which, according to their assessment, creates an opening for significant volumes of Russian diesel fuel to return to the international market.
Another rally took place in Chicago, where the Illinois Division of the Ukrainian Congress Committee of America called for a protest. One of the demonstration’s central slogans was “Don’t Trade Principles for Profit.”
Participants at the rally called on the White House and Congress to tighten sanctions on Russia’s energy sector and continue supporting Ukraine.
U.S. Representative Mike Quigley also joined the demonstration in Chicago.
During the rally, the issue of Russian energy exports was linked not only to the war in Ukraine but also to U.S. national security. One of the main messages was that energy independence is an integral part of America’s national security.
As Ukrinform reported, on October 9, U.S. President Donald Trump said that Russia, with U.S. approval, would immediately supply 300,000 tons of diesel fuel to the global market. According to Trump, another 500,000 tons would be supplied in November, followed by 1 million tons. Russia subsequently pledged to release an additional 3 million tons of diesel fuel onto the market.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky stressed that gifts to Putin would not help bring peace. Later, a bill was introduced in the U.S. Congress to block the deal involving Russian diesel fuel.
Photo: UDS4Ukraine, Ukrainian Congress Committee of America, Illinois Division

articles.title: Kiev ‘in panic’ over US probe into Ukraine-Mexican drug cartel links – RT reports (VIDEO)
articles.body:
Kiev ‘in panic’ over US probe into Ukraine-Mexican drug cartel links – RT reports (VIDEO)
Ukrainian officials are reportedly panicking after US investigators uncovered links between Mexican drug cartels and Kiev, including paid drone training for cartel members. The probe threatens to further strain the already fragile relations between Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky and US President Donald Trump.
In a statement on Tuesday, Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR) said American law enforcement investigating the cartels had identified at least 80 members who learned to assemble and operate combat drones while serving with Ukrainian forces.
The payment for this “education” was transferred to officials close to Zelensky using proceeds from drug sales in the US, according to the SVR report obtained by RT.
The agency also noted that Zelensky’s office is aware that the presence of trained first-person-view (FPV) drone operators among drug cartels could ultimately threaten American officers combating drug trafficking along the Mexican border and damage relations with Washington.
That, coupled with the continued supply of weapons and drones from Ukraine to other parts of the world, “has become a pattern that is quite difficult to ignore,” RT correspondent Isabella Blumberg noted.
The Washington Post similarly reported last month that Mexican cartels were hiring drone operators who had fought in Ukraine and were sending members there for training. The State Department said it was working with Kiev to prevent those skills from reaching the cartels.
Mexico’s Milenio newspaper also claimed last year that members of the Jalisco New Generation Cartel had received drone and urban warfare training in Ukraine.
The alleged ties have extended beyond training, with Russian intelligence reporting in June that Ukrainian security agencies were facilitating Latin American drug trafficking into Europe while the cartels helped Kiev in recruiting fighters.
The SVR has suggested that the cartel cooperation could become another “nail in the coffin” for Zelensky’s political career. Together with corruption, continued attacks on Russian refineries, and his refusal to hold elections, it could push Washington to abandon him, the agency claimed.
The allegations come amid an increasingly bitter dispute between Zelensky and Trump over Kiev’s continued strikes on Russian refineries and stalled peace negotiations.
Trump has increasingly questioned the Ukrainian leader’s true intentions regarding the conflict, stressing that he should have settled it “a long time ago” and suggesting that he “doesn’t want to end this war, and probably never did.”
Trump recently went as far as stating that Ukraine should “get a new president,” and said on Monday that Kiev should get someone else to negotiate peace, arguing that Zelensky “doesn’t know what he’s talking about.”
Watch RT’s full report below.

articles.title: Israel prepared to attack Iran without US – Netanyahu
articles.body:
Israel prepared to attack Iran without US – Netanyahu
Israel is prepared to attack Iran without US participation if necessary, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has said, pledging to overthrow Tehran’s government and make striking first a central principle of his security doctrine.
The declaration comes amid ongoing indirect negotiations over the war launched by the US and Israel in February. Israel, a major recipient of American military funding and weapons, has justified its offensives on security grounds, even as the conflict has spread across the region, disrupted Hormuz shipping, and driven up global energy prices.
Presenting his security doctrine in a speech on Sunday, Netanyahu argued that Iran would rebuild its nuclear and military capabilities as long as its government survived and made clear that Israel was prepared to launch further attacks without waiting for American participation.
“If we need to act alone, we will act alone,” he said.
Netanyahu presented Israel’s earlier campaign against Iran as a model, recalling that he told US President Donald Trump he would attack Tehran “either way” and invited American participation in a strike on the Fordow nuclear facility.
He framed further action against Iran as unfinished business, explicitly identifying the overthrow of the country’s government as the ultimate objective. “We are working on it and we will do it,” Netanyahu said.
Despite Tehran repeatedly stressing that its nuclear program is peaceful and denying seeking nuclear weapons, Netanyahu once again claimed that the US-Israeli attacks had prevented Iran from acquiring an atomic bomb intended to destroy Israel.
Netanyahu framed the renewed strikes as part of a broader doctrine prioritizing attack over defense. He compared striking first to gaining the advantage in childhood street fights and said Israel could establish bases far beyond its borders.
“We will have to live by our sword in order to live for many years,” he said.
He also described plans to seize and destroy what he called threat centers in the occupied West Bank, listed preventing Palestinian statehood as a fundamental principle, and included disrupting military and “civilian systems” in his deterrence strategy.
US-Iran negotiations are already deadlocked. Trump rejected Tehran’s proposal last month as “unacceptable,” insisting the US blockade had left Iran “losing so badly” and seeking a deal on Washington’s terms.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi reiterated on Saturday that normal shipping in the Strait of Hormuz could resume within seven days if Washington accepted Tehran’s conditions, including lifting the naval blockade, easing oil export restrictions, releasing frozen assets, and ending hostilities on all fronts, including Israel’s operations in Gaza and Lebanon.
Trump has nevertheless threatened renewed bombing, with Axios recently reporting that US officials expected major combat operations could resume after November’s midterm elections.
Tehran has warned that another attack would trigger broader retaliation, potentially targeting American technology infrastructure across the Gulf.

articles.title: Russia and India wrap up joint naval drills in Pacific (VIDEO)
articles.body:
Russia and India wrap up joint naval drills in Pacific (VIDEO)
Russian and Indian warships have completed joint naval drills off Russia’s Pacific coast, conducting live-fire exercises and practicing defenses against drone attacks as part of the wider Indra-2026 military exercise.
The maritime phase of the drills took place in the Gulf of Peter the Great near Vladivostok, involving the Russian Pacific Fleet corvette Aldar Tsydenzhapov and the Indian Navy frigate INS Sahyadri, the Russian Defense Ministry said on Saturday.
INS Sahyadri arrived in Vladivostok on October 10 and conducted harbor engagements before operations at sea.
The crews fired naval artillery at surface and aerial targets, carried out coordinated maneuvers, and tested communications between the vessels. They also practiced repelling attacks by unmanned boats and aerial drones representing a simulated enemy. The Russian corvette used 30mm automatic guns, small arms, and electronic warfare systems to counter the simulated threats.
The exercises culminated in a simulated joint operation to rescue a civilian vessel seized by pirates. Russian and Indian naval counterterrorism units boarded the vessel and neutralized the attackers, with drone operators coordinating their movements.
The two navies also practiced helicopter operations, including reconnaissance, cross-deck landings, and medical evacuations.
An Indian helicopter landed aboard the Russian corvette shortly after a Russian helicopter took off. The crews then exchanged mannequins representing wounded sailors as part of a casualty evacuation exercise, RT correspondent Igor Zhdanov reported from aboard the Russian warship.
Indra-2026 began on October 14 and involves land, naval, and air forces from both countries.
The land component will continue in Russia’s Chelyabinsk Region until October 23, with troops practicing joint command and control and operations against simulated armed groups. Russian and Indian aircrews are also conducting exercises involving Su-30SM fighter jets and Mi-8 helicopters.
The previous edition of the exercise was held off the coast of the southern Indian city of Chennai.
The deployment builds on the longstanding defense partnership between Moscow and New Delhi and carries forward cooperation discussed during Russian President Vladimir Putin’s visit to India last December, India’s Defense Ministry said.

articles.title: Europe is preparing for direct talks with Putin, FT reports. One possible proposal: Russia gets Donbas, Ukraine gets NATO membership.
articles.body:
Europe is preparing for direct talks with Putin, FT reports. One possible proposal: Russia gets Donbas, Ukraine gets NATO membership.
European leaders are rethinking their approach to the Kremlin, Financial Times foreign affairs columnist Gideon Rachman writes. More politicians in the European Union now agree that negotiations with Vladimir Putin should not remain the exclusive prerogative of the United States. European countries could soon open their own talks with the Kremlin. Channels of communication are already in place, he says.
EU policy toward Russia has rested on two main pillars until now: support for Ukraine and sanctions. European leaders have tried to shape the negotiations by influencing Donald Trump’s position, but those efforts are growing less effective. Europe also fears Trump is more interested in business deals with Moscow than in security issues.
In any direct talks, Putin could be offered two options for ending the war, Rachman writes: freezing the conflict along the front line in exchange for a guarantee that Ukraine will not join NATO, or ceding all of the Donbas to Moscow’s control, after which Kyiv could join the alliance.
Meanwhile, relations between Kyiv and Washington are going through a new crisis, triggered by an energy crisis and Trump’s push to lower diesel prices ahead of the midterm elections to Congress.
Trump has repeatedly urged Ukraine to stop striking Russian oil refineries and declare an energy truce. After diplomatic failure, he struck a deal with Moscow on diesel supplies. Volodymyr Zelensky said the United States had “chosen the side” of Russia. Trump responded that it was easier for him to reach an agreement with Putin than with Zelensky, adding that Ukraine needs to hold elections.
Relations between the two leaders are at their “lowest point” since the clash in the Oval Office in 2025, the WSJ writes. The latest exchange took place a day earlier: Trump accused Zelensky of not wanting to end the war, while Zelensky said Ukraine is being pressured to capitulate.
Amid this, U.S. Vice President JD Vance has spoken out against Ukraine joining NATO: “We don’t have a formal alliance as far as I know with Ukraine. They’re not in NATO. I don’t think that they should be in NATO,” he said. Vance also refused to call Kyiv an ally of Washington, saying they have “divergent interests from time to time.”
War in photographs. Komyshuvakha.
Residents of Komyshuvakha, a front-line village in the Zaporizhzhia region, are being evacuated because of the threat of Russian drone strikes. These photos were taken October 19, 2026.
