articles.title: Greece to shut 187 military camps in major defense overhaul
articles.body:
Greece plans to shut down 187 of its 831 military camps as part of a sweeping restructuring of its armed forces under a new force structure covering 2026-2035, with the move expected to generate significant savings and free up resources for modernization, Greek media reported on Oct. 20.
Defense Minister Nikos Dendias outlined the plans during a closed-door briefing to members of parliament’s committee on defense and foreign affairs, highlighting the financial benefits of consolidating military units and facilities alongside the integration of advanced technologies.
The camps slated for closure operate with no more than 30 percent of their planned personnel capacity and have been assessed as having limited operational significance, according to sources familiar with the matter.
The closures are expected to save approximately 100 million euros annually, amounting to 1.7 billion euros over the next decade.
The funds will be redirected toward a housing program for military personnel and smaller-scale procurement projects, while staffing levels at strategically important units could reach 70 percent in peacetime.
The restructuring forms part of a broader defense overhaul announced by Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis, who said that Greece would invest 25 billion euros through 2036 in what he described as the most far-reaching transformation of the country’s armed forces in modern history.
The modernization drive also includes the development of a multilayered air defense system, dubbed Achilles’ Shield, designed to counter missile, aerial and drone threats. Athens has cited rapidly evolving geopolitical challenges and strained transatlantic ties as key factors behind the overhaul.

articles.title: Streeting rejects claim Scotland’s coast is undefended
articles.body:
Suggesting that Scotland’s coast is undefended is both inaccurate and irresponsible, the Defence Secretary told the Commons, offering in the same answer to work with the Scottish Government on the defence of the United Kingdom regardless of constitutional differences.
Lara Bird, the Scottish National Party member for Arbroath and Broughty Ferry, asked the Secretary of State to station a warship permanently on Scotland’s north coast, and set the request against what she described as a sevenfold difference in defence spending between south east England and Scotland.
Bird said: “Scotland is currently on the front line of defending the High North. And yet, despite the very real threats that we face, the UK government currently spends seven times more on defence in the south east of England than in the whole of Scotland combined. And so, given those very real threats that we face, and given that our coastline is currently undefended by the Royal Navy, will the Secretary of State commit to placing a surface level vessel permanently on the north coast of Scotland?”
Wes Streeting, the Secretary of State for Defence, said: “Can I just sort of say gently to the hon. Member that I think it is both inaccurate and irresponsible to suggest that Scotland’s coast is undefended, and in the same spirit, just to underscore to her, I am very willing to work with the Scottish Government in defence of the United Kingdom, regardless of our constitutional differences. It is important that we work together and I hope we can do so in the question.”
His Majesty’s Naval Base Clyde at Faslane is the Royal Navy’s largest site in Scotland and the home of the submarine service, holding the Vanguard class boats that carry the deterrent and the Astute class attack submarines alongside them, with the whole submarine flotilla consolidating there.
RAF Lossiemouth flies the P-8A Poseidon maritime patrol aircraft that track Russian submarines through the Greenland Iceland United Kingdom gap, and holds Typhoons at quick reaction alert for the northern half of British airspace. River class offshore patrol vessels work Scottish waters on fishery protection and maritime security tasking, and the Fleet Ready Escort is held at short notice to shadow Russian warships as they transit.
HMS Prince of Wales and her strike group deployed to the High North this month on Operation Firecrest, with F-35B Lightning jets flying from the carrier in the North Atlantic, and the Royal Navy has spent the year building the pattern of surface deployments north of Scotland that the deployment sits within.
Versions of the claim have reached the Commons before, and this publication has examined an earlier assertion that there are no Royal Navy vessels in Scottish waters, and has tested the related argument that Scotland is short changed on defence spending.
Figures published last month put Ministry of Defence spending with Scottish industry at £2.53 billion, a thirteen per cent real terms increase on the previous year, worth £460 a head and supporting 12,200 jobs. The House of Commons Library, working from the previous year’s regional statistics, puts spending with industry in South East England at £7.9 billion, or £820 a person, against a United Kingdom average of about £460.
The Arctic Policy Framework published last week named Russian activity around undersea cables and pipelines as a threat to critical national infrastructure and described the shadow fleet as a systemic risk, which puts official policy close to Bird’s description of where Scotland sits. The Lunna House Agreement signed with Norway commits the two navies to protecting those links across the North Atlantic, and the Defence Committee is running an inquiry into the High North, with written evidence submitted this month setting out how uncrewed platforms and Type 26 frigates would provide persistent anti-submarine surveillance in the gap.

articles.title: Trump's backing of Netanyahu, Hegseth's secret visit fuel Iran war fears ahead of Israel's election
articles.body:
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu insists he promised U.S. President Donald Trump nothing in return for his public endorsement ahead of Israel's October 27 election. But with Trump, political gifts rarely come without expectations. For Netanyahu, whose ultimate ambition remains the fall of Iran's Islamic Republic, the American president's support may come at a price, potentially requiring Israeli concessions on other issues, particularly Washington's 20-point plan for Gaza.
One such concession is already taking shape. Netanyahu has agreed to the establishment of an "Emirati bubble" in Gaza, where reconstruction could begin before the Strip is demilitarized and Hamas is disarmed. The arrangement suggests the prime minister may be prepared to accommodate Trump on Gaza if doing so helps secure American backing for what he considers his defining strategic objective: bringing down the regime in Tehran.
The timing of Trump's endorsement, followed by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's unannounced visit to Israel, has sharpened speculation about the possibility of another round of fighting with Iran. Netanyahu has repeatedly described the confrontation with Tehran as his life's work and said in recent days that he instructed Israel's defense establishment to bring down the Iranian regime.
Hegseth had been scheduled to visit Israel in July, but that trip was canceled at the last moment. His arrival now, just eight days before Israelis go to the polls, comes amid discussions about the possible resumption of major military operations against Iran. The proximity of the visit to Trump's endorsement has added to questions about Washington's intentions and Netanyahu's calculations.
Yet one senior Israeli official offers a markedly different interpretation. According to the official, Netanyahu is eager to attack Iran but cannot currently do so because Israel lacks the necessary intelligence. The Americans, the official said, are not interested in another strike at this stage, and Hegseth did not come to coordinate an operation. Rather, the purpose of his visit was to ensure Netanyahu was not preparing any surprises before the U.S. midterm elections on November 3.
That assessment illustrates the competing interests at play. Netanyahu sees regime change in Iran as the ultimate strategic prize, while the Trump administration must weigh the consequences of another confrontation against its own political timetable. For both leaders, the coming weeks carry significant military and political risks.
The danger of an Iranian preemptive strike
The increasingly heated rhetoric could itself become a trigger for war. With Israeli leaders issuing warnings, security consultations taking place late into the night and Hegseth making an unannounced visit, Iranian officials could conclude that Israel is preparing an imminent attack. Tehran might then attempt to strike first, setting off a rapid escalation that neither side had necessarily intended to initiate at that moment.
Israel's message in recent days has been consistent: If Iran makes a mistake, the Israeli response will be unprecedented. The warning appears to refer not only to the scale of a possible operation but also to the targets Israel could choose. Previous reports have indicated that Israeli planners considered striking Iranian infrastructure and energy facilities in the belief that such attacks could accelerate the collapse of the regime.
But the central assumption remains uncertain. Even another devastating military campaign would not guarantee the fall of Iran's leadership. As one Israeli source put it, nobody is promising that this time the regime in Tehran will collapse.
The costs of another war would also extend well beyond the battlefield. Israel would face the prospect of extensive damage to civilian infrastructure, a prolonged reconstruction effort and potentially significant casualties. During Operation Roaring Lion, 30 Israeli civilians were killed by direct Iranian missile strikes, while 12 soldiers and one civilian were killed on the Lebanese front. Another major confrontation could expose the Israeli home front to further missile attacks.
The election timetable adds another layer of complexity. IDF Chief of Staff Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir has made clear to American officials that renewed fighting before October 27 could force Israel to postpone its election. A military confrontation in the final days of the campaign would therefore have consequences extending beyond national security, potentially disrupting the country's democratic process.
An Israeli source familiar with the situation put the chances of renewed fighting before the election at 30%, compared with a 70% likelihood that war would not resume before October 27. The figures represent that source's assessment rather than a certainty about either side's intentions.
The next deadline is November 3, when Americans vote in the midterm elections. Trump has indicated that the confrontation with Iran would be brought to a conclusion after that date, one way or another. As a result, the timing of any possible military operation is being considered against two closely spaced elections, each carrying its own political constraints.
Opposition questions Netanyahu's motives
Within Israel's opposition, the renewed discussion of war with Iran has prompted suspicion that political considerations may be influencing the timing and intensity of Netanyahu's warnings. Opposition figures believe the atmosphere of urgency surrounding the Iranian threat may serve the prime minister's interests in the final days of the campaign.
The signals have been difficult to ignore: late-night security consultations, briefings suggesting Iran could attempt to disrupt Israel's election and the unannounced arrival of Hegseth, widely regarded as one of the more hawkish members of Trump's administration. Together, they have contributed to the impression that another confrontation could be approaching.
There is also the question of who within Israel's security establishment might challenge the prime minister's calculations. Zamir appears to be the senior defense official most likely to scrutinize the timing and motives behind a proposed operation. The heads of Mossad, the National Security Council and Shin Bet are all Netanyahu appointees, although their appointments do not establish how they would respond to a decision to strike.
For Israel to initiate a discretionary war against Iran, Netanyahu would need Security Cabinet approval. An Iranian preemptive attack, however, could fundamentally change the circumstances, turning the question from whether Israel should launch a new operation into how it should respond to an attack already underway.
That is where the greatest danger may lie. Netanyahu's determination to bring down the Iranian regime, Trump's political backing and the signals surrounding Hegseth's visit have created an atmosphere in which intentions can easily be misread. Even if Washington and Jerusalem ultimately decide against launching an operation before the elections, Tehran could reach a different conclusion and act first. The result could be a war triggered not by a carefully coordinated decision, but by a miscalculation at one of the most politically sensitive moments for both Israel and the United States.

articles.title: Deferring mobilisation for drivers to keep transport services resilient
articles.body:
Bohdan Hevko, President of the Association of Road Transport of Ukraine, Candidate of Economic Sciences
Revising the rules on mobilisation deferments for employees presents the state with a difficult task: replenishing the armed forces while preserving the transport services on which defence production, exports and supplies to the public depend. For road transport, this comes down to the number of trips completed. A truck without a driver cannot deliver fuel or components, even if the vehicle is in good working order and the contract has been paid for.
Russian strikes on ports, railways and warehousing facilities are forcing businesses to change routes and transshipment locations. Road transport makes these adjustments possible and delivers goods to their final recipients. It cannot fully replace maritime and rail transport, but it maintains the connections between them. In autumn and winter, this flexibility is particularly important for supplying fuel, food and equipment to restore energy infrastructure.
The scale of the workforce shortage
In July 2025, Deputy Minister for Development of Communities and Territories Serhii Derkach estimated the shortage of category CE drivers at 30,000–40,000. According to information the ministry received from hauliers, around 30% of approximately 130,000 trucks were idle because of a lack of drivers. The official also cited a company where 30 new vehicles remained parked despite contracts being in place. This was an estimate at the time of the report, not a current census of the sector.
A World Bank study presented in February 2026 confirms a persistent shortage of truck and bus drivers. An analysis of more than 240,000 job advertisements also identified increases of 20–33% in advertised salaries for transport occupations facing shortages. These figures indicate pressure in the labour market; they should not be equated with an increase in the cost of all transport services.
Vehicle downtime reduces revenue, while some leasing, insurance and depot overheads remain. Consider an illustrative calculation: if seven equally productive vehicles operate instead of ten, unchanged shared fixed costs per unit of transport output rise by approximately 43%, reflecting a ratio of 10 to 7. This illustrates the mechanism; it is not an estimate of the sector’s actual losses.
The available data do not establish how many businesses have been lost or how much revenue has been foregone specifically because of restrictions on mobilisation deferments. Mobilisation, migration, an ageing workforce and working conditions all contribute to the shortage. To assess the impact of new rules, the government needs comparable data on unfilled driver positions, idle vehicles and unfulfilled contracts. The absence of such records does not negate the already documented shortage of workers.
Aligning mobilisation deferments with defence needs
The armed forces also need qualified drivers. Every expansion of mobilisation deferments reduces the pool of people available for mobilisation and therefore needs to be justified by specific transport operations. On 19 October, the prime minister explained the review of the rules in terms of mobilisation needs and efforts to tackle abuse, including fictitious staffing increases at critical enterprises. Any sectoral proposal must directly address this concern.
The procedure established by Cabinet of Ministers Resolution No. 76 provides for a general quota of up to 50% of employees liable for military service at the relevant category of critically important enterprises, along with exceptions and a procedure for increasing that quota. This is a share of the workforce, not the vehicle fleet. It is sufficient for some operators; for businesses whose workforce consists mainly of drivers, it may leave some essential trips without the staff needed to operate them.
I propose introducing separate sectoral criteria for critical enterprise status and allowing mobilisation deferments for 100% of drivers liable for military service at licensed, critically important transport enterprises, within the limits of verified staffing needs. International freight and passenger operators should be given priority. For freight transport, the justification is maintaining export and import flows; for passenger transport, it is maintaining essential connections. Holding a licence alone should not automatically confer an increased quota.
An enterprise should demonstrate that it holds a valid licence, actually performs transport operations, uses vehicles lawfully and formally employs its drivers. Staffing needs should be determined by routes and shift patterns, taking mandatory rest periods and relief cover into account. This would preserve the necessary driver workforce without extending the special quota to all administrative staff.
The ministry responsible for the sector should agree the parameters of this regime with the Ministry of Defence, taking mobilisation needs into account. Oversight should rely on data exchange covering employment, vehicles and trips, without duplicating paper reports. The cessation of operations or established cases of fictitious employment should trigger the consequences prescribed by law. At the same time, technical errors in a register require a mechanism for prompt correction and appeal.
Licensing domestic road freight transport
The next step is to introduce licensing for domestic commercial transport of non-dangerous goods. The current list of activities subject to licensing covers international road transport, passenger transport and the carriage of dangerous goods, but imposes no general licensing requirement on this domestic freight segment.
Licensing should establish verifiable records of operators and vehicles, along with requirements for professional competence and the organisation of safe operations. This requires coordinated amendments to the Laws of Ukraine on Licensing of Types of Economic Activity and on Road Transport. Electronic processing and an adequate transition period should prevent the reform itself from disrupting supplies.
Once licensed and confirmed as critically important, domestic freight enterprises should have access to the same regime for retaining the drivers they need. Domestic passenger transport and dangerous goods operations, which are already licensed, should also be covered where a critical function is verified. General rules would continue to apply to other enterprises.
Decisions needed now
The immediate minimum is to preserve existing access to mobilisation deferments and avoid making it harder for transport enterprises to obtain critical status before a dedicated mechanism is introduced. That mechanism needs to be incorporated into Resolution No. 76 and aligned with sectoral criteria. A solution for international operators should not have to wait for the completion of legislative reform of the domestic market.
In parallel, measures are needed to train young drivers, bring more women into the profession and support veterans in adapting to civilian employment. Older workers remain an important part of the sector; safety should be assessed on the basis of medical fitness, qualifications and working schedules. Overworking drivers is not an acceptable way to compensate for a shortage of staff.
The results of these changes should be measured by reductions in vehicle downtime and the recovery of transport operations, weighed against the number of additional drivers granted mobilisation deferments. This approach would enable the state to identify exactly what supply capacity it is preserving and the corresponding cost to the personnel available for defence.

articles.title: Z.AI founders worked on research funded by China institute that UK tied to spies
articles.body:
Z.ai founders worked on research funded by China institute that Britain tied to spies
- Four Z.AI founders worked on a 2018 to 2021 AI project partly funded by CGTRI, which MI5 said had “very strong ties” to China’s spy agency.
- The project, worth 2.94 million yuan, aimed to analyse social media, spot events and map people’s links, including a knowledge base of “China-related key persons”.
- The report links Z.AI to wider US scrutiny, including tech access limits, data extraction claims and concerns over its vulnerability ledger being shared with Chinese state databases.
AI generated
LONDON - Four founders of one of China’s most promising artificial intelligence companies, Z.ai, worked on research in a joint project with a technology institute that the British government accused of having “very strong ties” to China’s main spy agency, according to publicly available research papers from China and an “espionage alert” from Britain.
The nearly four-year AI research project, which overlapped with the company’s start in 2019, was co-funded by Beijing-based China General Technology Research Institute (CGTRI) and the National Natural Science Foundation of China, according to a previously unreported 78-page report that the project’s leaders compiled to detail their findings.
A CGTRI engineer and one of Z.ai’s founders were among the project’s leaders, and three other Z.ai founders contributed to the research, according to the report.
The report was published on a Chinese government website that provides research funding records.
Britain’s MI5 intelligence service, in the Sept 30 espionage alert, accused CGTRI of primarily existing to fund academic research that directly improves China’s main spy agency’s “technical capability for espionage”.
The first-of-its-kind bulletin said the institute has “very strong ties” to China’s Ministry of State Security and warned of potential criminal consequences for “any institution or individual continuing to conduct research ultimately funded by CGTRI following publication of this espionage alert”.
A spokesperson for China’s embassy in Britain called MI5’s allegations against CGTRI “baseless”.
The Z.ai founders’ work on research partially funded by an alleged Chinese intelligence front highlights the risks cited by some US officials regarding China’s growing prowess in AI – and could add to further scrutiny of Z.ai in particular.
The two countries are racing to develop a technology that is transforming the global economy and could give their military services an advantage.
The US restricted Z.ai’s access to American technology in 2025 based on allegations that the company aided the military with AI research.
More recently, US officials accused the company of systemically extracting proprietary knowledge from American rivals.
It is not clear what, if anything, any of Z.ai’s founders may have known about CGTRI’s alleged relationship with Chinese intelligence.
The MI5 alert did not mention Z.ai.
Z.ai did not respond to e-mailed requests for comment, nor did the four founders involved in the research project.
The company previously said the US decision to restrict its access to technology “lacked factual basis” and would not have a substantial impact on its business.
Reached by phone, a CGTRI representative said the institute does not do any external communication with anyone. Efforts to e-mail CGTRI for comment were unsuccessful.
Liu Chang, a spokesperson for the Chinese embassy in Washington, declined to address specific questions about Bloomberg’s report.
“I’m not familiar with the specifics,” he said. “The development of AI in China comes from greater self-reliance and strength in science and technology. China advocates AI for good. We firmly oppose attempts to throw mud at China by distorting facts.”
A White House spokesperson referred questions about Z.ai to the Commerce Department, which declined to comment.
In an indication of the importance of AI to US intelligence, President Donald Trump in October appointed Jay Clayton, the director of national intelligence, as his new AI czar.
In-Q-Tel, an independent non-profit investment firm set up by the Central Intelligence Agency in 1999, has made AI-related investments as part of its focus on start-ups used by the military and intelligence agencies.
Chinese AI models have gained in popularity because they are cheaper than US rivals and are closing the performance gap.
In the last year, however, US AI labs OpenAI and Anthropic have raised concerns about Chinese rivals including Z.ai, DeepSeek, Moonshot and MiniMax allegedly extracting data from American models to try to reproduce some of those capabilities through a technique called distillation.
It is a practice that is common across the industry, but violates terms of service when used to create a competing technology.
OpenAI and Anthropic have warned that models created through this method often lack safeguards designed to block misuse of cyber and biological capabilities.
The Chinese companies have not responded to the allegations, though China’s Ministry of Commerce denied intellectual property violations and threatened to take all necessary measures to respond to actions that harm its interests.
The project involving CGTRI and the Z.ai founders ran from January 2018 through December 2021 and had a total approved project budget of 2.94 million yuan (S$563,000), according to the researchers’ report.
It sought to develop AI tools to analyse social media posts, spot key events and map peoples’ connections, according to the researchers’ report.
A key goal of the project was developing a knowledge base of “China-related key persons”, according to the report, which did not elaborate on who such people would be.
James Mulvenon, who leads intelligence research and analysis at Virginia-based Pamir Consulting, a national security contractor, reviewed the researchers’ report at Bloomberg’s request.
He said the project involved research with both military and civilian uses that seeks to revolutionise how people use AI to identify and track specific individuals.
China’s Ministry of State Security “had an obvious interest in funding this research and reaping the targeting benefits”, said Mulvenon, co-author of a book on Chinese industrial espionage.
Z.ai, also known as Zhipu, was spun out of research done at China’s elite Tsinghua University.
The company has received backing from local governments in China, as well as tech giants including Alibaba Group and Tencent, Bloomberg has reported.
In January, Z.ai became the first major Chinese generative-AI start-up to go public with its Hong Kong listing.
Its shares have outperformed Hong Kong’s Hang Seng Index, rising more than 300% since its initial public offering versus a 6% decline in the benchmark.
Z.ai’s current market capitalisation is about US$32 billion (S$40.9 billion).
In an interim financial report filed in September, Z.ai listed five founders as “key persons” who are part of the company’s “single largest group of shareholders”.
Four of them are listed as participating in the AI research project, which was jointly conducted by CGTRI, Tsinghua University and Southeast University, according to the researchers’ report.
Neither university responded to requests for comment.
Z.ai co-founder Li Juanzi, a professor in the computer science and technology department at Tsinghua University in Beijing, led the research project alongside CGTRI’s Cao Weibing and another professor from China’s Southeast University, the researchers’ report says.
It describes the three as being “jointly responsible for the design of the overall technical plan, coordination of tasks among the three participating institutions, and the overall research progress of the project”.
That report lists three other founders of Z.ai – Tang Jie, Xu Bin and Zhang Peng, who is the company’s chief executive officer – as co-authors of papers, co-inventors on patents, or holders of software copyrights in a directory of all the project’s research achievements.
The report explicitly states that non-participants cannot be included.
Only one person identified in Z.ai’s interim report as a company founder and “key person” was not named in the project’s documentation, chairman Liu Debing.
Z.ai’s recent handling of a ledger it posted online detailing vulnerabilities it had found in other companies’ software also raised alarms, according to a report by the China-focused consulting firm Garnaut Global.
The company is run by John Garnaut and Matt Pottinger, former national security officials from Australia and the US.
Garnaut Global said its analysis of Z.ai’s ledger, which was established on Aug 14, showed that Z.ai found 2,436 vulnerabilities in software from Microsoft, Intel, Alphabet’s Google and other leading Western companies.
Microsoft declined to comment, while Intel and Alphabet did not respond to requests for comment.
In the last year or so, some of the more advanced AI models have proven adept at finding flaws in software, some of which hackers might be able to exploit.
In some instances, the companies or computer researchers who find vulnerabilities alert the affected parties so they can be fixed before a hacker exploits them – sometimes for a cash reward.
But Z.ai chose to leave most of the affected vendors in the dark, disclosing just 5% of the vulnerabilities to the companies, according to the Garnaut Global report, which was reviewed by Bloomberg.
Ten days later, Z.ai took the ledger down, replacing it with a notice that the Chinese government would be managing vulnerabilities discovered by the company’s AI models through several databases, including one run by the Ministry of State Security, the Garnaut Global report said.
“Rather than sharing vulnerability details with the affected companies, Zhipu has given China’s peak cyberespionage agency access to these vulnerabilities,” said the report. BLOOMBERG

articles.title: Z.ai founders worked on research funded by China institute that Britain tied to spies
articles.body:
Z.ai founders worked on research funded by China institute that Britain tied to spies
- Four Z.AI founders worked on a 2018 to 2021 AI project partly funded by CGTRI, which MI5 said had “very strong ties” to China’s spy agency.
- The project, worth 2.94 million yuan, aimed to analyse social media, spot events and map people’s links, including a knowledge base of “China-related key persons”.
- The report links Z.AI to wider US scrutiny, including tech access limits, data extraction claims and concerns over its vulnerability ledger being shared with Chinese state databases.
AI generated
LONDON - Four founders of one of China’s most promising artificial intelligence companies, Z.ai, worked on research in a joint project with a technology institute that the British government accused of having “very strong ties” to China’s main spy agency, according to publicly available research papers from China and an “espionage alert” from Britain.
The nearly four-year AI research project, which overlapped with the company’s start in 2019, was co-funded by Beijing-based China General Technology Research Institute (CGTRI) and the National Natural Science Foundation of China, according to a previously unreported 78-page report that the project’s leaders compiled to detail their findings.
A CGTRI engineer and one of Z.ai’s founders were among the project’s leaders, and three other Z.ai founders contributed to the research, according to the report.
The report was published on a Chinese government website that provides research funding records.
Britain’s MI5 intelligence service, in the Sept 30 espionage alert, accused CGTRI of primarily existing to fund academic research that directly improves China’s main spy agency’s “technical capability for espionage”.
The first-of-its-kind bulletin said the institute has “very strong ties” to China’s Ministry of State Security and warned of potential criminal consequences for “any institution or individual continuing to conduct research ultimately funded by CGTRI following publication of this espionage alert”.
A spokesperson for China’s embassy in Britain called MI5’s allegations against CGTRI “baseless”.
The Z.ai founders’ work on research partially funded by an alleged Chinese intelligence front highlights the risks cited by some US officials regarding China’s growing prowess in AI – and could add to further scrutiny of Z.ai in particular.
The two countries are racing to develop a technology that is transforming the global economy and could give their military services an advantage.
The US restricted Z.ai’s access to American technology in 2025 based on allegations that the company aided the military with AI research.
More recently, US officials accused the company of systemically extracting proprietary knowledge from American rivals.
It is not clear what, if anything, any of Z.ai’s founders may have known about CGTRI’s alleged relationship with Chinese intelligence.
The MI5 alert did not mention Z.ai.
Z.ai did not respond to e-mailed requests for comment, nor did the four founders involved in the research project.
The company previously said the US decision to restrict its access to technology “lacked factual basis” and would not have a substantial impact on its business.
Reached by phone, a CGTRI representative said the institute does not do any external communication with anyone. Efforts to e-mail CGTRI for comment were unsuccessful.
Liu Chang, a spokesperson for the Chinese embassy in Washington, declined to address specific questions about Bloomberg’s report.
“I’m not familiar with the specifics,” he said. “The development of AI in China comes from greater self-reliance and strength in science and technology. China advocates AI for good. We firmly oppose attempts to throw mud at China by distorting facts.”
A White House spokesperson referred questions about Z.ai to the Commerce Department, which declined to comment.
In an indication of the importance of AI to US intelligence, President Donald Trump in October appointed Jay Clayton, the director of national intelligence, as his new AI czar.
In-Q-Tel, an independent non-profit investment firm set up by the Central Intelligence Agency in 1999, has made AI-related investments as part of its focus on start-ups used by the military and intelligence agencies.
Chinese AI models have gained in popularity because they are cheaper than US rivals and are closing the performance gap.
In the last year, however, US AI labs OpenAI and Anthropic have raised concerns about Chinese rivals including Z.ai, DeepSeek, Moonshot and MiniMax allegedly extracting data from American models to try to reproduce some of those capabilities through a technique called distillation.
It is a practice that is common across the industry, but violates terms of service when used to create a competing technology.
OpenAI and Anthropic have warned that models created through this method often lack safeguards designed to block misuse of cyber and biological capabilities.
The Chinese companies have not responded to the allegations, though China’s Ministry of Commerce denied intellectual property violations and threatened to take all necessary measures to respond to actions that harm its interests.
The project involving CGTRI and the Z.ai founders ran from January 2018 through December 2021 and had a total approved project budget of 2.94 million yuan (S$563,000), according to the researchers’ report.
It sought to develop AI tools to analyse social media posts, spot key events and map peoples’ connections, according to the researchers’ report.
A key goal of the project was developing a knowledge base of “China-related key persons”, according to the report, which did not elaborate on who such people would be.
James Mulvenon, who leads intelligence research and analysis at Virginia-based Pamir Consulting, a national security contractor, reviewed the researchers’ report at Bloomberg’s request.
He said the project involved research with both military and civilian uses that seeks to revolutionise how people use AI to identify and track specific individuals.
China’s Ministry of State Security “had an obvious interest in funding this research and reaping the targeting benefits”, said Mulvenon, co-author of a book on Chinese industrial espionage.
Z.ai, also known as Zhipu, was spun out of research done at China’s elite Tsinghua University.
The company has received backing from local governments in China, as well as tech giants including Alibaba Group and Tencent, Bloomberg has reported.
In January, Z.ai became the first major Chinese generative-AI start-up to go public with its Hong Kong listing.
Its shares have outperformed Hong Kong’s Hang Seng Index, rising more than 300% since its initial public offering versus a 6% decline in the benchmark.
Z.ai’s current market capitalisation is about US$32 billion (S$40.9 billion).
In an interim financial report filed in September, Z.ai listed five founders as “key persons” who are part of the company’s “single largest group of shareholders”.
Four of them are listed as participating in the AI research project, which was jointly conducted by CGTRI, Tsinghua University and Southeast University, according to the researchers’ report.
Neither university responded to requests for comment.
Z.ai co-founder Li Juanzi, a professor in the computer science and technology department at Tsinghua University in Beijing, led the research project alongside CGTRI’s Cao Weibing and another professor from China’s Southeast University, the researchers’ report says.
It describes the three as being “jointly responsible for the design of the overall technical plan, coordination of tasks among the three participating institutions, and the overall research progress of the project”.
That report lists three other founders of Z.ai – Tang Jie, Xu Bin and Zhang Peng, who is the company’s chief executive officer – as co-authors of papers, co-inventors on patents, or holders of software copyrights in a directory of all the project’s research achievements.
The report explicitly states that non-participants cannot be included.
Only one person identified in Z.ai’s interim report as a company founder and “key person” was not named in the project’s documentation, chairman Liu Debing.
Z.ai’s recent handling of a ledger it posted online detailing vulnerabilities it had found in other companies’ software also raised alarms, according to a report by the China-focused consulting firm Garnaut Global.
The company is run by John Garnaut and Matt Pottinger, former national security officials from Australia and the US.
Garnaut Global said its analysis of Z.ai’s ledger, which was established on Aug 14, showed that Z.ai found 2,436 vulnerabilities in software from Microsoft, Intel, Alphabet’s Google and other leading Western companies.
Microsoft declined to comment, while Intel and Alphabet did not respond to requests for comment.
In the last year or so, some of the more advanced AI models have proven adept at finding flaws in software, some of which hackers might be able to exploit.
In some instances, the companies or computer researchers who find vulnerabilities alert the affected parties so they can be fixed before a hacker exploits them – sometimes for a cash reward.
But Z.ai chose to leave most of the affected vendors in the dark, disclosing just 5% of the vulnerabilities to the companies, according to the Garnaut Global report, which was reviewed by Bloomberg.
Ten days later, Z.ai took the ledger down, replacing it with a notice that the Chinese government would be managing vulnerabilities discovered by the company’s AI models through several databases, including one run by the Ministry of State Security, the Garnaut Global report said.
“Rather than sharing vulnerability details with the affected companies, Zhipu has given China’s peak cyberespionage agency access to these vulnerabilities,” said the report. BLOOMBERG

articles.title: Washington holds up Patriot missiles for Ukraine amid Trump-Zelensky tensions: report
articles.body:
WASHINGTON, Oct. 19 (Xinhua) -- The U.S. administration has not approved the transfer of Patriot interceptor missiles to Ukraine amid tensions between U.S. President Donald Trump and his Ukrainian counterpart Volodymyr Zelensky, The Washington Post reported on Monday.
At least some of the missiles are being transferred from countries friendly to Ukraine, but the handovers require approval from U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, the report said, citing a U.S. official and three other people familiar with the matter.
Hegseth has neither formally rejected the transfers nor completed the required steps to approve them, according to the report.
The United States retains control because the weapons are U.S.-made and are shipped abroad under the agreement that transfers to other countries require U.S. sign-off, said the report.
A Ukrainian official told the newspaper last week that only "a couple" of interceptor missiles remained in Ukraine's stockpile.
The delay comes as Trump has repeatedly criticized Zelensky in recent weeks.
"I think it's time for somebody else to negotiate on behalf of Ukraine," Trump told reporters on Monday. Earlier this month, he called for Kiev to "get a new president."
"Zelensky doesn't know what he's talking about," Trump said. "Zelensky is a man that should have had this war settled a long time ago."
"Russia, frankly, has been fine on Ukraine. They haven't been doing much," Trump said.
In an interview on Sunday, Zelensky said he did not want to believe that Washington was seeking to end the Russia-Ukraine conflict at Ukraine's expense. "But that's how it looks," he said. ■

articles.title: Witkoff hopes to visit Russia after meeting Zelensky in Oslo — Axios reporter
articles.body:
WASHINGTON, October 20. /TASS/. US Presidential Special Envoy Steve Witkoff hopes to visit Russia and meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin after holding talks with Vladimir Zelensky in Oslo on Tuesday, Barak Ravid, a correspondent for Axios and Israel’s Channel 12, said on X, citing sources.
According to the sources, Witkoff is currently flying to Oslo for a meeting with Zelensky scheduled for Tuesday. Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store, as well as representatives of the United Kingdom, Germany, Italy, France, the European Union leadership, and NATO, are expected to take part in the talks.
"The objective is to continue aligning on a comprehensive proposal that can form the basis for renewed negotiations with Russia," Ravid said.
According to one of his sources, Witkoff hopes to visit Russia after Oslo, where he intends to discuss with Putin the proposals developed jointly with Ukraine and European partners. Last week, representatives of the United States, Ukraine, and Europe worked on developing these proposals at the technical level. They include the release of Stephen Hubbard, a 72-year-old US citizen convicted in Russia of fighting on the side of the Ukrainian armed forces.
"President Trump has directed an intensive process to develop a comprehensive peace proposal with Ukraine and Europe, and the next step is to test whether that work can form the basis for serious negotiations with Russia", a US official told Ravid, adding. "These discussions remain fluid, and substantial work remains. President Trump’s objective is clear: to end the killing, bring the war to a close, and establish the conditions for a lasting peace that benefits Ukraine, Russia, Europe, and the United States."
Jared Kushner, a special envoy and son-in-law of the US president, will not accompany Witkoff in person this time because he has the flu. He will participate in the consultations remotely.
On October 1, Putin said Russia would like to end hostilities in Ukraine through a peaceful settlement as soon as possible. Moscow is ready for negotiations but sees no willingness on the part of the Kiev government to engage in talks, the president added.

articles.title: Taiwan tracks 14 Chinese military aircraft, 14 ships
articles.body:
TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Ministry of National Defense tracked 14 Chinese military aircraft, seven naval vessels, and seven official ships between 6 a.m. on Monday and the same time Tuesday.
In response, Taiwan deployed aircraft, naval ships, and coastal-based missile systems. Eight People’s Liberation Army aircraft sorties crossed the Taiwan Strait median line in the country’s northern, central, southwestern, and eastern air defense identification zones, according to the ministry.
So far this month, Taiwan has tracked Chinese aircraft 134 times and ships 237 times. Since September 2020, China has increased its use of gray zone tactics by incrementally increasing the number of military aircraft and naval vessels operating around the country.
Gray zone tactics are defined as “an effort or series of efforts beyond steady-state deterrence and assurance that attempts to achieve one’s security objectives without resort to direct and sizable use of force.”

articles.title: ‘I don't recognise the country I grew up in anymore’: some Israelis are tempted by exile
articles.body:
‘I don't recognise the country I grew up in anymore’: some Israelis are tempted by exile
From our special correspondent in Tel Aviv – Since 2023, Israel has experienced an unprecedented brain drain. With the October 27 legislative elections approaching, many graduates are considering leaving the country if the right-wing and far-right coalition led by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu remains in power.
The impressive Tel Aviv University campus is getting ready for the start of the academic year. At the cafeteria terrace, students greet each other among groups of soldiers who have come to visit the Museum of the Jewish People.
In his office, Itai Ater, an economist at the university’s Coller School of Management, does not hide his staunch opposition to Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s government. In February 2026, the researcher and his team triggered a controversy by publishing a study based on government data showing that, since 2023, 50,000 Israeli graduates have been leaving the country each year.
Brain drain under Netanyahu’s government
The Israelis who emigrate are for the most part doctors or engineers and 80 percent of them are under 40 with high incomes.
“For us, it’s clear that such a jump can only be explained by an event that occurred in Israel,” Ater said. “We’ve seen a sharp increase in departures starting in the summer of 2023, before October 7. And we can attribute the beginning of this phenomenon to the judicial overhaul introduced by Netanyahu in January 2023 [a judicial reform bill aimed at limiting the powers of the Supreme Court].”
According to him, this brain drain is not driven by economic factors or by cuts in funding for public services, research, or innovation, but is primarily a reaction to the political situation.
“You look at what has happened in Israel over the past four years and it’s crazy, no matter how you look at it: October 7, the wars in Lebanon and Gaza, the reservists’ draft, Iran,” he said. “And on top of that, you look at the government allocating huge sums to ultra-Orthodox Jews. So, if you’re secular, you do your military service, you pay taxes, and you look into the future and ask yourself, ‘do I want to raise my kids here in Israel?’”
A country ‘gone mad’
Ater makes no secret of his left-wing political commitment and wants to warn the public of the consequences of this brain drain.
“The Israeli economy depends heavily on human capital. We don’t have natural resources, oil or things of the sort, unlike Venezuela or Iran … As a citizen and as an economist, I want Israel to become a sane country again – a normal country.”
He added that, as Israel’s image around the world deteriorates, academics “suffer from a lot of boycotts” and that some “research collaborations are terminated because we are from Israel”.
While 150,000 graduates have already packed their bags since 2023, a victory by the right and the ultra-nationalist far right in the October 27 elections could – in his view – lead to even more departures.
If the ruling coalition is re-elected, Tamar*, 32, a product manager at a company specialising in AI, said she would seriously consider leaving the country with her husband and her one-year-old son.
The “endless wars”, the influence of Minister of National Security Itamar Ben-Gvir and “Benjamin Netanyahu’s lies” have become unbearable, she said.
Read moreHow Netanyahu survived the political fallout from the October 7 attacks
“Because of the war, I can't sleep anymore,” she added. “My husband has served more than 400 days of reserve duty in the army for the past three years and I'm very angry at the government for allowing the ultra-Orthodox to avoid military service. I don’t recognise the country I grew up in anymore – even though my mother’s side of my family has lived in Jerusalem for 14 generations.”
A divisive government
As elections approach, Israelis are still traumatised by Hamas’ unprecedented attacks from October 7, 2023. Between those who constantly demand revenge and those who want to understand how such an attack could have happened, dialogue seems to have fractured. The right and the far right use a constant messianic and religious rhetoric to discredit anyone who opposes them.
During this year’s commemorations of the October 7 massacre in southern Israel, Yinon Magal, a journalist from Channel 14 – which very aggressively supports Netanyahu’s government – caused a scandal by asking loved ones of former Israeli hostages held in Gaza to apologise to the government.
The polemicist was targeting the authors of a collective book published in 2024,“Mr. Abandonment: the legacy of the man who forsook the hostages”, in which relatives of hostages criticised Netanyahu’s handling of the crisis.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Read moreTrump endorses embattled Israeli PM Netanyahu ahead of October 27 election
The journalist called the authors “the most despicable people who live in the State of Israel”. The sister of Yarden Bibas – one of the hostages whose wife and two children died in captivity – responded to Magal’s comments by stating: “These remarks are part of a deliberate campaign to incite hatred and sow the seeds of division for the sole purpose of keeping in power the person who, to this day, refuses to take responsibility for the greatest failure we have ever experienced.”
Liberals in right-wing crosshairs
In this toxic climate, Tamar feels she no longer knows “where this country is going” and is considering moving abroad if the same government is re-elected.
“I love this country, but it’s become unbearable, I’m looking into my company’s offices abroad, in Europe and in the United States,” she said. “I know it won’t be easy because this government has destroyed our relationship with countries all over the world. I have family living in New Jersey who are now afraid to say they’re Jewish. If I leave, I hope it will be for a few years and not for the rest of my life … I’m not afraid of being called a traitor because my husband and I have done our military service.”
Like many Israelis, Tamar is frightened by the brutality of the Netanyahu government, which makes no secret of its hatred for the “Tel Aviv liberals”.
“My biggest fear is how can I raise my son here in Israel, when there are no liberal values and where a small number of religious fanatics control everything,” she said, adding that, in Israel, “saying you're on the left has become a bad word. I want to live in a democratic state.”
Maya*, a general practitioner from Tel Aviv whose husband also works in tech, came to the same conclusion as Tamar.
“These last four years, there was October 7, Iranian missiles hit Tel Aviv,” said the mother of three young children, the last of whom was nearly born in a shelter during a strike. “With war and the mobilisation of reservists, we’re shortstaffed in the healthcare, education, and early-childhood sectors. I feel violence creeping in everywhere – it's completely crazy.”
Intimidation and violence
For Maya, the driving force behind the polarisation of Israeli society is none other than Netanyahu, who was already in power when she was in sixth grade (she is now 42 years old).
With tears in her eyes, she said she fears for her parents’ safety, who have displayed signs in their window showing their support for The Democrats, the left-wing party that succeeded the Israeli Labor Party created by Israel’s founding fathers.
“My mother is 73, and for the past four years, she has taken part in every protest against Netanyahu,” Maya said. “The ones against judicial reform, the ones calling for the release of hostages in Jerusalem, and she was knocked down by a police officer on horseback. She’s a calm woman who wants to help others. And yet her photo was posted on social media because, as a lawyer, she defended Palestinians from the West Bank. I think this campaign was orchestrated by very powerful people.”
Drying her tears, Maya spoke about her upcoming with sadness.
“My husband really wants to leave, I do a little bit less,” she explained. “But he’s really worried. He’s worried that the election results will trigger violence in Israel and I think he’s right. Even if I don’t really see myself living in another country, I’ve been looking into where I could work. After the elections we’re going to visit friends who have moved to Portugal. We’re also thinking about Athens – many Israelis moved there after October 7 and it’s close to Israel.”
‘War crimes committed in my name’
Israel’s first elections since the October 7 attacks reveal a society fractured by fear and anger. The left, the centre, the right, and the far right are clashing over military service exemptions for the ultra-Orthodox, Benjamin Netanyahu’s refusal to create a commission of inquiry into the massacre committed by Hamas, and whether or not political parties representing Israeli Arabs should be included in a future opposition coalition.
Read moreNo longer the same Israel? October 7 and the future of the Jewish State
Maya also expressed deep unease when asked about the destruction of the Gaza Strip.
“I feel that, in my name and with money from my taxes, horrible war crimes are being committed,” she said. “It’s something that’s very difficult to bear and to put into words. I’m not ready to stop treating people like human beings because of the place they were born in or the language they speak; that’s the path that, morally, leads to hell. And men who come back from their reserve duty in the army are traumatised, become violent and are desperate because their professional activity is crumbling.”
On October 27, Tamar will vote for Gadi Eisenkot – the main opponent to Netanyahu, or former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett; while Maya will cast her ballot for Yair Golan’s Democrats – both with the hope of not having to leave their country.
*Tamar and Maya’s first names were changed at their request.
This article has been translated from the original in French.

articles.title: Russian attack damages Accounting Chamber premises in Kyiv, building not fit for purpose – photos
articles.body:
Russian attack damages Accounting Chamber premises in Kyiv, building not fit for purpose – photos
One of the Accounting Chamber's premises in Kyiv has been severely damaged in a Russian attack, with equipment and other property destroyed or damaged. The Accounting Chamber is Ukraine's supreme audit institution, responsible for overseeing how public funds are collected and spent, including the state budget.
Source: Olha Pishchanska, Head of the Accounting Chamber
Details: The security guard at the premises was injured but did not require hospitalisation.
"This is the third time this building has been damaged since the start of the full-scale war. Experts are currently assessing the damage and dealing with the aftermath of the strike," Pishchanska wrote.
Around 100 employees of the Accounting Chamber worked in the damaged building. It housed two audit departments – one responsible for the state budget, financial institutions and debt, and the other for the humanitarian and social sectors – as well as the Accounting Chamber's territorial office in Kyiv.
The Accounting Chamber continues to operate and carry out its duties. The building is temporarily not fit for purpose, so the body is quickly arranging additional workspaces in other premises.
Background:
- A Russian ballistic missile attack on Kyiv on the night of 18-19 October damaged the building of the National Commission for State Regulation of Energy and Public Utilities.
- On 14 October, the Verkhovna Rada (Ukrainian parliament) launched an independent competition to select new members of the Accounting Chamber. This is a condition for financial assistance to Ukraine from the European Union and the International Monetary Fund.

articles.title: Trump has made a deal with Moscow, but Zelensky has other ideas
articles.body:
Trump has made a deal with Moscow, but Zelensky has other ideas
The diesel deal between Moscow and Washington has once again shaken up the geopolitical chessboard, with each passing day bringing fresh and unexpected developments. Most striking is Kiev’s behavior. Despite his enormous dependence on Washington, Vladimir Zelensky has decided to challenge Donald Trump directly, adopting an unusually confrontational approach.
A more pragmatic politician might have announced a moratorium on strikes against Russian oil refineries until the US congressional elections, particularly as Washington had demanded no further concessions. Instead, Zelensky has chosen confrontation, creating a diplomatic crisis of his own making, but whether it develops into something more serious remains to be seen.
Relations between Kiev and Washington have deteriorated before, most notably following the notorious Oval Office confrontation, although that rupture lasted only a few weeks. Western European leaders and congressional hawks worked tirelessly to repair the damage. This time, however, the circumstances are different.
The NATO Europeans appear to have abandoned attempts to charm Trump, Senator Lindsey Graham is no longer on Capitol Hill, while Keith Kellogg, previously sympathetic to Kiev, has departed the administration, thus the pressure on Trump has diminished, although that hardly guarantees a fundamental change in American policy.
For one thing, the diesel agreement has done little to clarify the prospects for peace, given, according to leaks from Washington, American officials continue to promote proposals, including freezing hostilities along existing lines, that Moscow considers unacceptable.
Even if Washington succeeds in forcing Kiev back to the negotiating table, there’s no guarantee that the understandings reached at Anchorage can be revived and Trump could just as easily reverse course, as he has done before, and blame Russia for another diplomatic deadlock. Meanwhile, influential figures within his administration, particularly Secretary of State Marco Rubio, remain deeply skeptical of Moscow, so their relative silence should not be mistaken for acquiescence.
Nor is there much reason to believe Russian diesel exports to the US will quickly bring down fuel prices or transform the electoral landscape.
The agreement is primarily a political gesture, intended to reassure Trump’s increasingly disillusioned core supporters that their president understands their economic difficulties and is attempting to find a way out, yet it’s unlikely to prevent Republicans from losing control of the House of Representatives. The Senate remains uncertain, but its fate will depend on numerous factors, with diesel prices only one consideration.
A Democratic-controlled Congress would almost certainly confront the White House over Ukraine, seeking to preserve American assistance to Kiev, while another impeachment campaign cannot be ruled out either. Such a confrontation could consume Trump’s attention and leave greater responsibility for foreign policy in the hands of officials such as Rubio, whose instincts towards Russia are considerably less accommodating.
There’s also the possibility of a more fundamental reshaping of the Ukrainian political project, where replacing Zelensky, under external pressure, with a leader more acceptable to Washington could help reconcile American and Western European approaches and the growing crisis of governance in Kiev makes this scenario increasingly conceivable.
None of this diminishes Moscow’s diplomatic achievement in securing the diesel agreement, where it’s demonstrated that Washington is prepared to negotiate directly with Russia when American interests demand it, regardless of Kiev’s objections.
But diplomatic success shouldn’t breed complacency and the underlying contradictions remain unresolved, the prospects for a durable settlement are uncertain, and too many powerful interests still favor prolonging the confrontation.
The diesel deal may have changed the immediate political calculations, but it hasn’t altered the fundamental dynamics of the conflict.
This article was first published by Kommersant, and was translated and edited by the RT team

articles.title: Zelenskyy: In any case, we have more in common than US and Russia do
articles.body:
Zelenskyy: US has more in common with Ukraine than with Russia
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said he believes that Ukraine and the US have more in common than Russia and the US, and that Ukraine would like to continue to have an open, pragmatic and honest relationship with the United States.
Source: Zelenskyy in an interview with Corriere della Sera
Quote: "We have always had important, strong strategic relations with the United States of America. Our bilateral relationship began developing particularly actively during the full-scale war. I am grateful for all the support.
But we have always built our relationship on honesty, fairness and, most importantly, transparency. Because when you lie while your people are at war, it is very painful. That is why I have always wanted to hide nothing and never lie to the president of the United States.
In any case, we have more in common than America does with Russia. Most people in Ukraine and the United States of America understand this.
We would like to continue having the same open, honest, and pragmatic relations with America that we have today."
Details: Zelenskyy added that Ukraine is in favour of a mutual energy ceasefire and said that if Russia ignored it, Ukraine's partners could provide enough air defence systems to enable the country to protect its energy infrastructure.
Quote: "The position is very simple. We support a mutual energy ceasefire. If we are talking about the idea that we should not strike back at Russian energy facilities after they strike our gas, electricity, oil – everything. The Russians are striking. America cannot stop them.
Let's believe that America really wants to but cannot. Then, as a partner, I am willing to meet President Trump halfway: if they strike us and we cannot strike back – that is neither honest nor fair – but if this is what you need, if you cannot rein Putin in, then give us interceptor missiles so I can protect our energy infrastructure. You couldn't stop Putin – but you helped Ukraine."
Background:
- On Sunday 18 October, Zelenskyy accused US President Donald Trump of trying to pressure Ukraine into capitulating to Russia and of delaying deliveries of Patriot interceptor missiles.
- Trump accused Zelenskyy of never having wanted to end Russia's war against Ukraine.
- On 19 October, Trump said he is willing to meet Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping to discuss ending the war in Ukraine, even without Zelenskyy taking part.

articles.title: Lebanon: Tunnel found near Beirut sparks fresh Hezbollah tension
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Lebanon: Tunnel found near Beirut sparks fresh Hezbollah tensions
The discovery of a tunnel northeast of Beirut has sparked fresh tensions in Lebanon, with opposition lawmakers demanding a security crackdown amid suspicions over possible links to Hezbollah.
Lebanese army engineers launched an investigation on Monday after a tunnel was discovered in the Fanar-Zaitariyeh area of the Metn district, prompting calls for a comprehensive security sweep and the arrest of those responsible.
The discovery comes just over a week after Lebanese security forces intercepted a shipment of explosives belonging to Hezbollah in Dahr al-Baydar, raising tensions between the group and its political opponents.
However, a Lebanese military source told The New Arab that initial investigations suggested the newly discovered tunnel was small and was not intended for military or security purposes.
"Inspections and investigations are continuing, but so far it has emerged that the tunnel is small and was not prepared for military or security use," the source said.
Fanar mayor Michel Salameh told The New Arab that a resident discovered the tunnel on Sunday evening and alerted the municipality, which subsequently contacted the security authorities.
Salameh said the tunnel was located in a remote wooded area that was difficult to access, with the excavation concealed by trees.
تواصلت صباحاً مع وزير الدفاع، وطلبت منه اجراء الجيش والقوى الأمنية مسحاً شاملاً لمنطقة الرويسات - الجديدة ومحيطها، عقب اكتشاف نفق في المنطقة. وأبدى تجاوباً مع المطلب. نفق في المتن، شحنة متفجرات في ضهر البيدر، ومواجهات مع قوى الأمن في الضاحية… مؤشرات خطيرة تفرض وضع حدّ نهائي لازدواجية السلاح والتنظيم العسكري لحزب الله على كامل الأراضي اللبنانية. استمرار عمل السلاح غير الشرعي والتنظيم العسكري والأمني لحزب الله يشكل خطر داهم، وعلى الدولة الحسم حفاظاً على لبنان.
— Samy Gemayel (@samygemayel) October 19, 2026
When the vegetation was removed, a ladder, basic digging equipment and freshly excavated sand were discovered nearby.
"The tunnel is located in a wooded area in a remote spot that is difficult to reach," Salameh said, adding that the municipality had immediately informed army intelligence, which dispatched an engineering unit to inspect the site.
According to the mayor's preliminary assessment, the tunnel was approximately four metres deep, extended horizontally for two metres and then continued for another four metres.
He suggested that the excavation appeared recent, possibly dating back no more than a week, although its location made it difficult to detect.
Hezbollah accused as lawmakers demand security sweep
The discovery quickly prompted accusations against Hezbollah, which maintains influence in parts of the surrounding Zaitariyeh-Roueissat al-Jadideh area.
However, no evidence establishing Hezbollah's involvement in the tunnel's construction has been announced.
Lebanese Kataeb Party leader and MP Sami Gemayel said he had contacted Defence Minister Michel Menassa on Monday morning to demand a comprehensive security sweep of Roueissat al-Jadideh and its surroundings.
Gemayel said the minister had responded positively to his request.
"A tunnel in Metn, an explosives shipment in Dahr al-Baydar, and confrontations with security forces in the southern suburbs... dangerous indicators that require a definitive end to the duality of arms and Hezbollah's military organisation across all Lebanese territory," Gemayel said.
He warned that the continued operation of Hezbollah's military and security structures outside state authority posed a serious threat to Lebanon.
Kataeb MP Elias Hankach, who represents the area, also called for immediate army intervention.
He said he was contacting the Lebanese army command to demand searches of streets and buildings in Roueissat and neighbouring areas, the confiscation of weapons, arrests of those involved and the establishment of permanent security checkpoints and patrols.
The accusations come amid growing calls from Hezbollah's opponents for the Lebanese authorities to accelerate efforts to bring all weapons under exclusive state control.
Explosives seizure deepens political divisions
The tunnel controversy follows the seizure of a shipment of explosives in Dahr al-Baydar, on a route linking Beirut to the Bekaa Valley and Syria, more than a week ago.
Hezbollah acknowledged ownership of the explosives, insisting they were intended exclusively for use against Israel, and demanded their return along with the release of those detained.
The case has become a major point of contention between Hezbollah and the Lebanese government, with authorities pledging to pursue those involved in transporting and possessing weapons outside state control.
Further tensions erupted on Friday evening in the Galerie Semaan area at the entrance to Beirut's southern suburbs, when Hezbollah members confronted security personnel who had arrived to seal a pharmaceutical warehouse.
The incident was subsequently contained, but it fuelled criticism from Hezbollah's opponents over the group's continued security presence in areas where it holds considerable influence.
Lebanese security forces have intensified operations in recent days, including in Beirut's southern suburbs and the eastern Bekaa and Baalbek-Hermel regions, targeting wanted suspects, smuggling networks and unauthorised crossings along the Syrian border.
Hezbollah warns government over rising tensions
Hezbollah MP Ali Fayyad, a member of the Loyalty to the Resistance parliamentary bloc, warned on Monday that the Lebanese authorities bore "full responsibility for pushing the country towards dangerous internal tensions".
In a statement distributed by Hezbollah's media relations office, Fayyad accused the government of confronting a major component of Lebanese society and pursuing policies dictated by foreign powers.
He argued that the dispute had expanded beyond Hezbollah's weapons to encompass the movement's social, institutional and political presence.
"The authorities deliberately, knowingly and persistently expanded the dispute with the resistance, so that it is no longer limited to the issue of weapons," Fayyad said.
He also accused the government of compromising Lebanese sovereignty and failing to confront Israel's continued occupation and attacks.
Prime Minister Nawaf Salam, meanwhile, reiterated on Sunday that lasting stability could not be achieved without extending state authority across all Lebanese territory.
"Stability will not be established in the country unless the state's authority is extended over all its territory, even gradually, exclusively through its own forces," Salam said.
The prime minister said he had contacted army commander General Rodolphe Haykal and Internal Security Forces chief Major General Raed Abdallah to commend the increased deployment of security personnel across Greater Beirut.
The measures followed overnight gatherings in the capital that had raised public concerns about security.
Salam also met Justice Minister Adel Nassar and Public Prosecutor Rami al-Hajj to review the investigation into the Dahr al-Baydar explosives shipment and ensure that everyone involved in possessing or transporting unauthorised weapons was brought before the judiciary.
He stressed that there would be no limits to the investigation beyond those imposed by law.
Salam further urged political groups to prioritise Lebanon's national interests over foreign agendas, reiterating that decisions over war and peace must remain exclusively in the hands of the state and its constitutional institutions.
His comments followed a telephone conversation last week in which US Secretary of State Marco Rubio urged Lebanese President Joseph Aoun to hold those responsible for ordering, financing and directing the explosives shipment accountable.
Rubio also insisted that returning the seized explosives to Hezbollah should be ruled out entirely.
The latest incidents have heightened concerns over internal instability as Lebanon faces continued Israeli military attacks and occupation in the south.

articles.title: Britain sends Typhoon jets to shield Saudi skies from Houthi drones, missiles
articles.body:
Britain sends Typhoon jets to shield Saudi skies from Houthi drones, missiles
LONDON – Britain will fly Royal Air Force Typhoon fighter jets on defensive missions to help protect Saudi cities and critical national infrastructure from Houthi aerial attacks, the Ministry of Defence said on Oct 20.
The ministry said the warplanes would operate only in a defensive role and would not conduct offensive strikes against the Iran-aligned Houthis, whose attacks Britain says threaten regional stability and risk disrupting energy supplies and trade routes.
“The continuing attacks from the Houthis on our ally Saudi Arabia are absolutely despicable. The targeting of the airport in Riyadh, in particular, shows the lengths the Houthis are going to escalate the situation in the region,” Defence Minister Wes Streeting said in a statement.
“That’s why today I have approved further UK military support,” he said. “RAF Typhoons will fly defensive air missions to help protect Saudi airspace from drones and missiles.”
The additional support follows a request from Saudi Arabia’s government, which Prime Minister Andy Burnham said earlier in October Britain was prepared to consider.
Britain will also deploy an Atlas A400M transport aircraft and military advisers, expanding assistance announced in September that included an RAF Voyager air-to-air refuelling aircraft but not fighter jets.
Houthi attacks against Saudi oil facilities and other infrastructure have intensified in recent weeks as the conflict in Yemen has escalated.
Inside Yemen, the authorities said a Houthi strike on Oct 19 against a training camp for Saudi-backed government security forces killed 58 people. REUTERS

articles.title: Five children from same family killed in Russian missile strike laid to rest in Dnipropetrovsk Oblast
articles.body:
Five children from same family killed in Russian missile strike laid to rest in Dnipropetrovsk Oblast
Five children from the Voronov family – Dominika, 16, Viorika, 14, Zakharii, 13, Federika, 9, and 18-month-old Artem – have been laid to rest in Radushne, Dnipropetrovsk Oblast. Their lives were cut short on the night of 29-30 July when a Russian missile struck their family home.
Source: Suspilne Dnipro
Details: The children had been considered missing for around two and a half months, but forensic examinations have now confirmed their deaths.
The children's grandmother, Nelia, said all that remained of the house after the strike was the foundation. Throughout this time, she had been praying that all the dead would be identified.
Quote from Nelia: "We didn't know how they would be separated. But now they will all be together as one family there in the cemetery. No miracle was possible. The only thing I asked God for was that they would all be found and identified. There was no one else there, only members of the family – 10 people."
Inna lives near the place where the Voronov family's home once stood. She said she ran outside immediately after the explosion and saw only rubble where the house had been.
Quote from Inna: "The missile hit right in the middle of the house, we were told, in the children's room. We were putting out a fire in the neighbouring house, where two children were trapped under the rubble. When we got them out and went to the [Voronovs'] house, there was no one left to look for… We knew them. All the children were friends with each other. They were good people."
Details: The Voronovs' neighbour Mykola said they had always been a happy, close-knit family.
"In a large family, everyone is like that – they help one another and live as one family. It's hard to comprehend what happened. Such pain," he said.
Dominika's best friend, Karina, also attended the funeral. She said they often spent time together.
Quote from Karina: "[Dominika] was a very kind and sincere person. She really loved beadwork. I even have a pendant from her. She was so wonderful that I just don't have the words. She loved children so much. She was even planning to have a family of her own one day. She wanted two children."
Details: Dominika's classmate Sofiia remembered her as a cheerful, smiling person.
"I didn't know her family, but Dominika was a very cheerful person who was always smiling. I never saw her sad. It is so sad that this happened," Sofiia said.
Ihor Kozachenko, headteacher at the school where Dominika studied, described her as a good friend and an optimistic person who always had a smile on her face.
"She was someone who supported others during difficult times, when some people were in despair. She always had a kind word for others. This is a huge loss for our school. Her family were very close – that is rare these days," he said.
Tetiana Usenko, headteacher at the school attended by Federika, Zakharii and Viorika, said the children's classmates still cannot talk about them without crying.
What is known about the tragedy
On the night of 29-30 July, Russian forces attacked the Kryvyi Rih district. A ballistic missile struck a house in the settlement of Radushne, where the Voronov family lived.
Artem Voronov, 47, and his wife Olena, 41, had 10 children. Seven of them were at home with their parents that night: Mark, 17, Dominika, 16, Viorika, 14, Zakharii, 13, Azarii-Ilai, 11, Federika, 9, and Emiliia, 6.
Their 18-month-old grandson, Artem, was also visiting. He was the son of their eldest son, Danylo, a serviceman based in Mykolaiv. Artem had been due to return home that weekend and had already been enrolled in nursery.
Until the latest forensic findings were released, the deaths of only five family members had been officially confirmed: the parents, Olena and Artem, and three of the children – Mark, Azarii-Ilai and Emiliia.
