articles.title: Iran says 20 to 30 aircraft destroyed during war with US, Israel
articles.body:
Between 20 and 30 aircraft were destroyed during Iran’s war with the US and Israel, the head of the country’s state-owned flag carrier said Monday, according to the semi-official Tasnim news agency.
Taher Abdolhai, CEO of Iran Air, also known as HOMA, said at a news conference that Iran needs approximately 1,000 passenger aircraft but currently has only around 300.
Of those, between 130 and 140 aircraft were operational before the war, with 20 to 30 destroyed during the conflict, he said.
Abdolhai also said between 70 and 80 aircraft were targeted during the war.
He claimed Israeli attacks had caused particularly severe damage to Iran Air aircraft, saying some planes belonging to other operators were struck by single missiles, while one of his airline’s aircraft was completely destroyed.
READ: Iraq seeks to host talks between Iran and Gulf States in Baghdad
The airline chief also said international sanctions and restrictions have gradually weakened Iran Air’s operations, reducing its operational fleet and limiting access to profitable routes.
He cited difficulties obtaining spare parts, financial constraints and staffing challenges as major obstacles facing the airline.
Abdolhai said Iran Air employs more than 9,000 people, stressing the need to improve efficiency as the number of operational aircraft declines.
He also opposed privatizing the national carrier, arguing that Iran Air serves strategic national interests beyond commercial aviation.
The remarks come amid the continuing consequences of the US-Israeli war against Iran, which has caused extensive damage to the country’s military and civilian infrastructure.
US sanctions have restricted Iran’s access to new aircraft, spare parts, maintenance services and international financing. Washington’s withdrawal from the nuclear deal in 2018 and reimposition of sanctions disrupted aircraft purchases from Boeing and Airbus, leaving some planes grounded and increasing maintenance costs.
READ: Vance acknowledges ‘failures’ in US handling of Iran war

articles.title: Iran warns UN over Trump, Israel military threats
articles.body:
Iran's ambassador and chargé d'affaires to the United Nations, Gholamhossein Darzi, warned the UN secretary-general and the Security Council over what the letter called the "arrogant threats" of US President Donald Trump and the Zionist regime.
In the letter to UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres and the Security Council president, Darzi said the threats are part of US and Zionist regime wars of aggression against Iran that began on June 13, 2025 and Feb. 28, 2026, along with deliberate attacks on civilians and critical infrastructure. He said they risk further serious violations of international law with catastrophic humanitarian consequences and dangers to regional and international peace and security. He warned that responsibility rests with the United States, the Zionist regime and anyone who directly or indirectly supports their aggression and state terrorism.
The letter cited US media reports on Oct. 15, 2026 that the White House and Pentagon had prepared military options including the possible use of the GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast, known as the "mother of all bombs," against Iran. It said Trump discussed the weapon in a television interview the same day and threatened Iran with further attacks.
It said Israeli war minister Yisrael Katz announced on Oct. 18, 2026 that Israel was ready to attack Iran and that in any new aggression "all energy facilities" would be targeted, with the aim of returning Iran to the "Stone Age." Katz also claimed the United States and Israel had dropped 35,000 bombs on Iran in total and said their military campaign was not over.
The letter said that on the same day, the Zionist regime's prime minister, who is a war criminal under international prosecution, again openly declared his criminal intent to preemptively start another war of aggression against Iran. It said the silence and explicit support of some Security Council members had made him more brazen in pursuing genocidal thinking.
The letter said the threats amount to gross violations of international law, including the threat to use the MOAB against civilian infrastructure and to target all of Iran's energy infrastructure. It said attempts to spread fear among Iran's population or any threat to deliberately destroy critical civilian infrastructure are new instances of gross violations of international humanitarian law with severe and possibly long-term humanitarian and environmental consequences, increasing the responsibility of the United States and the Zionist regime. It said both have repeatedly shown they do not consider themselves bound by any rules of international law, including obligations under the four 1949 Geneva Conventions and customary international humanitarian law.
Iran asked the UN secretary-general and the Security Council to demand that the United States and the Zionist regime immediately end their unlawful threats and fully comply with their obligations under the UN Charter and peremptory norms of international law. It also asked them to explicitly and unambiguously condemn threats to attack Iran, including its critical civilian infrastructure, used as a tool of coercion and intimidation.
Iran further urged the Security Council to take urgent measures within its powers and duties, including holding an emergency meeting to address the threats to regional and international peace and security and to ensure accountability for the United States and the rogue Zionist regime. It called on the Council to guarantee accountability and full compensation for damages caused by wrongful international acts that the United States and the Zionist regime commit against Iran daily.
The letter said the Security Council cannot remain silent in the face of explicit threats of further aggression and destruction of critical civilian infrastructure, warning that inaction would further weaken the Charter and the international legal order on which the UN system is built.
Iran reaffirmed its inherent right to self-defense under Article 51 of the UN Charter and its determination to take all necessary measures against any source of threat endangering its people, sovereignty, territorial integrity and vital national interests. It said that if the Security Council fails in its responsibilities, Iran will exercise its right of self-defense and give a decisive response in line with international law to protect its supreme national interests.
It said the United States and the Zionist regime will bear full responsibility for the consequences of any further aggression, including the risk of unpredictable and uncontrollable escalation.
Iran requested that the letter be distributed as an official document of the General Assembly and the Security Council.
MNA

articles.title: Qatari official says Iran-US talks continue amid risk of wider regional war
articles.body:
Negotiations between Iran and the US remain ongoing, with both sides continuing to engage as regional tensions deepen, Qatari Foreign Ministry spokesperson Majed al-Ansari said on Tuesday.
“The negotiation is ongoing. We are seeing engagement from the parties,” Ansari, who also serves as an adviser to the Qatari prime minister, said at the Global Security Forum in Doha.
He said discussions were taking place with regional partners and expressed hope that the process would eventually produce an agreement, while warning that conditions on the ground were becoming increasingly difficult.
“Escalation left unchecked will mean that we are spiraling towards a regional war that will expand beyond the borders of our region,” he warned.
Ansari said the current process followed an earlier attempt to use a ceasefire as a pathway towards negotiations, but that effort ultimately failed and fighting resumed.
“Any ceasefire is basically a door that opens towards a destination rather than the destination itself,” he said, adding that the previous ceasefire “broke down again.”
On Yemen, Ansari said the conflict could be linked to tensions involving Iran but also had its own dynamics, describing the latest developments as part of an “escalatory ladder” that began in 2023.
“The only way to make sure that that doesn't continue is to start defusing all of these conflicts at the same time,” he said.
The spokesperson voiced concern over political statements coming from Israel, saying regional instability should not be used for domestic political purposes.
“We are concerned about a lot of the statements coming out, political statements that are coming out, especially from Israel,” he said, adding that exploiting regional instability for political infighting was “not something that any responsible statesman should do.”
No peace partner in Israel
Turning to Gaza and the broader Palestine, Ansari said prospects for a political settlement were being undermined by the absence of a viable peace process.
“Sadly, right now we do not have a partner for peace in Israel,” he said, questioning whether Israeli political parties and candidates were offering any path towards peace with Palestinians.
“The only thing that we hear coming out of Israel right now is about war and death and destruction,” he said, warning that “war begets war, conflict begets conflict.”
Since October 2023, Israel has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians and injured over 175,000 others during its genocidal war on Gaza, while around 90 percent of the enclave's civilian infrastructure has been damaged or destroyed.
Ansari said successful mediation did not require the parties to trust one another, but rather to have confidence in the process itself.
“It is trust in the process, not trust in each other, that allows for mediation to succeed,” he said.
The remarks come amid escalating hostilities between Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Houthi militia, with the Saudi-led coalition carrying out air astrikes against Houthi militia positions and the group launching missile and drone attacks targeting the kingdom.
The escalation has coincided with continued tensions between the US and Iran following their military confrontation, with diplomatic efforts aimed at reaching an agreement remaining deadlocked.

articles.title: UK to fly RAF missions defending Saudi against Houthi attacks
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
UK to fly RAF missions defending Saudi Arabia against Houthi attacks
Britain will deploy Royal Air Force fighter jets on defensive missions to help protect Saudi Arabia from escalating Houthi attacks, Bloomberg reported on Tuesday, citing British officials familiar with the matter.
RAF Typhoon fighter jets will help defend Saudi cities and infrastructure against aerial attacks by the Iran-backed group, while Britain will also provide an Atlas A400M transport aircraft and military advisers, the report said.
Britain's Ministry of Defence did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
In September Britain said it would provide additional defensive military assistance to Saudi Arabia following renewed Houthi attacks, including an RAF Voyager air-to-air refuelling aircraft. That announcement did not include fighter jet support.
Houthi attacks have intensified in Saudi Arabia in recent weeks, with Yemen authorities saying on Monday that a strike on a government security forces training camp had killed 58 people.

articles.title: US vice president says US and Ukraine are partners but differ on energy strikes on Russia
articles.body:
US vice president says US and Ukraine are partners but differ on energy strikes on Russia
US Vice President JD Vance has stated that Washington will continue cooperation with Kyiv on specific issues whilst simultaneously calling on Ukraine to cease attacks on Russian diesel production facilities which, he claimed, are driving up energy costs for Americans.
Source: Vance in an interview with 2WAY TONIGHT, as reported by European Pravda
Details: In response to a direct question on whether Ukraine is an ally of the United States, Vance said that "they are certainly a partner in some ways".
Quote: "But I think we, you know, have some divergent interests from time to time. Like, for example, do I think they should be bombing Russian diesel facilities that raise the cost of energy for Americans? No. But obviously, we work with them on some things. We're going to keep on working with them on some things. But I think they should stop bombing Russian energy."
Details: In response to a follow-up question regarding whether the concept of "partner" implies a less close relationship than "ally", Vance noted that the US does not "have a formal alliance, as far as I know, with Ukraine".
Quote: "They're not in NATO. I don't think they should be in NATO. I think they're a very admirable country, a beautiful country with a lot of amazing people. We're going to work together on some things, but also we're going to be opposite on some things, too."
Background:
- On 14 October, against the backdrop of a diesel agreement concluded between Russia and the US, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy stated that Ukraine is losing a strong partner.
- The Ukrainian president also stated that easing pressure on Russia would not help stop the war but instead sends a signal to Russian ruler Vladimir Putin that his actions have support.
- He made these remarks when commenting on Trump's order to suspend certain sanctions, restrictions and tariffs against Russia provided for under the Graham Act.

articles.title: US state issues arrest warrant for Raul Castro
articles.body:
US state issues arrest warrant for Raul Castro
A Florida judge has issued an arrest warrant for former Cuban President Raul Castro, 95, the state’s attorney general announced on Monday. The move marks another escalation in Washington’s months-long pressure campaign against Havana.
The warrant pertains to the 1996 shooting down of two American planes operated by anti-communist Cuban exiles off Cuba’s coast. US authorities accuse Castro of ordering the attack.
“Today, we are announcing state charges against Raul Castro with an arrest warrant for conspiracy to commit first-degree murder,” Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier said at a press conference in Miami. Prosecutors had gathered evidence and witness testimony linking a Cuban spy network to the operation that allegedly led Castro to order the planes shot down, he said.
In May, the US Justice Department separately indicted Castro and five others on charges including murder, conspiracy to kill US nationals and destruction of aircraft. Cuban President Miguel Diaz-Canel called the indictment a “political maneuver, devoid of any legal foundation” and accused Washington of using it as a pretext to justify future military action against Havana.
In February of 1996, Cuban fighter jets shot down two US planes operated by Brothers to the Rescue, a Miami-based Cuban exile group, killing four men. Havana has maintained that it acted in self-defense against aircraft that violated its airspace.
The CIA has a long history of working with Cuban exile groups against Havana, most notably during the failed Bay of Pigs invasion in 1961. Washington imposed a broad trade embargo on Cuba the following year.
US President Donald Trump has intensified pressure on Havana as part of what he called the “Donroe doctrine” – a modern interpretation of the 19th-century hegemonic political strategy known as the Monroe Doctrine, which aims to assert US dominance in the Western Hemisphere.
After US forces kidnapped Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro in January, Trump imposed a near-total energy blockade of Cuba and announced that the island will be “next” in line for regime change. The restrictions have led to a widespread energy crisis and frequent blackouts in Cuba.
Russia, China, Mexico and several other nations have provided humanitarian aid to Cuba. Moscow delivered around 700,000 barrels of oil to the island in March.

articles.title: Albania on fire: Who’s behind the riots?
articles.body:
Albania on fire: Who’s behind the riots?
Anti-government rioters have torched Albania’s education ministry and supreme court, as protests spread across the Balkan nation. Prime Minister Edi Rama is refusing to step down and blames the unrest on Russia. What’s really going on?
As of October 19, the Albanian capital of Tirana has been rocked by seven consecutive days and nights of rioting, while protests and clashes between demonstrators and police have been reported in the cities of Lezhe, Vlore, Elbasan, and Shkoder. A large group of rioters breached the perimeter of the education ministry in Tirana on October 14, setting the building on fire.
Running battles between demonstrators and police have broken out around the ministry on several occasions since. On October 19, hundreds of demonstrators pelted rocks at riot police, who responded with tear gas and rubber bullets. The previous night, offices of the Albanian Supreme Court were set on fire, and arson attacks on several police stations in the city were reported.
Some 500 demonstrators had been detained and 167 of them formally arrested as of October 17, according to Reuters. 295 people had been injured, including 196 police officers, as of October 19, according to Interior Minister Ervin Demo.
What do the protesters want?
The protests follow more than a year of unrest in Albania, which began when Rama banned TikTok in the runup to last March’s parliamentary elections, following similar measures inposed by the EU during every major election across the bloc since 2024. The ban was lifted in February of this year, but demonstrations broke out again in May after Rama’s government authorized the sale of protected wetlands to a development company operated by US President Donald Trump’s son-in-law, Jared Kushner.
The protesters demanded the resignation of Rama and his entire cabinet, and the cancellation of a planned twin-phase resort project on the wetlands and on nearby Sazan Island.
The protesters’ core demand – that Rama resign – remains unchanged. However, the movement is now calling for a root-and-branch reform of the entire Albanian establishment, with demonstrators accusing both Rama and opposition leader Sali Berisha of corruption. Unemployment, underfunding of schools, and declining living standards have also been cited by protesters as grievances.
What did Rama say about the protests?
Despite the repeated chants of “Rama resign” heard at the protests, Rama has claimed that the demonstrators do not oppose his government, but Albania’s “mission” of joining the EU.
“I am not being challenged,” he said in a video address on October 18. “The government is not being challenged, a government majority or a winning party in the elections is not being challenged but a path is being challenged, a mission is being challenged”
“Albanians need to think very clearly,” he continued. “Do they want this, do they want that, or do they want the EU?”
Rama has refused to resign, and blamed the protests on “foreign hands that do not wish for Albania to be at peace.” Back in June, Rama accused “the enemies of Albania and of Israel” of waging a “hybrid war” to stop the wetlands development. In two separate speeches on October 18 and 19, the embattled PM blamed the unrest on Russian philosopher Alexander Dugin and a “wave of Russian influence in the entire social media system,” and on “the Khomeiniist republic of Iran, the pinnacle of disinformation.”
Was Russia involved?
In short, no. Rama has not backed up any of his accusations, and they are being treated with skepticism and ridicule by demonstrators and opposition media. Albania’s Publik Media news outlet criticised Rama for “return[ing] to the Berisha, Russia and Iran alibi,” while Pamfleti, an investigative outlet, dismissed his claims as an “ignorant reaction to those protesting his misgovernance”
Even the US-run Radio Free Europe noted that Rama “did not present public evidence” to back up his allegations.
Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova has rejected Rama’s accusations. “No, Edi Rama,” she said on October 18, “it is the citizens of your country who have taken to the streets in protest.”
“This has all the hallmarks of the ‘highly likely’ British approach,” Serbian journalist Nebojsa Malic told RT on October 19, referring to British Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s failed attempts to blame the 2016 Brexit vote on Russia and a recent ‘terror plot’ at a US airbase on Iran. “We’ll just make an accusation and provide no evidence but say ‘oh it’s highly likely that Russia’s behind this’, and everybody is going to take it for granted.”
Rama is “doing this because he’s hoping it will stick,” Malic said. “He has nothing to lose. He’s seen plenty of leaders in western Europe essentially getting away scot free with covering for their malice and incompetence by blaming Russia.”
“Rama is just as opportunistic as [French President Emmanuel] Macron or any British prime minister in the last ten years,” Malic concluded. “They will say or do whatever, because they think that Russia is not able to defend itself.”
Why did Rama mention Israel?
Rama’s claim that “enemies of Albania and Israel” were behind this summer’s environmental protests stems from the involvement of Kushner in the wetlands project. A close associate of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, Kushner has extensive family and financial ties to Israel. His investment firm, Affinity Partners, has funneled Emirati, Saudi, and Qatari cash into multiple Israeli businesses, including five arms manufacturers.
However, all available information suggests that the funding for Kushner’s Albanian projects comes from Albanian, American, and Qatari individuals and entities. Affinity Partners is leading the €1.4 billion Sazan Island project, while Kushner himself is a minority partner in the wetlands development.
Rama visited Israel and addressed the Knesset in January. Less than 24 hours later, Israel’s Channel 12 claimed that the Albanian PM had struck a deal with Netanyahu to accept up to 100,000 Palestinian refugees from Gaza. As speculation spread that the Palestinians would be resettled on land developed by Kushner, Rama clarified that no such deal had been, or would be, made.
Regardless, Rama’s close relations with Netanyahu are at odds with public opinion in Albania, where a 2024 poll found that 73% of the population believe that Israel should be sanctioned over its war on Gaza. Kushner is widely seen in Albania as representing Israeli interests, and Rama’s decision to amend environmental laws and grant “strategic investor” status to Affinity Partners has fueled accusations that the PM is placing Washington and West Jerusalem’s interests above Tirana’s.
Will there be an Albanian Maidan?
Some images emerging from Tirana – burning barricades, police officers set on fire with Molotov cocktails, and smouldering government buildings – are reminiscent of the scenes that played out during the 2014 ‘Maidan’ coup in Ukraine. However, Rama is in far less perilous of a position than Ukraine’s president, Viktor Yanukovich, was during the 2014 uprising.
Unlike the present unrest in Albania, the Maidan coup was planned and directed by foreign actors, namely the US State Department and the British embassy in Kiev. Rama, on the other hand, is a close partner of the EU and US, and neither Washington nor Brussels have backed the protesters. Instead, Rama has apparently been given carte blanche to squash the demonstrations, with columns of military vehicles seen entering Tirana between October 15 and 19.
The EU has condemned the use of violence by protesters, with the European Commission criticizing them for “arson, attacks on State institutions and the destruction of public and private property.” In a statement on October 18, the commission praised Rama’s progress toward EU membership and welcomed his “commitment that the right to protest will be protected.”
One week earlier, an EU delegation in Tirana said that Brussels was “aware of allegations of excessive use of force by the police against protesters and journalists,” adding that the government’s response to protests and riots “must remain within the law.”
The EU took a far more interventionist position in 2014, sending officials to meet with demonstrators in Kiev and endorsing protests even as they devolved into violent riots. Brussels prepared sanctions on Yanukovich, and once he had been toppled, it gifted an €11 billion aid package to Ukraine, which would elect the pro-EU Petro Poroshenko president months later.
The West is still firmly on Rama’s side, and he is unlikely to face any calls for resignation from abroad. However, he is still facing the most sustained public pressure campaign of his 13-year stint in power, and if the protests continue and more buildings burn, he may be left with no choice but to admit defeat and step down.

articles.title: Zelensky says he wants to run for president again
articles.body:
Zelensky says he wants to run for president again
Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky has said he wants to run for president again if an election is held before the conflict with Russia ends. His five-year term expired two years ago, prompting Moscow to question his legitimacy, while US President Donald Trump has called for him to be replaced.
Zelensky has refused to call a new election since his term expired in May 2024, citing martial law, which was imposed after the conflict with Russia escalated in February 2022. During his 2019 election campaign, he promised to only serve one term.
Speaking to NBC News’ ‘Meet the Press’ on Sunday, Zelensky said he would seek another term if an election is held while the fighting continues.
“If it will be during the war – of course. It’s my responsibility, because I have to defend my country from the very beginning to end of this war,” he stated.
Zelensky once again demanded a ceasefire of at least 60 days to prepare for the election, claiming that the country needs time to amend its laws and put election infrastructure in place.
Moscow has rejected the demand. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has said Kiev could use an election as a pretext to secure a 60-day ceasefire to “regroup,” recover its military losses, and resume the fighting. He added, however, that Russia is prepared to suspend strikes on election day.
Russian President Vladimir Putin has argued that Zelensky’s presidential powers should have passed to the parliament after his mandate expired, and questioned whether he can sign binding peace agreements. He called Zelensky’s refusal to hold elections a “strategic mistake.”
Zelensky’s ambitions also face opposition at home. A survey in September by the Kiev International Institute of Sociology found that 53% of respondents believe he should only serve one presidential term, up from 46% in December 2025.
Trump has stepped up pressure on Zelensky, accusing him of prolonging the conflict while receiving billions in Western assistance. Earlier this month, he called for a new president, arguing that Zelensky has repeatedly rejected opportunities to end the fighting.
“I suggest they get a new leader who can make a deal,” Trump told reporters.
He also blamed Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries for the worsening global diesel crisis and rising prices which hurt American farmers, accusing Zelensky of creating “problems for the world” despite his repeated demands to stop the attacks.
In a Truth Social post on Sunday, Trump said Zelensky “doesn’t want to end this war, and probably never did,” arguing that he could have secured a better deal with Russia two years ago. He added that Ukraine is “in shambles,” describing its male population as “low, wounded, and/or dead.”

articles.title: Ukraine’s Signum Drones Break Past the Front and Start Hunting Targets Deep in Russian Rear
articles.body:

Ukraine’s Signum Drones Break Past the Front and Start Hunting Targets Deep in Russian Rear
Ukrainian drone operators from Signum have released footage showing a series of middle-strike missions against Russian targets well beyond the immediate front line, the 59th Assault Brigade of Unmanned Systems reported on October 20.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The compilation shows strikes against a vessel, Russian mobile fire groups, a semi-truck, passenger and cargo vehicles, as well as Russian infantry operating deeper in the rear.
Signum said it is increasingly relying on middle-strike drones for missions of this kind, giving its crews the ability to reach targets far beyond the line of contact and disrupt Russian logistics, personnel movements, and defensive units before they approach the front.
The unit gave the strike on the vessel a particularly pointed caption: “Russian warship, is that you?” referring to the final communication made on 24 February 2022, the first day of the Russian invasion of Ukraine, when, during the Snake Island campaign, a Ukrainian border guard spoke to the Russian missile cruiser Moskva.
Previously, reports emerged that Ukraine’s repeated strikes on Russia’s Black Sea Fleet have created a growing maintenance problem for Moscow, leaving damaged warships with few safe places where they can undergo lengthy repairs without becoming stationary targets.

articles.title: Drone strikes across Sudan kill more than 160 in past days
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Wave of drone strikes across Sudan kill more than 160 over past days
A wave of drone strikes targeting war-torn Sudan's army-held capital Khartoum and two western areas controlled by paramilitary forces has killed more than 160 people since Friday, according to residents, medical workers and paramilitary sources.
A drone strike by the Sudanese army killed 53 people at a market in an area disputed between Sudan and South Sudan, local authorities said Tuesday.
Yesterday, a rare drone attack on Sudan’s capital killed three children Monday, a rights group said, as both sides in the country’s war step up airstrikes that have killed dozens of civilians in the Kordofan region in recent days.
The strike, which the group blamed on Sudan’s paramilitary Rapid Support Forces, killed children ages two, four and six in Imtidad Nasser, a neighborhood east of Khartoum’s airport.
The deadliest drone strike hit near a market on Sunday evening in Al-Dibab town in the southwestern state of West Kordofan, which is controlled by the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) that have been at war with Sudan's military since April 2023.
Residents and medical workers said a drone struck a transport hub where villagers had gathered after a market day to find rides home, killing 80 people.
Ahmed Abakar Wadi, a resident who helped bury victims, told AFP at least 50 bodies were recovered at the scene, including that of his brother.
Another 47 wounded people were taken to the nearby town of Al-Mujlad where 30 later died from their injuries, according to a medical source.
"The drone struck once, and then came back 10 minutes later and struck again," Wadi told AFP.
The RSF's self-declared administration, known as Tasis, and the Sudanese rights group Emergency Lawyers accused the army of carrying out the attack.
The military has not commented.
The strike was one of the deadliest single attacks in Kordofan, an oil-rich region linking western and eastern Sudan where the army and the RSF have been battling for territory.
Dams targeted
Hours later, early on Monday, another drone attack hit the RSF stronghold of Nyala, the capital of South Darfur.
Medical and RSF sources said 17 people, including seven RSF officers, were killed and 23 wounded when a drone struck the city centre and destroyed two homes.
On Monday morning, violence also reached the capital Khartoum, where a drone strike hit a house in a neighbourhood east of Khartoum airport, killing four people, including three children aged between two and six, according to a medical source.
An army official said Sudanese air defences had intercepted drones launched by the RSF that were targeting the airport and nearby areas.
In eastern Sudan, a military source said on Sunday that air defences also intercepted several RSF drones targeting the Atbara and Setit dams in Gadaref state, about 420 kilometres east of Khartoum.
There is no definitive toll for Sudan's conflict, but aid workers estimate it has killed more than 200,000 people and created what aid agencies describe as the world's largest hunger and displacement crisis.
More than 1,100 people were killed in drone attacks across Sudan during the first half of this year alone, according to the United Nations.
Kordofan—home to oil deposits and the RSF's most powerful paramilitary allies—has come under repeated drone attacks in recent months as the army seeks to roll back RSF gains made last year after the paramilitary group consolidated control over much of Darfur.
On Friday, a drone strike on a cattle market in Nyala, Sudan's second-largest city and the seat of the RSF's self-declared administration, killed 30 people and injured 47 others, according to a medical source.

articles.title: Israel threatens to impose ‘Gaza model’ on Lebanon (VIDEO)
articles.body:
Israel threatens to impose ‘Gaza model’ on Lebanon (VIDEO)
Israel is threatening to turn its occupation of southern Lebanon into a permanent military presence while pursuing the so-called “Gaza model.” RT correspondent Steve Sweeney reports from Beirut on the destruction of entire villages, mass displacement and efforts to secure an Israeli withdrawal.
Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz declared over the weekend that troops would not withdraw from areas they currently control and warned that the military could advance further towards Nabatieh and the Litani River if Hezbollah launches additional attacks on Israel.
Katz claimed that more than 60 villages and 23,000 homes had been destroyed across an Israeli-controlled area of approximately 700 square km in southern Lebanon and that around 200,000 residents had been displaced.
“All the villages have been wiped out,” he said. “This is the Gaza model, and this is the model we are implementing.”
The reference is to Israel’s military campaign in Gaza, launched in response to the Hamas-led attack in October 2023, which killed around 1,200 people and saw 251 taken hostage. The offensive has left much of the Palestinian enclave in ruins, displaced most of its population and killed more than 74,000 people, according to local health authorities.
Fighting in Lebanon has subsided since a US-brokered ceasefire took effect in June, although Israeli strikes and demolitions have continued in the south. The UN estimated that approximately 330,000 people remained displaced as of late September.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has also insisted that the IDF would remain in southern Lebanon until Hezbollah is disarmed.
Lebanese President Joseph Aoun has accused the Jewish state of violating the June agreement through continued attacks and demolitions. He has also warned that the occupation itself is preventing the Lebanese army from deploying along the internationally recognized border, as required under UN Security Council Resolution 1701.
The latest escalation began in early March, after Hezbollah attacked Israel following the start of US-Israeli strikes on Iran. Israel responded with a major air and ground campaign.
The June agreement envisages a gradual Israeli withdrawal alongside Lebanese army deployments and the removal of Hezbollah’s weapons and infrastructure from designated areas. However, its implementation has stalled.
At least 4,389 people have been killed and 12,424 injured in Lebanon since March 2, according to recent Health Ministry figures.
A Lebanese military delegation is due to attend US-brokered talks in Tampa, Florida, on Tuesday, where Beirut will seek an end to Israeli attacks and a timetable for withdrawal. 
“The question is whether these talks can deliver an end to occupation or whether Israel intends to make its presence in southern Lebanon a permanent reality,” Sweeney said.

articles.title: Army corps commander explains how Operation Vivaldi was kept secret
articles.body:
Army corps commander explains how Operation Vivaldi was kept secret
Operation Vivaldi was kept secret because it was not mentioned in official reports and the commander reported directly to the commander-in-chief. Ukrainian open-source intelligence analysts also cooperated with the military and refrained from posting information about the operation.
Source: Brigadier General Andrii Biletskyi, Commander of the 3rd Army Corps, speaking at a meeting with journalists
Quote: "Both former commander-in-chief General Syrskyi and Commander-in-Chief General Drapatyi, knew about the operation and both agreed that there should be no official reports.
We did not record our advances in the DELTA battlefield management system either, because leaks can happen – not from the system itself, but from individual units. We did not include them in written reports. Roughly once every few weeks, I personally reported to the commander-in-chief.
The current commander-in-chief was even more closely informed because he commanded the Joint Forces grouping and was our direct superior – we worked closely together. All of this, combined with the Russians' lies, helped maintain effective secrecy."
Details: Preparations for the offensive also played an important role. The first sign of offensive action is the formation of an offensive grouping.
"These days, you can conceal a brigade's redeployment for three or four days at most. It leaves a huge electronic footprint. A brigade has 3,000-4,000 personnel. They have phones, use social media, call their families and friends and sometimes post things online. For open-source intelligence analysts, identifying that a brigade has moved to a new area is a matter of days. Taking away their phones is unrealistic."
There were suspicions within Russia's West grouping that something was wrong. However, one reason the Russians concluded that nothing serious was happening was the absence of reinforcements: they did not have the forces needed to conduct an offensive operation.
Biletskyi said the 3rd Army Corps' press service had also played its part: "We all understand that the 250 prisoners of war announced at the time dealt a blow to Russian morale. We can see this from their bloggers, military chat groups and elsewhere."
Biletskyi also expressed his gratitude to DeepState and the Institute for the Study of War (ISW): "They approached this in a very systematic way. When necessary, we could even use them to spread disinformation."
Quote: "We reached out to Western and Ukrainian open-source intelligence analysts, and the overwhelming majority cooperated with us and refrained from posting this information.
This had a positive impact on the course of the operation. Credit goes to the corps' press service, which handled this directly and, in my opinion, did an excellent job."
Background:
- During Operation Vivaldi, Ukrainian forces thwarted Russian attempts to outflank Ukrainian-held parts of Donetsk Oblast via Dobropillia and Barvinkove. Russian forces have now abandoned these plans, while the 144th Division of Russia's 20th Army has been defeated and has effectively ceased to exist.
- Ukrainska Pravda first reported on Russia's plan to outflank Ukrainian-held parts of Donetsk Oblast via Dobropillia and Barvinkove in the summer of 2025. The Dobropillia salient was intended to form one of two pincers in Russia's plan to encircle almost all of the part of Donetsk Oblast not under Russian occupation.
